#403. The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

From Picasso to Andy Warhol, a surprising number of artists have portrayed the German breed. But the dachshund has also at times been co-opted as a political symbol.

Pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter, and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

The plate and the photos are on show at the new exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with Picasso's adoptive pet.

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, says exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

Alongside Picasso, a surprising number of important artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

Bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented on in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to issue a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

Still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the World War I because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Doberman or dogs that looked big and dangerous."

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian says. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character."

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a new image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany."

Still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

But altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

The feedback Reckert's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events.

"It's really crazy," she says, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really."

#402. Are Memories Transferable? Meet the Scientists Replicating an Infamous Study to Find Out

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

It was the dead of winter in Boston. The surface of the Charles River was frozen solid. But Zachary Kelso braved the biting cold to finally put to rest a mystery that has haunted neuroscience labs for over half a century.

To do that, Kelso, a research assistant in the Harvard lab of the neuroscientist Sam Gershman, needed some worms. Specifically, planarians: arrow-headed flatworms, which are among the simplest creatures to possess a brain and a nervous system with bilateral symmetry like ours. Normally, labs order these widely used model organisms from biological supply companies. But the mail-order worms weren’t up to snuff. So Gershman had dispatched Kelso to the Charles’ icy banks to catch some wild ones. “I thought, ‘I’m going to look crazy because I’m using a hammer to beat through the ice,’” Kelso recalled. “So I wore the more business end of business casual.”

It wouldn’t be the last time Kelso found himself in this situation. The Charles River planarians, it turned out, didn’t cut it either. Neither did the worms he sourced while stream-hopping around Eugene, Oregon, in March 2025. Nor did the ones he fished from Michigan lakes that June—this time in thigh-high waders—while picnicking families gawked from shore. Kelso diligently turned over rocks, angled with bits of meat tied to a string, and even followed maps from a vintage guidebook called The Fresh-Water Triclads of Michigan. But his adventure was fruitless. Sure, he caught plenty of planarians. But back in Gershman’s lab, none of them would do what they were supposed to do.

In the 1960s, an eccentric behavioral psychologist named James McConnell convinced the scientific establishment that planarian worms, like Pavlov’s dogs, could be classically conditioned—and that memories of this training could be transferred from worm to worm through cannibalism. These bizarre findings were replicated by other scientists, and worm training became a staple of high school science fairs. Now, 60 years later, the worms have stopped learning, and nobody knows why.

I first learned about this scientific mystery while reporting another piece about what a cell can remember. As I dug into the historical literature on memory research, I kept coming across McConnell’s strange worm experiments, which captivated a generation of scientists before disappearing entirely. Planarian memory had itself been forgotten. I was content to dismiss it as a fluke of history until Gershman mentioned, in passing during an interview, that in addition to their work with the unicellular ciliate Stentor coeruleus, his lab was attempting to reproduce some wacky worm experiments from the 1960s. Had I heard of them?

Gershman, I learned, was keen to pick up where McConnell had left off. As part of a growing cohort of cognitive scientists looking beyond the brain for clues to the origins and basis of memory, he’s fascinated by any creature that seems to remember without the benefit of neural, synaptic networks. Little Stentor coeruleus, for example, can modify its behavior based on previous experience—quite a feat for a single-celled creature that can’t possibly have a neuron. Planarian worms, if McConnell’s findings were to be believed, might be the next great model organism for memory research.

The trouble was, it wasn’t going well. In fact, no matter how hard Gershman tried to train them, none of his planarians would learn a thing.

Can a worm learn? When McConnell posed the question in the early 1950s, the notion that memory had something to do with synaptic associations between neurons in the brain was just beginning to gain currency. McConnell, then a graduate student in psychology at the University of Texas, reasoned that planarians—among the simplest creatures with true neurons—should therefore be able to learn.

His early worm experiments were not particularly novel. He simply substituted worms for rats in what were, at the time, standard classical conditioning studies: repeatedly shocking the worms while exposing them to a bright light. After a period of this training, the worms came to associate the light with the shock and scrunched their bodies in anticipation whenever the light flashed. Voilà: worm learning!

Planarians have stranger features to offer for experiments. If a planarian is chopped in half, both halves will regrow into a new worm—the tail will grow a new head, and the head will grow a new tail. A fragment as small as 1/279 of the original worm can regrow into a completely normal adult worm in a matter of weeks, a regenerative capacity so powerful that, as one early naturalist put it, planarians are effectively “immortal under the edge of the knife.” For McConnell, this ability begged the question: When you chop a worm in half, do both halves remember?

This is where the real worm torture began.

In the ’60s, McConnell, by then a young professor at the University of Michigan, started beheading his trained planarians. The worms that grew back from the severed heads behaved as the originals had, associating the light with the shock—a result he expected, given the preservation of their primitive brains. What surprised McConnell was that the worms that regenerated from headless tails remembered, too. This meant that whatever form the worms’ memories took, they weren’t the exclusive purview of the brain. “It appeared that the memories were laid down throughout the animal’s body,” McConnell later reflected.

Thrilled, McConnell pushed his experiments further. He cut the worms into smaller and smaller pieces; each time, the regenerated segments retained the memory. He stitched the heads of trained worms onto untrained tails, but they kept falling off. He pureed trained worms and injected them into naïve recipients, a delicate process that the historian Larry Stern has compared to “impal[ing] a prune with a javelin.” Finally, remembering that some planarians are cannibals, he fed trained-worm puree to their brethren. In subsequent trials, the “cannibal” worms picked up the light response right away, as though they were remembering, rather than learning, what to do.

If McConnell’s experiments appear gruesome, his line of inquiry was of his time. The discovery of the DNA helix in the 1950s had revealed just how much information is packed into proteins and nucleic acids. The notion that the physical traces of memories, or “engrams,” might have some chemical basis seemed plausible enough to many scientists. Could McConnell’s cannibal worms have eaten an engram? McConnell certainly thought so. He was convinced that their memories were encoded in the structure of their RNA—and could be transferred from worm to worm.

“In the jargon of computer engineering, information is always ‘fed’ into a computer,” the journalist Arthur Koestler later wrote in an appreciative survey of McConnell’s work. “Here the metaphor became flesh.”

These were sensational findings, and McConnell took every advantage of the media attention they generated. Before becoming a scientist, he had had a brief career in radio, and he knew how to repackage nuanced ideas as pithy soundbites. In magazines such as Time and Esquire, he spoke grandly of a future of memory consumption—of “piano lesson pills” and “professor burgers.” He brought his trained worms onto The Steve Allen Show, and, belying his clean-cut hair and horn-rimmed glasses, dubbed himself “McCannibal.”

Students began writing to McConnell’s lab at the University of Michigan to ask for worm-training tips for their school science fairs, and McConnell shared advice. Science, he believed, should be for the people; he saw himself as a latter-day David pitching stones at institutional Goliaths. This made him one of the most famous public scientists of his era, but it did not endear him to more serious peers. It also didn’t help that he published all his research in The Worm Runner’s Digest, a countercultural journal he distributed from his lab.

While the Digest is now something of a cult classic, the mix proved confusing for many readers. McConnell eventually cut the publication in half, not unlike a planarian worm, and renamed the serious half The Journal of Biological Psychology (no relation to the current peer-reviewed journal Biological Psychology, founded in 1973). But McConnell’s reputation as a heretic and prankster was well established.

The wheels started to come off in the mid-1960s. Although McConnell enjoyed a period of fame and funding—including an accelerated path to tenure at the University of Michigan—attempts to replicate his memory transfers yielded inconsistent results. While many apparently succeeded, the failures were more visible. In 1965, the Nobel Prize–winning biochemist Melvin Calvin tried to replicate McConnell’s worm experiments and failed, even with the help of some of McConnell’s former assistants and using the same device. His high-profile publication of the results sparked an acrimonious debate about, among other things, proper worm handling.

By the 1970s, the planarian memory fad had come and gone. Scientists had moved on to rats, cats, goldfish, and even praying mantises. Researchers showing successful memory transfers in rats—by injecting brain RNA from one animal to another—had published their findings in prestigious journals such as Nature and Science, making the planarian model seem unimpressive in comparison. But when further experiments proved inconclusive, interest in the question of memory transfer petered out. As the science historians Harry Collins and Trevor Pinch put it, “memory transfer was never quite disproved; it just ceased to occupy the scientific imagination.”

McConnell closed his laboratory in 1971, and his long period of subsequent obscurity was broken only once, in 1985, when he became a victim of the Unabomber. (He lost his hearing temporarily after the blast.) He died in 1990. If a younger generation of scientists is familiar with his cannibal planarians, it’s as “a cautionary tale that neuroscientists tell to their students at bedtime to scare them away from ill-fated projects,” Gershman said.

Still, McConnell’s unconventional work and contrarian attitude has lingered in neuroscience lore, and the idea of memory transfer remains a subject of private fascination. What if McConnell really did manage to feed a memory to a worm? For Gershman, who is searching for a way to study memory at a molecular level and connect it to observable behavior, the question was an itch that had to be scratched. He decided to settle the matter once and for all.

It all seemed straightforward enough. In the spring of 2025, Gershman and Maddie Snyder, one of his postdocs, set out to reproduce the worm-training protocol of one of McConnell’s students, Alan Jacobson. Jacobson’s papers were the most rigorous of the planarian memory transfer era, and Gershman and Snyder followed them to the letter. “We wanted a behavioral basis to be able to study the circuits that are driving memory in these extremely unstable animals,” Snyder said. “Are those circuits at all being used for memory consolidation or storage? Because if you lose your head and all those circuits are gone, then what is the mechanism of storing memory?”

Despite their best efforts, however, they couldn’t do what Jacobson, McConnell, and so many others had done back in the 1960s: condition the worms to scrunch their bodies in response to light. (They reported the results on biorxiv.org in April 2026.) “I was really scratching my head about this,” Gershman said. He’d assumed that the memory transfer would be the dodgy part of the experiment—not getting the worms to form a memory in the first place.

They talked to other planarian labs. They tried different stimuli. They ran the planarian footage through a machine-learning pipeline. In desperation, Kelso and Snyder even visited the Harvard Science Museum to examine a vintage “inductorium,” an electric-shock contraption used in midcentury worm science. But it offered no clues.

Kelso searched for any of McConnell’s former collaborators who might still be alive, and through a stroke of luck he found contact information for Daniel Kimble and his wife, Reeva, who had both worked in McConnell’s lab. Now in their nineties, they live in Eugene, Oregon. When Kelso called them, he discovered that not only did they run many of McConnell’s experiments in the 1960s, but they’d also kept the entire print archive of The Worm Runner’s Digest in a box in their basement.

This, after all, is what McConnell did. Rather than using laboratory strains of planarians, he sourced his from a lake near the University of Michigan. And so, not wanting to leave any stone unturned, Kelso made one final trip to McConnell’s former fishing grounds in Michigan. He returned with plastic tubes full of worms, but not a single one was a learner. “At some point, we had like 12 different strains of planaria, none of which showed any learning,” Gershman said.

As Snyder tells it, the Kimbles were absolutely convinced that their conditioning experiments in the 1960s had worked. The worms learned—they were sure of it. The literature of the era seems to support their certainty; at least 36 labs reported similar results. So why is it that when the exact same experiments are done today, using the same laboratory protocol and even the same worms, fished from the same Michigan waters, planarian worms are utterly uneducable?

One explanation, Snyder said, is that McConnell, the Kimbles, and all the other “worm runners” were inconsistent in how they scored the planarians’ behavior and may have misinterpreted more anodyne worm “turns” for the definitive “scrunch” of the light reaction. Every scientist is a product of their time, after all, influenced in myriad, often invisible ways by sociological conditions, funding pressures, and, in this case, a highly charismatic leader. This interpretation made Snyder hyperaware of her own potential biases. “Throughout this entire project,” she told me, “I was like, ‘What are the things that I am taking for granted now in our models of neuroscience, and our assumptions of what is known and unknown, that I should really notice?’”

A more remote possibility is that planarian worms themselves have somehow changed over the last six decades—falling victim to pollution or genetic drift. Gershman finds this scenario unlikely. “What are the chances that a bunch of researchers just happened to do these studies at the particular time when this phenomenon happened?” he asked, incredulous. “They just got extremely lucky, in the millions of years of planarian evolution? And then our luck ran out?”

No matter the reason, in 2026, despite their nervous system and simple brains, planarians don’t learn. From an evolutionary perspective, this might actually make sense. “The reason that we learn associations, to some degree, is so that we can predict danger and avoid it,” Snyder said. But planarians have a different relationship to danger. Their regenerative physiology, so key to McConnell’s experiments, protects them from blunt trauma. Bitten in half, they simply grow back. What use is memory to such a creature? “That’s a whole other philosophical conundrum,” she said.

It’s a great time to be wrestling with such conundrums. Planarian learning may be a dead end, but memory transfer experiments with other organisms are back in scientific vogue—and those experiments appear to be working. In 2018, the neuroscientist David Glanzman of the University of California, Los Angeles, performed a memory transplant on the sea slug Aplysia californica, a darling model organism for memory research owing to its relatively simple nervous system and gigantic neurons. After training the slugs to respond to a shock to their tails, Glanzman was able to transfer the sensitization from one slug to another via a direct injection of genetic material. This suggested that some aspect of the memory was stored in RNA, which was McConnell’s contention.

Then, in 2021, the Princeton University geneticist Coleen Murphy found that Caenorhabditis elegans worms—microscopic roundworms with 302 neurons to their name—could learn to avoid a pathogenic bacterium by eating, or even just swimming around in, pureed worms who had learned the hard way. Murphy’s group identified a retrotransposon, a jumping segment of genetic material, called Cer1, that appears to “carry a memory” between individuals, she said. A few years later, a group at the Indian Institute of Science published a paper suggesting that trained C. elegans worms release extracellular vesicles—small lipid particles containing genetic information—that can impart their training to their naïve counterparts.

None of these researchers are half as flashy as McConnell was, but their work indicates that he may have been right about worm memory after all. He just bet on the wrong kind of worm—and doubled down on it, despite inconsistent evidence. In the end, he lost his reputation, but his sheer gusto sparked the curiosity of another unconventional scientist. Fortunately, this one’s following the evidence.

At Harvard, Gershman is shifting his focus from the inscrutable planarian to the more legible C. elegans. It may not regenerate when it’s cut in half, but C. elegans is a long-standing model organism in neuroscience—and it’s been consistently shown to learn. With new experiments underway, Gershman is cautiously optimistic. “I just hope we’re not going down another rabbit hole,” he told me. A wormhole, on the other hand—that’s for certain.

#401. Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot

A powerful feedback loop could drive more warming than predicted.

Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.

A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs, and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding.

None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.

A separate analysis published in One Earth in March, which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.

Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.

At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project, through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.

But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.

So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.

Several startups are also exploring possibilities. They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control.

Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile. But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.

The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.

#400. Ready to read in color? These are the 4 best color e-readers.

Color has finally come to e-readers, opening up a richer digital reading experience for anyone who uses Libby for graphic novels, prefers color EPUBs, or simply enjoys seeing a book’s cover in full color. But with more devices offering the feature, which one stands out? For us, the Kobo Libra Colour is the clear winner.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

When we write about e-readers, Kindle is usually the first name that comes to mind. But in the color e-reader market, Kindle has been late to the party. That delay opened the door for other brands to step in with stronger devices. We’ve rounded up the best color e-readers, and here are the ones that stood out.

This year has not been good for tech prices. Due to the global memory crisis, prices are increasing on tablets, phones, laptops, and even e-readers. Three out of the four color e-readers on this list increased in price this year. The only e-reader to avoid a price hike was the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft.

Having tested my way through a lot of e-readers — and now color e-readers — I’ve found a universal truth: While the colors are accurate, they often look a bit washed out. No matter which brand you use, that’s going to be the case. The muted tones don’t outweigh the convenience and portability of color e-readers, but it’s worth tempering your expectations.

Don’t expect the vivid, punchy colors of an iPad screen. An iPad has a max of 500 nits (a measure of brightness), while Kobo and Kindle e-readers max out at 100.

Read our full review of the Kobo Libra Colour.

Color enthusiasts: Picking the best color e-reader wasn’t easy, with so many strong contenders. But when considering who really wants a color e-reader, the choice was clear: The Kobo Libra Colour. The Libra Colour also stands out for annotators. Aside from the Kindle Scribe, it’s one of the only e-readers with writing capabilities, making it ideal for color-coding highlights and annotations.

Expert-approved: Besides the Kindle Paperwhite, the most popular e-reader among the Mashable team is the Kobo Libra Colour. Its seven-inch display offers ample space for reading graphic novels in detail, and the built-in gyroscope lets you switch between vertical and horizontal reading — a flexibility unique to the Libra. Not to mention it has the most sought-after feature for e-reader users: page-turning buttons.

The Kobo Libra Colour is one of our favorite e-readers, period. And when it comes to color e-readers specifically, it’s the clear winner. It stands out for its large display, screen rotation, and writing capabilities — but beyond that, it’s a thoughtfully designed device.

As with all color e-readers, colors appear more muted than in a physical book. That’s unavoidable, but the Libra maintains strong color accuracy despite the softer tones.

Like many e-readers, the price on the Kobo Libra Colour increased, but even at $259.99, it's still cheaper than any of Kindle’s color e-readers. While Kobo does offer a more budget-friendly color option with the Clara, the Libra is worth the extra cost for its writing features, internal gyroscope, and page-turn buttons. It has plenty of storage (32GB) and is waterproof.

If you were disappointed by the discontinuation of the Kindle Oasis, the Kobo Libra Colour offers a similar design, including page-turn buttons. Ergonomically, it’s the best e-reader I’ve tested. It's more square than a Kindle, as one side offers extra space for the page-turning buttons, which makes it easier to hold — especially while lying down and reading one-handed. It's the only e-reader (besides the iPad) on this list that has an internal gyroscope, so when you rotate the device, the display rotates with it. While reading in bed, if I flipped over, I could rotate the device to still be able to hold it on the side with page-turning buttons.

Finally, the Overdrive (aka Libby) integration is great. Log in with your library card, and your borrowed e-books instantly populate in the Overdrive tab.

Read our full review of the Kobo Clara Colour or watch our comparison of the Kobo Clara Colour and Kindle Paperwhite.

You want color on a budget: If you want a color e-reader for under $200, your only option is the Kobo Clara Colour. Luckily, that's a fantastic option. It’s affordable, compact, and speedy. While the Libra’s larger screen makes it the stronger choice for color reading, the Clara still delivers a great experience.

I love the Kobo Clara Colour. I’ve tried dozens of e-readers, and this one has nearly everything I want. At 6 inches, it’s the optimal size — comfortable to hold for hours without wrist strain. In past testing, I’ve found Kobo devices to be slower than Kindles, but the Clara doesn’t have that problem. It’s just as quick as the Kindle Paperwhite.

Like the Libra Colour, the Clara Colour has generally accurate colors, though in muted tones. With a 6-inch screen, it might feel a bit small for graphic novels, which is why we think the Libra is the better color e-reader.

In the grand scheme of color e-readers, the Clara is the most affordable. At $179.99, it’s $20 cheaper than the Kindle Paperwhite and only $30 more than a basic Kindle. If you want a Kindle in color, you’ll have to pay $289.99.

Its processing system is really smart and fixes one of my biggest e-reader pet peeves. When you adjust the font size on a Kindle, the device doesn’t recalculate how many pages are in the book, which makes it inaccurate — you never really know how many pages are left in a chapter. The Kobo Clara does recalculate page count accurately, giving you a more exact reading experience. Also, like the Libra, it has seamless OverDrive integration.

The Kobo Clara’s biggest downfall is its battery life. It’s supposed to last up to 42 days, although many users say it averages out at about two weeks. That’s pretty weak compared to the Kindle’s 12-week battery life; however, I’d trade a couple of weeks of battery life for a better reading experience any day.

Kindle users who want to upgrade to color: If you’re already deep in Amazon’s ecosystem and ready to make the jump to color, the Kindle Colorsoft collection is worth a look. The best option in the lineup is the Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, as it's compatible with the new Page Turn Cover,

The 2026 Kindle Colorsoft makes some modest improvements over its predecessor, introducing the same design changes as the rest of Amazon's 2026 Kindle lineup. That means the new Kindle Colorsoft has a slimmer build, magnetic Pogo pins, and edge-to-edge color, so the bezels now match the color of the rest of the device. Overall, it's an improvement, but it doesn't solve the problems of the original device, nor fully justify the $289.99 price (or $319.99 for the Signature Edition).

Unfortunately, E Ink technology has extremely dim and muted colors. Even if you crank the vibrancy settings all the way to the max, the colors are disappointing. When you compare the Kindle Colorsoft side-by-side with graphic novels or books with illustrations, the differences are extremely obvious. If you want to read comics or similar color artwork digitally, you're better off with a tablet.

With those major caveats, if you want a Kindle with color, this is the best option. On the plus side, we love the fig colorway (it matches the burgundy iPhone), and the color lockscreen artwork does look great.

Read our full review of the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft.

Journalers and annotators: If you're seeking an e-ink tablet like the ReMarkable, we recommend the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft. It's best for the person already deep into the Kindle universe, who wants a model for note-taking but with the perk of color. It's distraction-free without ads or internet browsing, but still has Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive integrations to easily access and send documents, which makes it perfect for students. While we love its writing feature, at the end of the day, it's also just a great e-reader as we've come to expect from Kindle.

Amazon finally released a Kindle that has color and writing capabilities, and it's phenomenal. The brand took a while to perfect the Scribe, its only e-reader with note-taking abilities, but it was worth the wait. The displays are better than ever with a new front light that creates a brighter screen, now reaching up to 100 nits. The resolution specs haven't changed much, with color resolution maxing out at 150 ppi and black and white resolution at 300 ppi.

Where the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft really stands out is its lack of ghosting. Many e-readers with writing capabilities suffer from previous screens or images appearing as shadows when you erase or navigate away. Yet, that's not an issue with this latest Scribe. It isn't completely innocent; it still has some ghosting, specifically when erasing writing or drawings, but it's very faint.

It's delightful to write and draw with, allowing you to swap between several different pen styles. It comes with the Kindle Premium Pen, a lightweight stylus that magnetically attaches to the side of the e-reader when not in use. The colors on the Scribe Colorsoft are limited, a pastel-leaning palette that works well within the parameters of the Scribe's limited resolution and brightness.

It's as fast as any Kindle, living up to the speed of the beloved Paperwhite. It has impressive battery life too, lasting up to eight weeks, although that may be shortened by how often you use the writing feature.

As of October 2026, we added the new Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition to this list. While the display and resolution haven't improved, its new aluminum casing makes it a sturdier e-reader.

In February 2026, we added the Kindle Scribe Colorsoft to this guide. After testing Amazon's latest e-reader, we were thoroughly impressed by both its speed and display.

You might notice that ReMarkable e-ink tablets are not on this list. We've tested both the ReMarkable Paper Pro and ReMarkable Paper Move, and while they're dynamic digital notebooks, they're limited in their e-reader capabilities. Getting e-books on these devices was a bit of a struggle, and we missed the Libby integrations available on Kindles and Kobos. So while we think they're great e-ink tablets, they're inferior e-readers.

To test the best color e-readers, I used the same criteria I apply to standard e-readers, with one key addition: color quality, the main draw of these devices.

Screen size is especially important for color e-readers, since many people use them for graphic novels. I gave preference to 7-inch screens, the optimal size for balancing viewing and portability.

To properly assess each e-reader’s color quality, I compared its display with both a physical copy of the book and the e-book on an iPad. I looked at overall color accuracy, as well as how brightness and warmth affected the color levels.

I analyzed each color e-reader’s range of features, including adjustable brightness and warmth, as well as page-turn buttons.

Color e-readers vary widely in price, so I made sure to include a budget option in an otherwise expensive market.

Samantha Mangino, is an e-reader expert. She's tested all the Kindle and Kobo e-readers, diving into the buzziest models. Her love of reading extends beyond the e-reader beat, covering books and authors, too. In the tech space, she covers tablets, smart rings, and headphones.

#399. We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time

Right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools. Here’s what we need to do instead.

This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.

AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences.  And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability: the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely.

Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important.

With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.

Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from.

Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it.

Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used.

No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.

AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist.

Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.

No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too.

Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance.

Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

#398. This boiled bag of offal is banned in the US. In Scotland it's a fine-dining treat

Anthony Bourdain loved haggis. But even the late, great American chef, writer and television host recognized that Scotland’s national dish, with its “sinister sheep parts” wrapped in a shroud of mystery and half-invented history, could be a hard sell.

“Don’t let them tell you otherwise, that’s really one of life’s great pleasures,” Bourdain said on one of his gastro-curious pilgrimages to Glasgow. “There is no more unfairly reviled food on Earth than the haggis.”

A mash-up of diced lung, liver and heart mixed with oatmeal, beef suet, onion and assorted spices, haggis was traditionally made by stuffing these raw ingredients into the stomach of a recently slain sheep and boiling the lot to a state of palatability.

Instagrammable is not the word that immediately comes to mind. In our 21st-century world, where “clean” eating and processed pap overlap, haggis can seem like an “Outlander”-style outlier from another age.

Yet, by some alchemy, once cooked to its required “warm-reekin’ (steaming)” state, it adds up to much more than the sum of its modest parts. It’s offaly charm has kept nose-to-tail eating alive among a younger generation of Scots that has largely turned its back on the tripe, liver and kidneys their predecessors enjoyed (or endured).

Carefully prepared, haggis tastes both oaty and meaty; it is dark and crumbly, a little crispy at the edges but still moist; earthy but also savory and spicy; deep-tasting and profoundly warming, the perfect foil for its traditional garnish of floury mashed potatoes and orange bashed turnip.

“It’s like a cuddle for the stomach,” says Nicola Turner, a 35-year-old office administrator from Helensburgh, a town on western Scotland’s Firth of Clyde.

For children of the 1960s and ’70s, like crime novelist Ian Rankin, haggis meals were a choice between the classic meat-and-two-veg plate and the battered and deep-fried, chip-shop iteration loved by both his friend Bourdain and his quintessentially Scottish detective character, Inspector John Rebus.

Now myriad other treatments have blossomed.

“I’m pretty sure the first time I dined with AB in Edinburgh we had haggis in filo pastry with a jam-style – maybe blackcurrant – sauce,” Rankin recalled. “He was a big fan of haggis and of chip shops. Rebus will have enjoyed the occasional haggis supper from his local chip shop. He was definitely a fan, as am I.”

“It is all about the spicing and the texture,” says the Scottish food writer, novelist and cook Sue Lawrence, a champion of haggis’ adaptability for use in other dishes. “If you didn’t know what was in it, you wouldn’t think ‘oh that tastes of liver or whatever.’ It is all nicely chopped up and the oatmeal gives it a lovely texture. It could easily be a nice, big mince dish.”

These US restaurants and chefs are James Beard Award finalists

Lawrence uses haggis as an alternative to beef and pork ragù in lasagna and in her pastilla, a version of the North African dish in which a hand-made haggis from the Isle of Mull substitutes for the traditional poultry or seafood filling. The filo pastry savory is flavored with the spice blend ras el hanout, apricots, chile, orange zest and almonds before being sprinkled with cinnamon and icing sugar.

Such cultural crossovers serve as a reminder that haggis could easily be a dish with nothing specifically Scottish about it at all. Records of similar quick and portable preparations of the fast-perishing innards of sheep and other animals date back to ancient Rome and Greece.

Haggis-like combinations of offal and grains are part of the culinary history of several countries. Spain has chireta, Romania drob and Sweden polsa, while chaudin, or ponce, is a rice and meat-stuffed pig stomach that is a staple of Cajun cooking.

In neighboring England, recipes for “hagese,” “hagws of a schepe,” “haggas” or “haggus” pop up in recipe books published between the 15th and 17th centuries, probably preceding written records north of the border.

Etymological evidence points to the term “haggis” having its roots in Old Norse, suggesting an early version of an oat-and-offal sausage might have arrived in Britain and Ireland on a Viking longboat.

But ever since it was first optioned by the poet Robert Burns in the late 1700s, the haggis backstory has been monopolized by Scotland and the Scots, sometimes mischievously.

It is, according to the kind of lore that Burns engendered, the dish a doughty Highlander would carry with him as he drove cattle through the glens to the markets of the central belt or the perfect picnic for a whisky smuggler plying his illicit trade by moonlight.

From such romantic notions it was a short step to turning the haggis into a wee wild beastie, one with longer legs on one side that was thus condemned to run round and round whichever hill it lived on. In 2003, a poll of American tourists in Scotland found that one in three of them believed they might encounter such a confused creature on a Caledonian vacation.

Bourdain, a native New Yorker, may have qualified as haggis’ biggest admirer since Burns, but his compatriots at the US Department of Agriculture remain unconverted to offal-filled paunch. Haggis imports into the United States were prohibited in 1971 as part of a ban on the consumption of all livestock lungs. Authentic versions of old school haggis remain culinary contraband in the US, as hard to lay your hands on as Cuban cigars.

Across the rest of the world, it’s a different story. According to leading producer Simon Howie, haggis is more widely appreciated and consumed now than it has been since Burns improvised his “Address to a Haggis” for the entertainment of well-to-do Edinburgh acquaintances.

Firmly tongue-in-cheek, the poem lauds the “Great chieftain o’ the pudding race,” as exactly the kind of unpretentious, hearty fare required to nourish a nation of braveheart warriors.

In comparison to the enfeebling foreign muck enjoyed by the capital’s claret-quaffing elites of the time – the olio, fricassée or ragoût that would “sicken a sow” – Burns urges his readers to wonder at the magical impact of haggis on his fellow sons of Scotland’s soil.

As the English translation of the original Scots language version puts it:

These days synthetic casings have largely replaced stomach but ovine and porcine innards remain at the core of most of the haggis produced in its homeland, said Howie, who estimates that his company Simon Howie Butchers, accounts for around 60% of the roughly two million haggises produced every year.

For Howie, versatility, value for money and convenience explain why this staple of the Scottish larder is thriving. Typically haggis retails in Scotland, which accounts for half of global consumption by volume, for around £6, or $7.70 per kilogram ($3.36/pound). That’s around half the price of less expensive cuts of beef or a third of the price of Scotch lamb while enjoying a fairly similar nutritional and calorific profile.

“You can give your kids a meal that is not full of things you don’t want to feed them – for a few pounds you can feed three strapping lads,” Howie said.

“From a kitchen perspective, it is very simple because when it leaves our factory it is already cooked. So when you or a restaurant owner gets it into the kitchen all you have to do is heat it up to be piping hot. It couldn’t be more basic: a student with no cooking skills or a Michelin-starred chef do exactly the same thing to put it out on the plate.”

Its texture means haggis can also be usefully deployed in fine dining alongside leaner meat like venison or as a stuffing for poultry and game birds. Its spicy intensity means it is also finding uses in canapés and as a crouton-borne garnish for soups.

Buoyant sales are also underpinned by the increasing consumption of haggis in forms inspired by Scotland’s ethnic minorities.

Glasgow’s Sikh community pioneered haggis pakora in the 1990s and samosas, spring rolls and quesadillas have followed in its wake, often using a vegetarian version of the protein in which the offal is replaced by a mix of vegetables, pulses and mushrooms.

Such dishes are more than culinary twists. They are badges of belonging, and an indication that, two centuries after Burns grabbed it for the nation, haggis is as intimately entwined with Scots identity as ever.

Just ask Ross O’Cinneide, a promising 14-year-old fly-half in the junior section of Stirling County rugby club.

“Most of my friends and I like haggis,” he says. “Mum makes it for us sometimes after rugby and it’s got a very nice warming feeling. And it’s nice because it’s purely Scottish.”

#396. Keurig Alta Brewer Review: Brand-New Tech, Classically Good Coffee

Ahead of my virtual taste-test briefing for the new Keurig Alta brewer, it was 9:50 am and I was panicking. Pesky time zones be darned; the meeting I thought was taking place in two hours was actually in 10 minutes. That led to the first of many positive interactions with this machine—I had it fully set up, connected to my Wi-Fi, and ready to brew in less than seven minutes. That's about as intuitive a setup process as one could hope for with a first-of-its-kind coffee machine. (We won't talk about the amount of packaging scattered all over my kitchen floor during the aforementioned meeting.)

The Keurig Alta looks like something straight out of a design convention. It almost looks like spaceship decor with its curved white lines and sleek components (it also comes in black and stainless steel). Whereas some inexpensive Keurigs—the kind that sell for $50 during shopping holidays—can feel cheap and plasticky, this machine feels high-end from top to bottom. The cup holder is metal, the cup and whisk for the steam wand are magnetic, and the reservoir bin is slim and reversible. Both drip trays tuck away seamlessly without adding extra bulk.

The top of the machine has two compartments. On the right side, you'll find the standard Keurig K-Cup basket, with the typical needle at the bottom to pierce the cup. On the left, though, is a new compartment for the brand-new Keurig AltaRounds ($11 for a box of 8). These little pucks are the latest in Keurig's coffee technology and are like nothing I've seen before. The whole package comes at a high price point, but compared to in-home espresso makers, it's not unreasonable.

If you've ever used an espresso machine or watched a barista pull shots, you'll be familiar with the process of filling a portafilter with ground coffee and tamping it down. The Keurig AltaRounds look similar to this puck of coffee. Each puck is coated in a substance derived from seaweed, and that layer of “glue” holding the AltaRounds together allows them to bloom inside the machine. They're available in four varieties right now: dark roast, medium roast, a caramel blend, and double-shot espresso, with light-roast coffee and single-shot espresso varieties coming soon. The AltaRounds are stamped with a QR code that the machine reads in a split second when you insert them into the left touchscreen compartment.

The machine then recommends different drink types (more on that in a second.) When spent, the pucks are collected in a waste bin and can be popped into your home compost or simply tossed in the garbage. While they're currently shipping in foil-based packaging, they'll eventually be wrapped in paper-based packaging, which will be curbside recyclable. This plastic-free coffee delivery system is a first for Keurig and really appeals to me. I've tested machines like the Bruvi BV-01, which has biodegradable pods, and technically Nespresso pods are recyclable, but most municipalities require that you send them to Nespresso for recycling via the mail, which is not exactly convenient. Keurig has a bad reputation for its K-Cups being wasteful; these little AltaRounds are the opposite.

The resulting brews I've tried have been fantastic. The Alta uses up to 10 bars of pressure to brew actual espresso, rather than using the concentrated coffee some pod machines label as “espresso.” Plain old coffee has a layer of crema and a rich oiliness that offers a full-bodied taste and viscosity that I wouldn't typically associate with pod coffee makers. I'm not usually a flavored-coffee person, but even the caramel blend is delicious, with a sweet scent and a cozy taste that isn't overdone. My friends who have gotten an under-oath sneak peek couldn't believe their eyes or taste buds, either. My initial skepticism was quickly overshadowed by sheer excitement.

The Alta brewer has a nifty touchscreen interface that will suggest different drinks based on which AltaRound you're using. You can favorite these drinks for quick access, but navigating the menu is pretty easy, even if it's first thing in the morning and you're groggy. There are options for every coffee drinker. Want a flat white, a latte, or a cappuccino? How about a cortado or Americano? All of these and more are possible, with options to customize size, temperature, and strength. The Alta features a built-in steam wand, complete with a dedicated vessel and a magnetic whisk. When you select a drink that requires milk froth, the machine will walk you through the process step by step. It'll tell you how much milk to add—there are measurements inside the vessel—and it can make intelligent adjustments based on whether you're using dairy, oat, almond, or soy. You can make tweaks for a wetter or drier foam, and it can also create cold foam or cold froth.

The milk toppers are all rich, silky, and exquisite additions to my standard coffee drinks. You can tell the difference between drinks as well. Lattes are creamy and smooth, while cortados have a light and airy whip on top. This wand can be used manually if you'd prefer ultimate control. Once the milk is ready, the wand purges itself into a separate drip tray. Simply wipe it down and rinse out the cup; the magnetic storage keeps it in place on the machine. I love that this is a built-in feature and that it's so easy to use. I just need to pick up some flavored syrups so I can make more intricate beverages when the mood hits. I'd also like to improve my latte art, which feels a bit like cheating when I don't have to manually steam my own milk. The entire process is seamless: The coffee brews, the milk froths, you mix the components, and you have a perfect drink in hand.

I do have a few tiny nitpicks regarding this machine. The footprint is huge (10.8" W × 11.8" H × 19.0" D), and the brewer is heavy at 22 pounds. I had to reconfigure my 15-inch baker's rack in order to make room for the machine, and even still, my microwave is hanging precariously over the shelf end. And while AltaRounds have largely been flawless, I did have one incident in which my Round burst open inside its compartment and made a real big mess that I still haven't fully been able to clean out. On a similar note, I don't like the coffee waste bin. It's separated into two compartments—one for the coffee grounds and one for the residual water that comes out of them—but there are three pieces in all, including the tray that holds them both. I always forget this and end up dumping out the entire water tray because I forget that I need to hold it in place rather than just flipping my hand upside down while holding the base.

It's a small detail, but as part of a machine that feels so engineered to be easy to use, it stands out as being disproportionately annoying. And there is a slight learning curve with all the fancy bells and whistles. These are first-world problems, but I sometimes find myself overwhelmed when navigating the menus on the touchscreen, and I'm trying to sort between all of the options to tweak customizations. It's also not easy to tell at a glance whether I'm making a hot drink or a cold drink unless I double-check—I'd love an easier visual cue for drink temperature specifically. I assume this will get easier over time, and I regret complaining about my lobster being too buttery. But if you have little patience for newfangled technology, you may want to keep this in mind. Yes, the machine is very easy to use—once you know all of the ways in which you can use it. I'm still learning some of them.

Overall, though, this promising brewer truly does seem like the next frontier of homemade pod-brewed coffee. It's rare that I find a gadget truly disruptive, if you'll forgive me for that overused word, but I've tested dozens of pod coffee machines and have never found one quite like this. In fact, I'm having so much fun with it, I may be overdoing it on the caffeine. (Perhaps there are decaf AltaRounds on the horizon.)

A lot of the pod coffee machines I've tried have made my morning caffeination process more convenient, but up until now, none have made it feel so automated. I don't have to think too hard at all—not for tamping my espresso grounds, not for frothing my own milk, and certainly not for brewing the right amount of coffee for the drink I want. It's more than basic convenience. It truly feels like a replacement for going out and ordering coffee … something that I haven't done since I started testing this machine. If that's not reason to have one around, I don't know what is.

#395. Many Turkish 'guest workers' hit by poverty in old age

West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers on October 30, 1961. Sixty-five years on, many so-called 'guest workers' can't live from their pensions.

Düsseldorf Airport is a historically symbolic location. This is where the first Turkish "guest workers," as they were called at the time in Germany, arrived 65 years ago.

At a ceremony there in in mid-September, North Rhine-Westphalia's premier, Henrik Wüst, commemorated the courage of this first generation of migrants and their contribution to Germany's prosperity.

By the time recruitment ended in 1973, some 870,000 Turkish men and women had migrated to Germany for work. They toiled in the coal mines, did piecework on assembly lines or cleaned factory floors. Most settled in Düsseldorf, Cologne or Duisburg. "They have made our country more diverse, more open and stronger," said Wüst. However, he also stressed: "We will have reached our goal only once name, skin color and religion no longer matter."

According to integration expert Haci-Halil Uslucan, Germany is still a long way from that.

Even 65 years later, he told DW, people of Turkish descent still suffer a great deal of discrimination in Germany.

But he believes that the German Turkish labor recruitment agreement was, in the main, a success story.

"We've seen success in many areas, such as education. Today, we have a large number of college graduates, and we've seen professional advancement. And successful political careers. Take Baden-Württemberg's state premier, Cem Özdemir, for example," he said.

Uslucan himself is one such a success story. His father came to Berlin from Turkey and worked in the textile industry. Two years later, his father brought his wife and two sons to join him in Germany.

Haci-Halil Uslucan subsequently earned his Ph.D. in psychology and a professor of contemporary Turkish studies at the University of Duiburg-Essen.

One of his most recent research topics addresses the dark side of the labor recruitment agreement. He is examining loneliness, an issue that affects and troubles many former so-called "guest workers."

But poverty is also increasingly taking its toll on some people of Turkish descent reaching retirement age.

With a rate of between 25-30%, poverty in old age is twice as high among migrants in Germany than among Germans, which is about 12-14%, he says, adding that the disability rate and the rate of early retirement are significantly higher among migrants because the first generation did very heavy physical labor.

They are also twice as likely to become unemployed 10 years before reaching retirement age, says Uslucan.

"In addition, their monthly income is lower, they are more likely to have had employment gaps and worked in low-wage sectors. As a result, their pensions are also low."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An analysis by Germany's pension insurance fund (DRV) for the Mediendienst Integration, an information service for journalists on migration topics, uncovered some alarming figures: In Germany, pensioners with Turkish citizenship receive, on average, about €890 ($997) in pension benefits per month. That is €360 less than German pensioners, who receive €1,250 per month on average.

Even more troubling is that in June 2026, more than three times as many retirees with Turkish citizenship relied on top-up welfare benefits as Germans (9.3% compared to 2.7%).

One reason for this is that many of the Turkish workers who came to Germany were already in the middle of their working lives and consequently has less years to contribute to their pension fund, social scientist Eric Seils of the Hans Böckler Foundation in Düsseldorf told DW.

"But, of course, the most important reason is that they earned less in wages and had a shorter work history. The guest workers who came to Germany often went straight to factories, mines or construction sites. There, they didn't earn high hourly wages because they were often less educated than the Germans," he added.

With deindustrialization in the early 1970s and the oil crisis, many Turkish workers in Germany also lost their jobs.

"There weren't as many good jobs available at traditional industrial companies. Those who weren't as well-educated were more likely to become unemployed than those with an education — and the same was true for Germans. And when working lives are interrupted, that naturally has an impact on retirement benefits at some point."

Janina Söhn of the Institute for Sociological Research (SOFI) at Göttingen University has also studied the issue of poverty among older immigrants in Germany.

It's a major problem in Germany that nearly one-third of immigrants are at risk of poverty, she said.

"This group faces even greater hardship than, for example, women in general, who already have a higher risk of poverty. And when you then look specifically at female migrants living alone, the figures are truly dire and alarming. If there were no family support, it would be an even sorrier situation."

Older Turkish migrants in Germany also often have limited opportunities to earn extra euros during retirement.

This is because either because they are poorly qualified or because the hard physical labor they performed when they were younger has left them physically unfit.

According to figures from Germany's Federal Employment Agency, the employment rate of for retired Turkish people living in Germany is only half that of Germans (5.2% compared to 10.8%).

"Basically, they face a whole series of disadvantages or hardships in life. That generation of guest workers was brought to Germany and then had to do the worst jobs here, whereas many Germans were able to progress through education and training," Söhn said.

The Turkish workers in Germany didn't get similar chances.

"The people who did these tough jobs, which are always necessary for any economy, paid for it with their health," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

#393. A college students jet-powered drone may have just broken a world record

Georgia Tech aerospace engineering student Tomas Salvo rocked the internet by sharing video footage of his custom-made Reaper RC drone launching to an astonishing 491 mph (790 kmh) while carrying a payload of 2.6 pounds (1.2 kilograms). According to reporting from Tom's Hardware, it held that incredible speed for a full four minutes, climbing to a maximum height of 6,500 feet, with a total range of 31 miles at full speed.

His original tweet has now been viewed more than two million times, making it one of Friday's most viral internet posts, but you have to go through his post history to understand the genesis of this project and his greater ambitions.

All of that engineering and space-grade technology doesn't come cheap, though. Salvo is estimating his total costs for the project will be roughly $70,000, including $40,000 just on the engines and testing expenses; $6,000 for fuel and fuel systems; and a further $20,000 in contingency expenses to replace damaged parts or redesign and remake underperforming parts.

His GoFundMe page is seeking to raise $50,000, with more than $16,000 already pledged. If you contribute $500 or more, you can get yourself added to a private email list for future updates, while if you pledge $5,000 or more, you can attend a test flight in person.

In the immediate future, Salvo wants to compete for the inaugural Boom Prize, announced by Boom Supersonic CEO Blake Scholl, for "the first amateur-built radio controlled airplane to break the sound barrier." The total payout of that prize currently sits at $800,000 ($750,000 in cash and $50,000 in Boom stock), but even at 491 mph, Reaper will need to gain an additional 276 mph in speed to reach Mach 1 and break the sound barrier.

The next test flight of the prototype Reaper M1 is targeted for a late-November, early-December window, but if you want to keep up with Salvo's progress you should follow him on X.

#392. Kwame Brathwaite, photographer of 'Black is Beautiful' movement, dies at 85

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, announced his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

Brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in New York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

Using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

“You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model

By the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

By the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands

Throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The New Yorker.

T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is currently on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.
