While German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in South Korea on Friday called for a better rule-based trade order, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier was in the Chinese capital in a bid to smooth out trade disagreements.

In Beijing, Steinmeier called for preserving the "win-win principle" characterizing Sino-German relations, borrowing from the expression "win-win cooperation," one of the most frequently used phrases in Chinese foreign policy statements.

Germany's economic ties with China have gone through a shock in recent years, with Chinese manufacturing growing into sectors once dominated by German firms, and Chinese electric cars taking over market share.

At the start of a meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Steinmeier cited a recent deal limiting exports of Chinese hybrid cars to the EU in exchange for select tariff cuts on EU exports to China as an example of a "a way to find solutions."

Steinmeier also brought up Germany's growing trade deficit with China, which grew to nearly €90 billion ($100 billion) last year.

Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.

Steinmeier said Germany would work to solve trade problems with China. "We are coming with the intention of maintaining and strengthening the framework for good economic exchange between our two countries," Steinmeier said.

Later in the day, the German president, who occupies a largely ceremonial role without policymaking power, was also recieved by an honor guard alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping.

During his final day of a whirlwind Asia tour this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul on Friday that Germany and Europe are ready to cooperate with Asian economies to foster a rules-based economic order.

Merz said the European Union is ready to take the lead in shaping a better deal for countries in Asia feeling the pressure of a destabilized rules-based trade order.

"Competition between the US and China is ramping up. Tariffs, technological decoupling strategies and a tough race for critical raw materials and new technologies are fundamentally changing the rules of our global economy," Merz said.

"These conflicts and systemic shifts in power patterns concern us all. They particularly concern economically aspiring partners in the Indo-Pacific, as well as in Germany and in Europe."

During stops in Singapore and Japan this week, Merz pushed for free trade partnerships and greater European cooperation with Asian economies.

In Singapore on Wednesday, Merz called for a free trade agreement between the EU and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), a sweeping multilateral free trade agreement connecting the Asia Pacific and the Americas.

The UK is the single European signatory, albeit outside of the EU bloc. The US pulled out during the first administration President Donald Trump in 2017, scuttling the original version, the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).

"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements,"he said in Seoul on Friday.

"We are resolutely joining forces against unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law," Merz added.

"When supply chains become political pawns, when access to key technologies is obstructed or when efforts to secure raw materials resemble displays of power rather than fair partnerships, this jeopardizes growth, prosperity and ultimately the security of entire regions."

Merz also tried to allay concerns about EU protectionism under the "Made in Europe" scheme intended to protect carmakers.

"There is a fear that we might be facing ‌a new wave of European protectionism - that we are closing ‌ourselves off from other nations," ‌Merz said.

"I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, ‌but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here," he added.

Citing Germany as an example, South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong Sook told the conference  "German companies are using Korea as a central hub to expand their presence in the Asia-Pacific region."

The question of who should become Germany's new president is becoming pressing.

Many want to see Germany's first female head of state. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is keeping his cards close to his chest.

Read DW's full report on who may be the next German president.

Good morning from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

Germany's chancellor and president were both in Asia this week, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz calling for more robust trade ties with middle powers and President Frank-Walter Steinmeier focusing on diplomacy   during a multi-day visit to China.

On Friday, Merz spoke at a German-South Korean business conference in Seoul, while Steinmeier is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Keep reading for the latest updates from Germany.

#357. Best Chromebooks and Googlebooks (2026): Laptops With a Google Touch

Chromebooks are dead. Long live Googlebooks. OK, that’s an exaggeration, but Chromebooks seem to be on their way out. Google has introduced a new line of laptops, Googlebooks, which certainly look like an evolution from Chrome OS. Google announced that standard Chromebooks will remain in the lineup for the foreseeable future, but it also stated some of the latest models will be eligible for an update to the new Googlebook operating system.

Five Googlebook models have been released so far, and I’ve been testing them for the past couple of weeks. Despite being some of the most premium laptops Google has ever had in its laptop ecosystem, that doesn’t mean you should rush out and buy one. First-generation products always come with their fair share of compromises, and that’s certainly true here. As someone who’s been testing Chromebooks for over a decade, here are my suggestions on which to buy—and which to skip.

For more recommendations, check out Best Laptops, Best Cheap Laptops, Best Android Tablets, and Best Android Phones.

Unlike my Windows or MacBook laptop recommendations, I’m starting with something on the cheaper end of the spectrum. Despite Google’s best efforts, I still believe most people looking for a Chromebook in 2026 choose price first. Chromebooks have always been pitched as a cheaper alternative to PCs and Macs, and that’s still their strongest attribute—even with the arrival of Googlebook. And that’s why the Acer Chromebook Plus 516 is at the top of my list.

It often sells for under $500, cheaper than any Windows laptop I’d recommend buying. One reason is the responsive, smooth-feeling touchpad. That goes a long way toward improving the day-to-day experience of using the laptop. I wasn’t annoyed every time I had to click-and-drag or select a bit of text.

The Chromebook Plus 516’s biggest weakness is definitely the screen, which is true of almost every cheap Chromebook I’ve tested. The colors are ugly and desaturated, giving everything a sickly green tint. It’s also not the sharpest, as it stretches 1920 x 1200 pixels across a large 16-inch screen. But for usability and performance, the Acer Chromebook Plus 516 is a great value, pairing an Intel Core i3 processor with 8 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage. At $350 when it's on sale, it’s a steal.

The Asus Chromebook CX14 and CX15 can sometimes drop to as low as $130. Unlike the Acer above, these are not “Chromebook Plus” models, so they can be configured with less RAM and storage and even use lower-powered processors. That’s exactly what you get in the cheaper configurations of the CX14 and CX15. I definitely recommend the version with 8 GB of RAM, but regardless of what you choose, the CX14 and the larger CX15 are mildly attractive laptops for the price.

I appreciate the relatively thin bezels and chassis of the CX14 and CX15, as well as the larger touchpad and comfortable keyboard. The CX15 even comes in a striking blue color. The touchpad isn’t great, nor is the display. Like the Acer Chromebook Plus 516, it suffers from poor color reproduction and only goes up to 250 nits of brightness. Its webcam is only 720p, which makes video calls a bit rough. But that’s true of nearly all the competition (and there isn’t much).

Of the two models, I definitely prefer the CX14. It lacks the number pad and off-center touchpad of the CX15—two laptop features I’ve always found awkward to use. Look, no one’s going to love using a computer that costs less than $200, but if it’s what you can afford, the Asus Chromebook CX14 will at least get you by without too much frustration.

Whatever you do, don’t just peruse Amazon and buy your kid whatever ancient Chromebook is selling for $100. It’s worth the extra cash to get something with better battery life, a more modern look, and decent performance.

Googlebooks share a lot in common with Chromebooks. These devices run a custom version of Android (Googlebook OS) that looks and behaves more like Chrome OS than the phone variant you might be used to. Like Chromebooks, Googlebooks get the full version of the Chrome web browser, which can be updated separately from the operating system—something Chromebooks can’t do. Googlebooks can also run Google Play Android apps natively, meaning they perform faster—more like they do on an Android phone or tablet.

The best aspect of a Googlebook is the seamless integration with Android. As a Google Pixel user, I love how easy it is to send and receive texts or even directly control apps my phone—similar to what Macs can currently do with iPhones. The Gemini-based AI features feel like smaller stakes by comparison, though the AI-based context menu can be handy. But like so much day-one software, it’s full of bugs and small issues that will hopefully be resolved. The inclusion of a year of Google Gemini is the same deal that was offered to Chromebook Plus devices.

The specs are also a major difference between Googlebooks and Chromebooks. All of the available Googlebooks come with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage, on par with high-end Windows laptops or the MacBook Air.

Price is the biggest hurdle with the Googlebook platform in this first iteration. That’s why the Acer Googlebook 14 feels like the best overall option right now, which comes in at the cheapest of the available options. It’s priced closest to higher-end Chromebooks like the Lenovo Chromebook 14 or Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514—two devices I like a lot. The OLED display on the Acer Googlebook 14 is far superior, though, with a 2880 x 1800 resolution and 120-Hz refresh rate. That display is sharper, brighter, faster, and more colorful than any Chromebook.

My runner-up pick is the Dell XPS Googlebook. This laptop best exemplifies the idea of the Googlebook, emphasizing portability, battery life, and high-end design. In comparison, the HP Googlebook is slightly thinner, the Asus Googlebook is lighter and has more ports, and the Acer Googlebook is cheaper. But the XPS Googlebook is the only one with a smaller 13-inch screen, which really shrinks the device’s overall footprint. It uses the same chassis as the latest Dell XPS 13, refreshed this year. The XPS 13 is one of my all-time favorite laptops you can buy right now, so it’s no surprise I like this Googlebook, too. Like the Windows version, the XPS Googlebook doesn't include a headphone jack—something to consider.

Both the Acer and Dell Googlebooks use the Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite processor, rather than the Intel chip the HP and Asus use. Unfortunately, none of the Googlebooks offer battery life that can compete with what you get on the Windows side. That’s a disappointment, because we know how efficient those Snapdragon chips can be. Plus, an M5 chip in the MacBook Air still considerably outperforms devices, even in browser speed (as tested in Speedometer 3.1). On the other hand, Chromebooks have also been behind in battery life for the past few years.

As good as the hardware is, don't be surprised if you run into a fair number of bugs in the Googlebook software. On Intel models, some Chrome extensions just plain won't load. Meanwhile, performance on Android apps can feel a little slow and clunky. And then there's the compatibility issue of Android apps themselves. While they run much faster than on Chromebooks, that doesn't mean they're all properly optimized for keyboard and touchpad. Google finally updated some of its own apps to support keyboard and touchpad (like Google Docs), but you still can't normally select text with the touchpad in Microsoft Outlook. An app like Spotify, meanwhile, technically works fine, but is still built for touch and looks weird to use on a laptop. This situation will almost certainly be improved over time, but in most cases, I just reverted to the web apps in Chrome to avoid having to guess and check on how optimized these apps are. On the other hand, that defeats one of the big advantages of Googlebooks over Chromebooks.

I also really wish Google had let manufacturers start with either less memory or less storage. The main issue I have with these Googlebooks is the expensive starting prices—and to me, that’s the main reason they don’t get much interest. It leaves you not appreciating the extra performance—and instead, wondering why you can’t get one for cheaper. So far, Googlebooks don’t feel like a proper Windows or Mac alternative as a premium offering when it comes to performance, nor the economic option like the Chromebooks they are intended to supplant.

Speaking of cheaper, there’s one Chromebook I’d recommend that has the premium hardware of a Googlebook without the exorbitant price. That’s the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514. It’s a compact, modern-feeling laptop at just 0.61 inches thick. The white chassis is pretty, too. The MediaTek Kompanio Ultra 910 processor is also important: a very efficient chip that delivers much longer battery life than your average Chromebook. The review unit I tested had a sharp display, which made the laptop feel premium. However, I can’t find that model for sale online right now, so only this more basic, lower-priced version is available. The touchpad and keyboard feel great; it comes with extra ports, 12 GB of RAM, and it can even handle up to three 4K monitors.

Google mentioned that some Chromebooks will be upgradeable to Googlebook OS at some point. Unfortunately, the company hasn’t yet revealed which models will be compatible (or when it will be available), but I imagine the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514 would be a perfect candidate.

We’ve tested dozens and dozens of Chromebooks over the past years, reviewing every major release across the price spectrum. Many of these are no longer available to purchase. I stand by my picks above, but here are a few standouts from our testing that are still worth considering for the right person.

Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 for $999: For a while, this was my absolute favorite Chromebook. In many ways, nothing quite compares to it. It came out in 2025 and set a level of quality that had never existed in Chromebooks. The OLED screen is certainly part of the equation, as is the MediaTek Kompanion Ultra processor, which gives it really solid performance and battery life, just like the Acer Chromebook Plus Spin 514. Unfortunately, the price of the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14 has risen substantially over the past few months, and discounts are incredibly rare. At $999, you’re better off getting a Googlebook.

Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 for $479: Chromebooks don’t tend to be lookers, but Asus breaks tradition with the Chromebook Plus CX34 (7/10, WIRED Recommends). It’s wrapped in a gorgeous white shell that, while plastic, felt durable in my testing. I’ve reviewed many bland, gray Chromebooks, and I found myself reaching for the CX34 more because of its attractive design. The hardware is typical for a Chromebook Plus, and it felt responsive even when I had my usual complement of more than a dozen tabs and a handful of apps running. Unfortunately, this model doesn’t come with a backlit keyboard, and its 14-inch, 16:9 display feels cramped compared to other Chromebooks I’ve used with taller 16:10 screens. If you can look past those shortcomings, though, the CX34 is a solid little workhorse that stands out. —Daniel Thorp-Lancaster

What Specs Should You Look for in a Chromebook?

Chromebook prices can vary widely, from $150 to $999, so specs can differ.

Processor: For the best experience, you should avoid older Chromebooks with Intel Celeron processors. The Chromebook Plus specifications offer a good baseline to guarantee speedy performance, and I recommend going with at least an Intel Core i3, Core i5, or AMD Ryzen 3 7000 processor. Just watch out for overspending on configurations with Intel Core i7 processors unless you need the extra horsepower for multitasking, Android games, Linux apps, and dozens of Chrome tabs.

While Intel and AMD dominate the processor scene, you’ll occasionally find Chromebooks using ARM processors like the Qualcomm Snapdragon 7c Gen 2. These can be fine for very basic tasks, but they won’t fare as well under sustained, intense loads. That said, a new generation of ARM chips is on the way, like the MediaTek Kompanio Ultra 910 powering the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14.

RAM: Always opt for at least 8 GB of RAM if you can afford it. You won’t find 4 GB of RAM in anything but basic, super-budget Chromebooks, and it severely limits multitasking. If you want to avoid slowdowns, aim for 8 GB of RAM, though if your budget is under $300, that may be difficult.

Storage: Unlike a Mac or Windows PC, much of your Chromebook work will be stored on the web. This means you can typically get away with less storage, but I wouldn’t recommend going below 128 GB. If you can afford it, get at least 256 GB. You’ll get the best speed from an NVMe solid-state drive, so look for that on the spec sheet when you’re comparing models.

Screen: Most Chromebook displays you’ll find are IPS LCD panels, and that’s just fine. OLED displays are finally starting to appear on Chromebooks, but IPS LCD screens are more common and offer a good balance of brightness, contrast, and color accuracy. If you’re shopping in the extreme budget range, watch out for TN LCD panels, as they’re generally lower quality and offer worse viewing angles. For resolution, make 1920 x 1080 (or 1200p for a 16:10 aspect ratio) your standard. You’ll get crisp visuals on 13- and 14-inch screens, and it’s passable on 15 inches. Higher resolutions will look even better, but they are fairly uncommon in Chromebooks.

Ports: USB-C ports are now commonplace on Chromebooks, so there’s no excuse to buy one without them. Try to get one that charges over USB-C so you can recharge with a portable power bank when you’re on the go. A microSD card slot can also be beneficial if you want an easy way to expand storage on the fly. Some Chromebooks also support Thunderbolt 4 over their USB-C ports. That’s an excellent option if you plan to plug your Chromebook into high-end monitors, but it isn’t necessary for most people. Instead, you can get similar external monitor support (and spend a lot less) with an HDMI port or DisplayPort over USB-C support.

For years, it had only been rumors and reports. Whispers of some kind of replacement or evolution of Chromebooks—perhaps one that might even merge Android and Chrome OS. Aluminium OS was the early code name. Such an operating system would benefit both Google and Android users, yet attempts to unify the two have not worked out so far (anyone remember the Pixel Slate?). But that’s exactly what Googlebook-based laptops are attempting to do, and as of October 2026, the first wave of Googlebooks has officially arrived.

The Googlebook OS is built entirely on Android, but it maintains the Linux kernel in order to provide the full desktop version of the Chrome web browser. This is what makes Googlebooks feel like Chromebooks, without many of the same limitations. You still can’t install traditional software like on Windows or Mac, but it can run Android apps natively. These first Googlebooks start at $899, so the company is clearly starting with high-end laptops. Cheaper Googlebooks, presumably, are to come.

Google has insisted that it won’t phase out Chromebooks right away and will support them for a long time. But it hasn't provided a timeline yet.

Almost every Chromebook we recommend has “Chromebook Plus” in the name. Google launched this initiative in late 2023 with its hardware partners to offer a new category of Chromebooks designed for a better, more premium experience. To be deemed a Chromebook Plus, a laptop has to meet or exceed the following hardware requirements:

The result? A new baseline that guarantees a certain level of performance when you see the Chromebook Plus name. With the rise in remote work, Google is focused on ensuring Chromebook Plus laptops deliver a superior video-calling experience, with higher standards for webcams and AI-powered camera enhancements. It’s also gradually folding new AI features into ChromeOS that benefit from the better hardware. When you buy a new Chromebook Plus laptop, you currently get a free 12-month subscription to Google AI Pro, which gives you access to AI features like NotebookLM and Gemini, as well as 2 TB of cloud storage.

Regular Chromebooks haven’t disappeared, and you’ll still find super-budget Chromebook models without the “Plus” moniker. Chromebook Plus models start at $399 and range up to $800, though you’ll often find them on sale for less. Expect non-Plus Chromebooks focused on basic needs to keep hitting store shelves in the sub-$300 range. The first wave of Googlebooks have targeted the price and specs category above Chromebook Plus models, but it's worth noting that future Googlebooks may more directly intersect with Chromebook Plus territory.

In 2023, Google announced a new policy guaranteeing 10 years of automatic updates for any Chromebook released in 2021 or later. That’s probably far beyond the usual upgrade cycle for most people, but it keeps secondhand Chromebooks and school-issued devices secure and up to date for a long time. When a Chromebook gets its final automatic update, ChromeOS will notify you that it’s time to throw in the towel.

The 10-year automatic update timer starts from when a Chromebook is first released. You can check when your Chromebook is set to receive its final update at any time in the “Update schedule” section of its settings menu (Settings > About ChromeOS > Additional details > Update schedule). Google also keeps a handy running list of automatic update timelines for every Chromebook model on its support site.

There are lots of things you can't do on a Chromebook. You can download and organize files, but you can’t install traditional software like you can on a MacBook or Windows laptop. Everything you do must happen in a web browser. You can open Chrome windows and tabs to your heart’s content, but when you go to download the desktop version of Photoshop or Microsoft Word, you’re stuck. Proprietary school or work applications likely won’t work, and you certainly can’t play Steam games. However, you might be surprised by how much you can actually accomplish in a browser window these days.

Android apps can, however, fill in some of the gaps. With access to the Google Play Store, you can install Android games or use Android versions of some apps. This can help in a pinch, though I've often found that web-based versions of these apps work better on Chromebooks when they’re available.

Other downsides of Chromebooks come down to hardware. Most Chromebooks are made of plastic and use cheaper components. Like many budget laptops, manufacturers often compromise on touchpads and displays.

Lastly, you may run into compatibility issues with certain accessories. Standard peripherals such as mice, keyboards, and external storage shouldn’t give you issues, and even most printers are compatible. Niche peripherals designed for highly specific uses just won’t work. For example, I use a USB colorimeter to test display quality, but Chromebooks don’t support it.

#356. 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid: Drives like an EV, but there's no plug involved

Nissan’s series hybrid e-Power system has been retuned for American roads.

Nissan has a new version of its bestselling Rogue SUV, and it’s launching the model here with the latest version of its e-Power hybrid system, which Ars tested in February. Most hybrid cars you can buy today are parallel hybrids, which means that they have an internal combustion engine and an electric motor, both of which drive some or all of the wheels—everything works in parallel. But there’s another approach. Instead of connecting the engine to the wheels via a transmission, it can act as a generator and charge the traction battery, which in turn powers the electric motor. Since the engine and motor work in series, this is known as a series hybrid.

That’s mostly how the Chevrolet Volt worked. As does Honda’s hybrid CR-V. Well, mostly; engineers worked out it was more efficient for those cars’ gasoline engines to directly drive the wheels at highway speeds, something that to this day makes a certain subset of hybrid car enthusiasts irrationally angry. If you know anyone like that in your life, send them to wherever the nearest Nissan dealership is, because the 2027 Rogue Hybrid is exactly what they’ve been asking for.

Under the hood, with its crisp shut line and slim horizontal lights that give me something of a Range Rover vibe, there’s a 1.5 L, three-cylinder turbocharged direct-injection engine that generates 148 hp (110 kW). It only revs to 5,200 rpm because it’s optimized to charge the battery, not cope with the various loads of an engine connected to a gearbox and the wheels. That also allows the engine to operate at a rather impressive 42 percent thermal efficiency—we would need to look at Formula 1 engines to find higher.

This charges a 1.67 kWh lithium-ion traction battery that has been optimized for its charge and discharge ability, which in turn powers a pair of electric motors. At the front axle sits a 202 hp (150 kW), 243 lb-ft (330 Nm) permanent synchronous magnet motor, at the rear another PSM providing 134 hp (100 kW) and 144 lb-ft (195 Nm), although given the battery’s limitations, combined power output is 225 hp (168 kW). And as you would expect, the motors will regeneratively brake under deceleration to return as much energy to the battery for reuse as possible.

Although this is the first time Nissan has offered the e-Power hybrid system in the US, it has been on sale in Japan for a decade now, with more than 1.4 million cars on the road in that time. Those versions weren’t considered quite sufficient for our roads, so Nissan retuned the system for the Rogue Hybrid to be able to cope with harder acceleration and bigger vehicles.

From behind the wheel, you could very easily forget this wasn’t just a new EV—a replacement for the gone-too-soon Ariya, perhaps. Throttle tip-in is immediate, like any good electric car, and there’s enough torque to get you on your way without any fuss, even if a 0–60 mph (97 km/h) time of 6.4 seconds isn’t particularly fast by 2026 standards. Nissan has had plenty of expertise in calibrating one-pedal driving setups, and when you access the Rogue Hybrid’s by pushing a button on the center console, you’ll find it’s no different here.

So keen was Nissan to demonstrate the smoothness with which the powertrain decelerates under regen braking that it put us through a mini school-run obstacle course, complete with a fishbowl full of water mounted to the cupholder. Nary a drop was spilled, versus the same test in what might be the Rogue Hybrid’s greatest rival, Toyota’s hybrid RAV4. (The RAV4, with no one-pedal driving, requires you to use the brake pedal to slow and stop.)

Acceleration is good at highway speeds, and cruising is quiet—on a wet and windy day it was the gusts we heard, rather than wind noise generated by the car. Speaking of generators, you don’t really hear the engine running much either. It never revs particularly high and shuts off whenever possible—with music playing on the infotainment system, the occupants might not even notice.

The ride absorbed bumps well, but it didn’t absorb sharp transient shocks as well as it did those of longer duration. A combination of low-rolling resistance tires and Californian roads that were seeing their first rain in some time conspired to create rather a lot of understeer as I entered a roundabout with perhaps a touch more vigor than normal. That said, I rather liked the Rogue Hybrid’s steering feel, and together with the smooth power delivery from the two electric motors and the easy one-pedal driving mode, my time behind the wheel was most pleasant.

The Rogue Hybrid SR we drove is rated at 41 mpg (5.7 L/100 km) in the city, 36 mpg (6.5 L/100 km) highway, and a combined 38 mpg (6.2 L/100 km), not quite as good as the RAV4 hybrid but still competitive with the segment.

The Rogue Hybrid provided a commendable amount of storage space, and I was glad to see so many physical controls. As our car was fitted with the Tech package, it included a larger 14.3-inch touchscreen infotainment system running Android Automotive OS with Google Automotive Services. Wireless Android Auto and Apple CarPlay are available with both this and the standard 12.3-inch system, and I was surprised to discover that the Rogue Hybrid would show Google Maps navigation from an iPhone through CarPlay on the main instrument display in front of the driver—usually only Apple Maps (and Waze iirc) appear on this screen, with Google Maps relegated to the infotainment display.

Seat comfort has long been a Nissan obsession, and its work on its “Zero Gravity” seats has paid off, as a day of driving did not result in a fatigued driver. The stitching and design of the seats were inspired by cozy puffer jackets, although I think the charcoal interior would be a better idea for life with a family or animals than the light gray of our test car.

Initially, Nissan will just have a single model of Rogue Hybrid for sale, the SR with the Tech Package, which will cost $41,490. In January, it will add the $35,490 SV and the $43,490 Platinum trims to the mix, prices that are benchmarked against the aforementioned Toyota. And for those who think you’ll only be able to find the most expensive ones at the dealership, Nissan says it expects the mix to be 30 percent SV, 50 percent SR, 20 percent Platinum.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#355. NYT Connections Sports Edition today: Hints and answers for November 2, 2026

Today's Connections: Sports Edition will be easier for football fans.

As we've shared in previous hints stories, this is a version of the popular New York Times word game that seeks to test the knowledge of sports fans.

Like the original Connections, the game is all about finding the "common threads between words." And just like Wordle, Connections resets after midnight, and each new set of words gets trickier and trickier — so we've served up some hints and tips to get you over the hurdle.

If you just want to be told today's puzzle, you can jump to the end of this article for the latest Connections solution. But if you'd rather solve it yourself, keep reading for some clues, tips, and strategies to assist you.

The NYT's latest daily word game has launched in association with The Athletic, the New York Times property that provides the publication's sports coverage. The sports Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words, and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake — players get up to four mistakes before the game ends.

Players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

A score in basketball: BASKET, BUCKET, FIELD GOAL, MAKE

#354. Giving Marjorie Taylor Greene a platform isn't good for America

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has announced plans to protest in New York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”

But on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.)

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.)

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.)

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”

Now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.)

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

#353. Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on November 2, 2026

The Moon has now reached its Waning Crescent phase, which means less than half of its surface illuminated. It will continue to decrease now until we reach the New Moon.

As of Monday, Nov. 2, NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waning Crescent phase, with 45% of its surface visible.

Tonight, without the use of visual aids you should be able to spot the Tycho Crater, Kepler Crater, and the Mare Imbrium. Binoculars will also help you see the Alphonsus Crater, the Clavius Crater, and the Grimaldi Basin. And, if you have access to a telescope, you'll also see the Apollo 12 landing spot, the Reiner Gamma, and the Schiller Crater.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

The Moon takes approximately 29.5 days to complete an orbit around Earth, going through a series of phases along the way. Depending on its position relative to Earth and the Sun, the amount of its illuminated surface we can see changes, creating the familiar sequence of crescents, quarter moons and the Full Moon. Once the cycle is complete, the pattern repeats, as explained by NASA.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere)

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

Lois Mackenzie is a freelance reporter at Mashable. Over the years she has written for many publications, covering everything from the local news to the best pair of running shoes. You can find bylines in publications including Fit&Well, Metro, and Coach magazine, usually covering deals on everything from earbuds to TVs, or guides on how to beat your half marathon time.

Lois also holds a Master's degree in Digital Journalism from Strathclyde University and obtained a Master of Arts in English Literature at the University of Aberdeen.

#352. What the rift within the Tsikhanouski family means for the Belarusian opposition in exile

Siarhei Tsikhanouski criticizes the work of his wife, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, and her office. He also questions her legitimacy. What are the implications for Belarusian political forces in exile?

Blogger and dissident Siarhei Tsikhanouski , 48, was detained in Belarus in May 2020, after he had announced to challenge the country's ruler, Alexander Lukashenko, in the upcoming presidential elections. In December 2021, Tsikhanouski was convicted to 18 years in prison, in part for organizing "mass unrest."

After his arrest his wife, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, took his place and challenged Lukashenko as presidential candidate. Despite allegations of large-scale vote-rigging, Lukashenko was declared the winner of the election in August 2020. This triggered unprecedented mass protests across the country. They were violently suppressed, and thousands of government critics were arrested or fled into exile. Tsikhanouskaya also fled her homeland and became the leading representative of the Belarusian democratic movement.

In June 2025, Siarhei Tsikhanouski was released after nearly five years in prison and was forcibly taken out of the country.

Some 14 months after his release, the blogger has re-activated his YouTube channel, where he not only denounces Alexander Lukashenko's regime, but also Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's office, Belarusian media in exile, political analysts and others. Thousands of people follow his streams.

In one of them, Tsikhanouski claims that while Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya obviously enjoyed "a certain legitimacy from the European Union," the people who were living "quietly and silently" in Belarus today had not granted her any. He said that many of those who had voted for her as joint candidate of Belarus' opposition were regretting this today.

Tsikhanouski has suggested that a supervisory board should be established under the label "United Office of Demoratic Forces." It would be made up of "former presidential candidates, protest leaders and iconic figures of the revolution," including himself and his wife. "There would not be a full legitimacy but one which was at least granted by Belarusians," Tsikhanouski said, adding that such a supervisory board could oversee the distribution of grant funds.

Speaking about his wife, he said: "Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya was a so-called technical candidate, who received the votes of all those who were against Lukashenko. The percentage of votes she received in the 2020 election was negligible because no one knew who she was. She was allowed to run because she did not pose a threat for the regime, and because she had neither supporters nor political experience."

Asked by DW what his goals were, Siarhei  Tsikhanouski refused to comment and referred to his livestreams instead. The former political prisoner is residing in the US and is, by his own account, currently unemployed. At the beginning of summer he said he was living in Los Angeles, learning English, preparing for university studies and writing a book. It is also known that his children — a teenage son and a younger daughter — temporarily stayed with him in the US. Today, however, they attend school in Poland, where Tsikhanouskaya resides.

Neither she nor her office have commented on the family situation or her husband's allegations. Even before the public dispute, the leader of the Belarusian democratic forces avoided commenting on her husband. Asked about his activities, she often suggested to approach him directly.

Speaking to DW in December 2025, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya merely said: "What happens in the public sphere and what happens at home, are different things. I understand Siarhei's deep traumatization and also his very strong reactions to certain events. Siarhei was in prison for five years, and I look at it with great understanding. This is why I'm not going public or making any comments. We'll deal with it among ourselves."

During the 32-year-long rule of the Lukashenko regime, the Belarusian opposition has weathered many crises and conflicts. Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's leadership role has been called into question more than once. However, she and her team have always managed to work themselves out of difficult situations during the last couple of years. But will she still be able to do that now, with her own husband having turned into her critic?

Siarhei Tsikhanouski had gone back to his own self, said political scientist Yury Drakakhrust: "With all his idiosyncrasies, his style of debate, which is not exactly in line with common practice. This is likely to strike many as odd, including Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's international partners."

Tsikhanouski, Drakakhrust pointed out, insisted that he was the key figure of the 2020 events, which is why he was entitled to all the benefits, privileges, recognition and invitations. But there was no way back.

"Even if we assume that Tsikhanouski is right, that he was the central figure, what good would it do today?" he asked. "If, suddenly, hundreds of thousands of Belarusians watched his livestreams, collected funds, formed local groups or associations in Tsikhanouski's name, then perhaps it would be possible to turn back the wheel. But this will hardly be the case."

Drakakhrust described the current situation within the democratic forces as a "crisis." He doubted that Tsikhanouski would be able to reach an agreement with all the members of the supervisory board he has proposed. Furthermore, his wife, in particular, had since established certain assets, resources, and a status for herself through her office.

"Tsikhanouskaya is being received at high levels, if not as an elected president, then as a leader for Belarus and Belarusian democracy. She's not regarded as just one of several democratic leaders from Belarus," the political scientist said.

He pointed out that not only Tsikhanouskaya, but also other actors from the 2020 election campaign are in exile. They, however, had not achieved a similar level of representation or comparable access to resources. "She has surpassed them as a politician, and that's what counts."

Drakakhrust said that the Belarusian government views disputes among the opposition with a touch of irony, occasionally adding fuel to the fire: "Basically, they don't care who wins. The main thing is that there is conflict, bickering and mutual vilification."

This article was originally published in Russian.

#351. Chatbots Are Leading Hikers Astray, With Dangerous Consequences

This story originally appeared on High Country News and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

By the time the three hikers called for help from a rocky face on Mount Shasta in Northern California, they’d made a series of bad decisions. They didn’t bring enough food, and they’d overestimated their fitness. Instead of turning back in late afternoon when they hadn’t yet reached the top, they summited at 7:30 pm and had to descend in the dark. Their lack of preparation and poor planning, as they admitted later, came partly from relying on Google’s artificial intelligence chatbot Gemini. By morning, they were lost on a gnarly part of the mountain, and one hiker had banged up his knee.

“We get plenty of people who come unprepared or don’t do any research at all. To these guys’ credit, they did try,” said Nick Meyers, US Forest Service program manager of the Mount Shasta Wilderness Climbing and Avalanche Center, which responded to the call. “But I think they kind of turned their brains off.”

The three 20-year-olds aren’t the only ones making missteps in wild spaces with the help of artificial intelligence. Another Mount Shasta visitor pitched her tent near a “No Camping” sign, insisting she had a right to do so because AI told her she could, Meyers said. His team also encountered a man wandering around at a trailhead with an AI-generated map that showed prominent features on the wrong side of a nearby mountain. In British Columbia, a helicopter crew rescued a 16-year-old hiker from a ledge in the Widowmaker Arete on the back of Crown Mountain. The teen had used Anthropic’s chatbot Claude to help him plan his trip. News stories focused on that fact went viral across Canada and the US, though the hiker said later that he also consulted Google Maps and the popular hiking app, AllTrails.

Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming has also seen a marked uptick over the past year in the percentage of visitors who report using AI for travel information, said Park Superintendent Chip Jenkins. “It went from zero to 26 percent. And I’m guessing that curve is not going to flatten.”

It remains to be seen whether increasing AI use will lead to an increase in backcountry accidents and search and rescues, Meyers said. His office, which oversees a massive wilderness area in Northern California, averages a dozen rescues each year, and 2026 is shaping up to be an average year. Calls to search and rescue in Wyoming have actually gone down compared to 2025, with only 312 calls so far in 2026 compared to a total of 466 in 2025 and 377 in 2024.

Some search and rescue veterans say that AI chatbots are just the latest tools giving people new ways to get into trouble. Roughly a decade ago, when hikers, backpackers, climbers and other outdoor enthusiasts began to source their destinations, inspiration, and information from Instagram and other social media sites, they faced sometimes deadly consequences. Before that, hikers and other recreationists were led astray by their reliance on Google Maps or smartphone connectivity.

“Over the last two decades, there’s been a phenomenal push in the media to get more people outdoors, and consequently we have more people outdoors and recreating,” said Jim Moss, a Colorado-based recreation attorney and search and rescue volunteer. It’s still unclear how questionable advice from a robot will influence all those people, he added.

Turning to an AI chatbot for guidance does come with unique risks. Chatbots can “hallucinate” persuasively presenting misinformation as real, and their use can lead to a phenomenon called “cognitive surrender,” said Chris Flathmann, a human-centered computing professor at Clemson University in South Carolina who has studied AI and search and rescue.

“When humans work with AI systems, they can get so deep into it they give up thinking critically for themselves,” he explained. When AI pretends to be an expert on an unfamiliar topic, “you can’t call BS on that because you don’t have the expertise.” And once you stop thinking critically, it can be hard to start again, especially in a stressful backcountry situation.

Chatbots also tend to tell users what they want to hear and to do so with authority regardless of whether the sources they’re consulting are reliable, Flathmann and others said. Claude or ChatGPT might answer a query with extensive directions and advice that sound credible but are actually scraped from Reddit threads and out-of-date YouTube videos—and might even be entirely fabricated.

TikTok and Instagram may offer a viewer inspiration, but AI tends to offer instructions—right or wrong—as well as encouragement, Flathmann said. “AI isn’t trying to trick people into going up mountains, but I think it’s the natural evolution of what happens when you get a tool like this.”

Regardless of the resources recreators use, experts have the same advice: When you’re headed to a new place, make sure you double-check your information against reliable, authoritative sources like up-to-date public-land agency maps and websites, trail association websites, or guidebooks. Even better, talk to a real-live guide, a national forest official, or a park ranger.

“If you’re going to go into places that will kill you,” Meyers said, “you should take your planning seriously.”

#350. Hurdle hints and answers for November 2, 2026

If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

There are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

An important note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.

#349. Hackers steal $6.3 billion from Binance in record crypto heist

Binance scrambles to freeze billions after record-breaking hack linked to North Korea.

Binance has suspended all withdrawals after the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange fell victim to what appears to be the biggest heist in history.

The exchange put the “estimated total impact” of the hack at about $6.3 billion and said around $3 billion of affected assets, mainly stablecoins that act as cash for the crypto market, had been frozen.

But analysts at Elliptic said the attacker had changed about $3.3 billion into digital assets that could not be frozen and was working to cash those out as traditional currency.

An “initial investigation” suggested hackers had been able to compromise an engineer’s laptop and withdraw funds from the platform, Binance said, adding on Friday morning that further investigation “has uncovered additional points of breach.” The company is working with law enforcement.

Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs linked the hack with a North Korean unit known as TraderTraitor, saying that the sums involved would make it “the largest crypto theft on record.” Last year, North Korean hackers stole crypto worth $1.5 billion in an attack on exchange Bybit.

Peter Ward, of the Sejong Institute in Seoul, said North Korea had considerable expertise and offered “near-total protection to its hackers.”

“Things may get a lot worse going forward,” he said.

Binance said on Friday that it had “already reserved over $6.34 billion of company funds to cover this incident,” with $5 billion of the funds “already held in the exact token assets that were impacted.”

The company said it was actively buying more tokens in order to cover the remaining amount. “This step can take longer because some tokens may have low liquidity,” and settlement “also takes time,” it said.

The hack is a major blow to Binance, which was co-founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao and holds about $140 billion of digital assets. In 2023, the company pleaded guilty to US criminal charges related to breach of anti-money laundering laws and paid a $4.3 billion fine.

Zhao, known as CZ, pleaded guilty to criminal charges relating to inadequate money laundering controls. He stepped down as chief executive and was pardoned last year by US President Donald Trump.

Bitcoin fell about 4 percent in the hours after the hack emerged late on Thursday before regaining ground to trade above $78,000.

The crypto market is in the grip of a prolonged downturn after a sharp sell-off late last year wiped more than $1tn from the combined capitalization of about 18,000 digital tokens.

Richard Teng, co-chief executive of Binance, told customers that their “money is safe, and we’re covering every loss” from a reserve fund as well as “company funds.” Binance’s reserve fund holds about $1 billion worth of bitcoin, according to a company update from mid-October.

Zhao said this leaves roughly $2 billion that the company still needs to cover, adding that the company owns shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX worth more than $1 billion.

“Remaining gap is (still painful, but) manageable,” he said in a post on X.

Binance co-chief executive Yi He said on Friday that the company’s annual revenue “is sufficient to cover the losses,” without giving further details. CZ said earlier this year that the company’s annual revenue is about $5 billion.

Crypto venues have become lucrative targets for hackers, with notable heists including $280 million stolen in April from the coffers of unregulated crypto exchange Drift.

Unlike traditional exchanges, crypto venues sit on big piles of customer assets. Some institutional investors in recent years have sought third-party custody arrangements in order to keep their funds elsewhere and mitigate the risks of their assets being stolen directly off the exchange.

Binance works with Swiss banks Sygnum and Flow, the FT previously reported.

Abu Dhabi’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority, which regulates Binance’s main global crypto exchange, said in a statement on Friday that it was aware of the “security incident involving unauthorized withdrawals of assets” from the company’s exchange and was “engaging closely with Binance.”

Binance was ordered to wind down its EU operations in July after it failed to secure a license under the bloc’s new regulatory framework. The exchange, which became regulated in Abu Dhabi in December 2025, had already agreed to block UK customers from signing up for the exchange after being barred by Britain’s financial watchdog in 2021.

In the US, Binance operates under a separate entity from the rest of its global operations that is registered with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network and authorized to operate as a money transmitter in 32 states.

Last month, nearly $390 million was stolen from crypto exchange Bitget, which reimbursed customers from its so-called User Protection Fund.

North Korean hackers stole about $2 billion in cryptocurrency in 2025, a 50 percent increase from the year before, according to data from Chainalysis.

Binance said it found no evidence that unique user codes, known as “private keys,” had been breached.

In a post on X early on Friday, Yi He said the exchange expected to allow withdrawals again “in the next 48 hours.”

Binance, which has no official headquarters, last year became regulated in Abu Dhabi, where Zhao and He, who are romantic partners, are based.

In a sign of the potential repercussions from the heist, Paolo Ardoino, chief executive of Tether, said his company had frozen about $1.5 billion of USDT, its $180 billion dollar-linked stablecoin.

Jeremy Allaire, head of Circle, the second-biggest stablecoin issuer, said $800 million of its USDC coin had been frozen amid “reports of a potential exploit” at Binance.

Crypto companies can freeze the wallets in which stolen funds are moved or held. Analytics firm Elliptic said it had verified $2.8 billion of frozen crypto—mostly USDT and USDC—but that the hackers had moved the remainder into assets that could not be frozen, such as the ETH crypto token.

“This is almost certainly the largest theft of any kind in history,” Elliptic said.

Additional reporting by Daniel Tudor in Seoul

I also appreciate the mug's stainless steel rim that's smooth to sip from sans lid. Just note that it’s not TPU powder-coated like most Hydro Flask bottles, so it's a bit less grippy and you’ll have to hand wash it.

If you’re a fan of the Owala FreeSip’s spout, then the lightweight SmoothSip Slider will not disappoint. Its triple-layer insulation helps to keep drinks hot for around six hours or cold for 24. The slider lid works fine for everyday use and didn't leak when I flipped it upside down. But I still wouldn’t toss it into a bag because of how easy it is to unlock. Alongside being available in fun colors, Owala also releases limited-edition designs you can shop. Also notable is that Owala bottles are lead-, BPA-, and phthalate-free.

After an unfortunate entanglement with a coffee mug and my computer, there was a period of time when the only bar where everybody knew my name was the Genius Bar. Now, lid security is my top priority for any liquid I tote around. For that singular concern, BrüMate's cupholder-friendly Strova gets a W from me. The brand claims its patented BevLock lid is fully leakproof, and after putting the mug through its paces—flipping, shaking, and dropping it—before I even considered placing it in my purse to intermingle with my water-sensitive electronics, I came to trust the promise: I couldn't make a single drop of coffee slip through the closed-mouthpiece edges or perimeter of the lid. Further, the mug's ceramic-lined interior both protects the temperature and taste of whatever you're drinking, and it comes in more than a dozen colors and designs any aesthete would be happy to show off.

The compromise you'll have to make is that the Strova is a bit awkward to sip. The mouth opening is quite small, running in a thin, tight line, like an expressionless face, as opposed to larger, easier-to-sip options that might conjure more of an open-mouthed cackle. The construction means you have to tip the mug up past your nose to sip when it's half full or less. This may look a bit aggro while you're drinking, but it’s frankly a small price to pay for confidently avoiding spillage. —Alexis Berger

A long morning commute can be a slog. Add in successive underwhelming sips of tepid coffee, and you're less and less likely to walk into work bright-eyed and bushy-tailed. For owners of the Ember Tumbler 2, that vignette is mere fiction. This travel tumbler, from the brand that normalized spendy warming mugs, holds a generous 16 ounces, fits into a car cupholder, and—most importantly—keeps your beverage hot. It claims to have a battery life of three-plus hours, but I noticed my brew losing its steam after about two. You can control the temperature on the tumbler itself by pressing a button on the bottom that toggles between five heat levels, or you can choose a precise temp via the Bluetooth-connected app. But if you're driving, you'll probably just want to default to the hottest temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit before you depart.

The Tumbler 2's slim profile is easy to pick up with one hand while you keep the other firmly on the steering wheel. Do keep the tumbler upright in that cupholder when you're not sipping, though. It dripped when I flipped it upside down, even with the sipping lid's slider closed, so I certainly wouldn't throw it into a purse or computer bag. (The tumbler also comes with a screw-off, top-handle lid, which is less leaky, but also less useful.) Drips aside, the drinking experience is nice, with the lid's smooth texture and curved lip allowing for easy, natural sips.

If cupholder compatibility isn't your priority, you might consider the new 16-ounce Ember Mug 3 ($160), the first edition of the brand's classic line that's available in this larger capacity. It's not formally a travel mug, but it does come with a sipping lid that helps your drink stay warm longer, making it a nice option for the work-from-home crowd. Both the Mug 3 and Tumbler 2 are conveniently top-rack dishwasher safe. —Alexis Berger

Fellow nailed it with the Carter Move. This sleek mug has a ceramic-coated interior that doesn't hold scent or taste, meaning your matcha today won’t taste like yesterday’s coffee. A 270-degree twist locks the lid effectively; I’ve tossed it in my bag without a second thought and have never experienced annoying leaks or regrettable spills. The included splash guard keeps ice cubes from smacking your teeth and protects against drips and splatters while you walk and drive. Fellow also drops limited-edition colors and sometimes releases design collaborations with artists. The mug fits into most car cup holders and is conveniently compatible with the Cold Lid + Straw ($12) and the Carry Lid ($12), allowing flexibility in how you drink and tote it.

The Carter Move fits most standard drippers but isn’t compatible with the AeroPress Coffee Maker or Prismo AeroPress Attachment. If that's a deal-breaker, you might consider the Carter Wide ($30), a great alternative to the Move that works with most manual coffee brewers. In that case, you'll have to compromise on a splash guard, which I really like in the Move.

For less than $25, the Ello Campy delivers a nostalgic charm, harking back to the enameled camp cups that ooze 20th-century Americana. The Campy isn’t enameled—just painted to look like it—but it pulls off the effect well. The cork-lined handle stays cool even when piping-hot brew fills the mug, while the vacuum insulation retains your drink’s heat. The screw-on plastic lid is designed to avoid heat conduction, and the mug also features a sliding lever for sipping. It’s not spill-proof, but if you hold it upright, it should keep its contents contained. However, it doesn't fit into cupholders, which may be a deal-breaker for drivers, and the paint is likely to chip off with wear.

Some travel mugs are perfectly good enough—just not as great as the top picks above.

KeepCup 12-ounce Coffee Cup for $31: This double-walled, insulated mug aims to replicate (and replace) paper cups from coffee shops. It's a solid option if you're looking for a glass cup (the rubber grip is plastic, though). That said, it’s not the best at preserving the temperature of your drink, and the lid is a tad wobbly.

Oxo Good Grips Thermal Mug for $29: WIRED reviewed this bottle in 2022, and it earned high marks for its sturdy build and dishwasher-friendliness. But since it's older, it now fluctuates in and out of stock.

REI Co-op Camp Mug for $23+: REI's stainless steel cup is decent enough, but it doesn't particularly stand out in the wider category of travel mugs. Our tester says the exterior coating was tough enough to show no scratches, even after knocking it over a few times outside.

Zojirushi Stainless Steel Mug for $40: In addition to having a lid lock that's effective for avoiding accidental spillage, the mug is also a great option for temperature control: A reviewer once left tea in it for 18 hours (unintentionally) and discovered the drink was still hot when she finally opened the lid. The downside is that the cover has three separate parts—a mouthpiece, a gasket, and a lid—that are deeply ridged and annoying to clean.

They can't all be winners. These two cups fell short compared to our favorites.

Greens Steel Beast 20-Ounce Insulated Tumbler for $23: The Beast Tumbler has more than 81,000 positive reviews on Amazon, but the rubber seal around the lid easily comes out of place. That meant it leaked like a sieve.

Toaks Titanium Double Wall 450-Milliliter Cup for $40: More often than not, we at WIRED champion Toaks gear as an affordable source of titanium camp cookware. But this mug costs $12 more than the Hydro Flask pick above, and has a rougher finish.

Since WIRED editors began testing reusable water bottles and travel mugs, we've discovered that some brands use lead soldering to seal their insulated bottles. While exposure is unlikely (you'd have to drop or damage the bottle or mug to detach the lead pellet), we still believe it's an unnecessary risk, especially since many of our top choices use safer sealing methods. We've removed mugs from brands that have admitted to using lead in their products.

There's no shortage of travel mugs available to buy. Narrowing down the best options for you depends on your priorities and how a given mug can satisfy them. Here are key considerations for selecting a great travel mug:

I’ve been running on caffeine since I was 12 (sorry, Mom and Dad) because I took middle school way too seriously. Fifteen years later, caffeine is basically part of my personality, and I’ve been unofficially testing travel mugs for most of my life.

To officially test the mugs in this guide, I, along with other editors, drank both coffee and tea at piping-hot and ice-cold extremes, rating heat retention and taste, ensuring no picks have any hint of metallic notes. Shape and design matter, too: How comfortable is it to hold a given mug? Does it fit into a car cup holder? Does it offer additional features worth considering? I aggressively shook the mugs that promised to be leakproof and dropped those that claimed to be durable from about 4 feet high onto both wood and concrete surfaces to evaluate how well they held up. Finally, travel mugs can be a pain to scrub, so I factored in ease of cleaning.

Simply put, I need a travel mug that pulls its weight. If it didn't keep my coffee warm, my bag dry, and make my life a little easier, it didn’t make the list.

#344. What Democrats Can Learn From New York’s Data Center Moratorium

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.

When New York became the first state in the country to enact a moratorium on data center development, Adrienne Yocina was excited. For the past two years, the mom of three has been organizing in western Genesee County to stop a 600-megawatt data center from coming to a site close to the Tonawanda Seneca Nation’s reservation and a federal wildlife refuge.

But almost four months after the one-year moratorium began, Yocina tells me that she’s “getting nervous.” She’s worried that Democratic governor Kathy Hochul won’t sign a stronger bill to impose a stricter moratorium, and is concerned that the state Department of Environmental Conservation is not adequately involved in the process of evaluating data centers in New York.

“I feel like she’s just trying to shut us up,” she says of Hochul.

Data centers are at the center of midterm races across the country, with politicians of both parties making promises to enact regulations or moratoriums on development. After next week comes the tough part: Newly elected officials must either break their word or follow through on those promises as they weigh large infrastructure projects coming to their states and residents who say they’ll reject data centers no matter what.

How will those compromises go—and will they appease voters? New York’s moratorium, and the continued opposition from some groups, may offer clues.

In July, just two months after dismissing the idea of a data center moratorium, Hochul signed the nation’s first executive order to put a pause on development. Her order was a compromise. Just weeks prior, the state legislature had passed an omnibus bill that would have implemented a one-year moratorium throughout New York. The bill contained several provisions that made it more aggressive than Hochul’s moratorium, including stricter limits on the size of data centers and a mandate that the Department of Environmental Conservation conduct a thorough environmental impact review of data center operations. Rather than sign the bill, Hochul issued her own order. (The governor has until the end of the year to sign that bill, and her office says they are still looking at it.)

One of the bill’s State Senate sponsors, Democrat Kristen Gonzalez, has been publicly supportive of Hochul’s moratorium. The governor’s office, Gonzalez says, proactively reached out to her after her bill passed to help design the moratorium for more immediate relief for New Yorkers.

Gonzalez went on a data center tour of New York at the end of the summer, talking to residents around the state about their concerns. She told me that the people she talked to overwhelmingly wanted Hochul to go further and implement more aggressive measures to protect communities from data centers.

“There are local communities statewide that are living near existing data centers, dealing with significant air pollution and noise pollution, who are struggling with rising utility bills and rising water bills,” she told me. “We see the moratorium as a first step, but it can’t be the last.”

Hochul has a comfortable lead over Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman ahead of Tuesday’s election—something that may have been helped by the moratorium’s passing. In a recent Quinnipiac poll of New York voters, 53 percent of respondents said they trusted Hochul to do a better job in handling AI and data centers, compared to just 31 percent trusting Blakeman. Blakeman, who has voiced support for data centers, called Hochul’s moratorium “crazy” when it was passed in July. His campaign didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Hochul has also touted her tough-on-data-center bona fides on the campaign trail. Early last month, she hosted a roundtable discussion on data centers with agricultural, environmental, and business leaders at a farm in the Hudson Valley. There, she told reporters that she wanted to work with the state legislature to implement more aggressive protections, including banning tax breaks for data centers. At the event, Hochul was flanked by Gonzalez and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, one of Washington’s most prominent data center critics.

I asked Hochul at the event how she anticipates handling continued opposition after her moratorium ends. How does New York balance economic development with community opposition if some people don’t want data centers in their backyards under any circumstances, even with the assurances from the state that Hochul’s office is working to create?

The purpose of her pause, she said, was that communities should be able to choose. “This is democracy in action,” she said. “If you want it, it should come with all kinds of guardrails and restraints, but if you don’t want it, it doesn’t come.”

More New Yorkers may end up choosing the latter option. A Siena poll from September found that 63 percent of New Yorkers would oppose data centers being built in their area even after Hochul’s moratorium expires. (It’s even higher for New York Democrats, with 75 percent saying they’d remain opposed to data center development post-moratorium.)

Many newly elected (or reelected) governors will face a similar dynamic: At least 20 gubernatorial candidates have promised a data center moratorium or pause, according to research compiled by government relations company MultiState. Even more have promised to regulate the industry more tightly. Formerly data-center-friendly incumbents like Texas’s Greg Abbott and Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro have also made pledges to be stricter on their development.

Come January, new governors will face highly engaged constituents who are finding a political home for the first time in the fight against data centers. That includes Yocina, who says she had never voted in a local election before.

She says she understands the need for industries and jobs in upstate New York: Her youngest son decided to join the Army after a fruitless job search and is about to be deployed. Now, her organizing group is moving from focusing on just stopping the data center to brainstorming new ideas for the site.

“We’re trying to figure out what we can say yes to that’s not a data center,” she says.

Buried in Anthropic’s IPO documents filed last week was a startling admission. The tech giant’s plan to develop its own data centers exposes it to financial risk, thanks to its projected reliance on natural gas. Of course, Anthropic isn’t alone in its reliance on gas, and the filing acknowledges that’s a real problem. The heavy demand could “drive up the price of natural gas” and make it harder to purchase. I took a look at Anthropic’s plans for data centers and the brewing competition between data centers over natural gas supply in the US.

#343. GM to pay $220 million after selling customer Smart Driver data

Owners of GM cars found their driving data had been sold to insurance companies.

General Motors marketed its Smart Driver system as a way for parents to monitor teen drivers or for adults to track their driving behavior. But in 2024, it emerged that GM had been sharing that data with brokers. Those brokers then sold the data to insurance companies, and some drivers found that their insurance became more expensive as a result. To make matters worse, many of those drivers claimed they had no knowledge of ever agreeing to share such data for such purposes.

Last year, GM and its OnStar subsidiary entered into a settlement with the FTC, prohibiting them from sharing some kinds of driver data with third parties. The settlement was finalized this January. That agreement banned the two companies from sharing geolocation data or driver behavior data for five years. At the time, GM also discontinued Smart Driver across its entire range.

Now the automaker has reached terms with the District of Columbia and 35 states after their attorneys general joined together to sue GM as well.

GM said in a statement that “[s]afer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how ⁠it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share.”
