#312. My Journey to the Center of America’s Political Spam Text Hell

I've gotten nearly 2,000 campaign fundraising texts that were meant for someone else. I tried to find out why—and uncovered a labyrinth of politicians, data brokers, and shady tactics.

Just as my kid is nodding off for the night, it arrives: a ding. It’s Nancy Pelosi, texting to tell me that if I don’t donate $5 immediately, American democracy will basically collapse. A few minutes later, it’s Cory Booker, with an urgent request. Don’t even get me started on James Talarico.

Sometimes I’m driving, or making dinner, or trying to focus on my work, and another three messages arrive. Barack Obama NEEDS me. There’s a critical deadline approaching. A generous donor has offered an 800 percent match. Everything is at stake.

As I was writing that last paragraph, I got a message from Angus, a cat belonging to Sam Forstag, a Democratic congressional candidate in Montana. Angus needed me to know that Sam was out there working to flip Montana’s First Congressional District, taking on his Republican opponent and the wealthy special interests backing him.

I’m not sure what Angus expected me to do about it.

Political fundraising texts are a fact of American life. They’re intrusive, melodramatic, and relentless.

In the first 20 days of October, more than 190 arrived—nearly 10 a day.

The strangest part is that most of these messages aren’t meant for me.

For years, I diligently opted out. I’ve replied “STOP” 49 times since 2021, by my phone’s count. Sometimes “Stop2End,” when that was the magic word. In November 2025, I told Jon Ossoff’s campaign some version of “stop.” It did not stop. Since then, I’ve received 13 more texts boosting his campaign, from nine different numbers.

When the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee texted to inform me that Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden were calling me personally to action, I replied “eat shit.” That didn’t work either.

Exhausted, I decided this month to figure out what the hell was going on. Why did so many campaigns have my number? Why did they think it belonged to someone else? And why wouldn’t they fucking stop?

For starters, I downloaded my Messages history and pulled out the political texts I’ve received in recent years. Since March 2022, I’ve gotten 1,735, from 812 different phone numbers. By any measure, this is simply too many texts—nearly none of which were meant for me.

James Carville had written 27 times, soliciting money for at least a dozen political organizations. Ken Burns wanted help electing Jacky Rosen, then Roy Cooper, then Sherrod Brown. On April 2, 2025, the day after Cory Booker finished his 25-hour Senate floor speech, I received the same first-person appeal from “Cory” three times in less than two hours, sent by three different fundraising operations.

The thing is that John—the person these campaigns had me confused with—isn’t a particularly big donor. Federal Election Commission records show roughly 160 contributions since 2017, totaling about $1,700. The median gift was $6. This year, John donated six times, for a total of $51.

In the same period, my phone received 725 fundraising texts literally begging for his money.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee alone sent 60 of them—22 in the first 20 days of October—from 28 different numbers. My relative had given it $5, once, in 2020. The DCCC sent another 41 messages; it had received $8. House Majority PAC, which has never received a dime from John that I could find, kept offering to multiply contributions by as much as 900 percent.

I understand the logic of these messages on some level. They are cheap, and the strategy isn’t all that different from how a lot of scams work—spray out messages and pray someone will bite. You don’t need many people to respond for it to pay off. What I couldn’t understand, though, was how I’d gotten wrapped up in all of this. I didn’t have to look far for the answer.

Almost every text contained a link that, after a few redirects, led to ActBlue, the platform Democrats use to process donations. Helpfully, many of those links carried tracking codes—strings of letters and numbers identifying the fundraising appeal, the message being sent, and sometimes where the campaign got the recipient’s contact information.

An October DCCC link, for instance, contained acq_sms.p2p_fr_2026.10.13_b1_dccc_rent_4mtch_st. Squint a little and you can make out abbreviations for acquisition (“acq”), peer-to-peer fundraising (“p2p_fr”), and a rented list (“dccc_rent”). But one word kept appearing in these strings across messages from otherwise unrelated campaigns: Sterling.

Sterling Data Company is a relatively small firm that uses AI to help Democrats find people likely to give them money. In 2022, Forbes reported that Sterling had assembled a database of roughly 30 million political donors, with hundreds of details about some of them, including what cars they drove and what they watched on Netflix. Sterling says it uses that information to predict who might donate to a particular candidate.

Sterling appears to get much of its information from other data brokers, combining details about people’s age, location, politics, and donation histories into voter profiles that campaigns can buy or rent.

Of the 725 texts I’d received this year, nearly half contained tracking codes that appeared to reference Sterling. They came from dozens of PACs and campaigns, including the DCCC, DSCC, James Talarico, and Mark Kelly.

FEC records show that a Biden joint fundraising committee paid Sterling about $1.87 million for donor lists over four months beginning in November 2023. Around the same time, a text from the committee reached my phone with a code containing strl2b.

The DSCC’s first reported payment to Sterling came on November 22, 2023—the very day I received one of its texts tagged STL2. According to FEC data, the committee has continued paying Sterling, including roughly $250,000 this summer, which preceded another wave of Sterling-tagged texts.

Those recent texts all appeared to link back to a common platform. Dozens of campaigns had their own web addresses, but I could see that they used nearly identical software and tracking codes, often ending in tier1. Sterling’s own website advertises something it calls “Tier 1 contact data intelligence,” though I couldn’t establish whether the two were connected or who ran the system. Still, the breadcrumbs were leading me to suspect that, at some point, a Sterling database mixup had lumped John together with my phone number.

“High-frequency solicitation is a necessary evil,” Martin Kurucz, Sterling’s CEO, tells me when I ask about all of this. “Few people give, so every campaign chases the same donors, and texting at scale works too well to skip.”

Kurucz declined to discuss Sterling’s proprietary data but confirmed that the company handles the texting itself and can rent the same record to multiple campaigns. Sterling limits how often individuals can be contacted, he said, though he didn’t specify what those limits are.

“No contact database is perfect,” Kurucz says. Even matches made with moderate confidence are generally accurate enough to be worth using, he says. Wrong numbers tend to drop out of circulation because the recipients don’t engage.

Kurucz wouldn’t confirm that Sterling has caused the deluge of misdirected text messages my way, but he also didn’t deny it. Instead he offered some advice for making them stop: Don’t respond at all.

I found that there’s another way out: lawsuits. At least two people have successfully gotten a settlement out of Democratic organizations over apparently misdirected campaign texts, which presumably included never being contacted again.

That seems like a lot of work, though. Meanwhile neither of those lawsuits established how the wrong names got attached to their numbers. I still don’t know for sure how mine got mixed up with John’s. But the outcome is the same: The DSCC now texts me more often than my mother. Replying “eat shit” another hundred times won’t change that.

#311. Over 25% of people lie to get antibiotics—and their lies aren't even good

Faked symptoms still point to infections that antibiotics don’t treat.

A significant number of patients in the US lie to their doctors to get antibiotics they likely don’t need, according to two new studies. While that may not be a startling revelation, the studies drill down on the phenomenon, finding that the lies patients tell are generally bad ones—and yet, they work almost all the time.

In the two linked studies published Friday in JAMA Network Open, a team of researchers led by Alistair Thorpe at the University of Utah analyzed online survey data from over 1,000 adults. They found that over a quarter of people reported having lied to a clinician at least once to get an antibiotic prescription for themselves or a child in their care. Patients lied by either exaggerating symptoms, making up symptoms, or—most often—both.

But interestingly, the lies people told to get antibiotics involved making up or exaggerating symptoms of infections that wouldn’t be treated with antibiotics. For example, the most common falsehoods were symptoms associated with colds, such as fever, cough, and sore throat. That’s despite the fact that colds are caused by viruses, not bacteria—which antibiotics treat.

Further, while the data suggests many patients were being dishonest, clinicians responded with what could be considered their own form of dishonesty; in most cases, the dubious fibs led to antibiotic prescriptions. Specifically, 77 percent of adult patients and 87 percent of caregivers said their lies worked, leading them to get the antibiotic prescriptions they wanted.

“These findings signal a significant issue for health professionals making antibiotic prescribing decisions and for the fields of antimicrobial stewardship and public health,” Thorpe and colleagues concluded.

For the study, the researchers reviewed survey responses from 1,371 online respondents and found 959 responses that were valid and complete. Of those, 268 (28 percent) respondents reported misrepresenting their symptoms to get antibiotics. Of those, 108 reported exaggerating symptoms, 19 reported fabricating symptoms, and 141 reported doing both. In a separate analysis of 263 respondents who identified as caregivers, 63 (27 percent) reported misrepresenting symptoms of a child to get antibiotics.

The most common reported reasons for lying were that people: felt their illness or the illness of a child in their care was particularly severe; believed that antibiotics were the only thing that would help them; believed antibiotics would help them return to responsibilities (work/school) faster; or felt they should have personal autonomy (thinking they know more about their health status than the clinician or feeling like they should get to decide their own treatment).

Those who misrepresented their symptoms tended to be younger and feel their symptoms were not taken seriously by clinicians. They were more likely to believe that antibiotic resistance is a hoax, such as a scare tactic by the government or a gimmick by drug companies to justify charging more for antibiotics. People who lied were also more likely to have more underlying conditions, view lying as more acceptable, and report needing help reading health-related materials. On the other hand, those who didn’t report misrepresenting their symptoms tended to have greater antibiotic knowledge and aversion to taking antibiotics.

For people who reported misrepresenting symptoms, the online survey gave them additional questions about the types of symptoms they fabricated or exaggerated. The most common falsehoods, reported by 65 percent of dishonest patients, were to misrepresent cold-related symptoms. After that were misrepresented stomach symptoms (49 percent), joint or muscle pain (46 percent), eye symptoms (34 percent), rashes and other skin conditions (32.5 percent), urinary symptoms (31 percent), or a general feeling of being unwell (37 percent). Respondents could also report not remembering what they lied about.

“To be clear, none of these are specific indications for antibiotics,” Jeffrey Linder, of Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, wrote in an accompanying commentary, highlighting that these lies shouldn’t have helped patients get unnecessary antibiotics. “In fact, of the 8 categories offered that patients could have exaggerated or made up to get antibiotics, only 1 of them (urinary symptoms) clearly justified antibiotic prescribing,” he wrote.

While symptoms of respiratory infections can be due to bacterial infections in some situations—namely, acute sinus infection, strep throat, or pneumonia—those conditions have specific clinical guidance and/or associated tests to confirm the diagnosis, Linder highlights.

Given the magnitude of the deception, the findings raise concern that the ill-gotten antibiotics could contribute to the rise of antibiotic-resistant infections. Misuse and overuse of antibiotics are known to drive the development and spread of drug resistance. This week, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention released an updated report on antimicrobial resistance threats, finding that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi are now causing 9.7 million infections and 50,800 deaths in the US each year.

But in the accompanying commentary, Linder said that an even more concerning consequence may be the “erosion of trust” between clinicians and patients. Linder acknowledged that drug resistance is a concern, but said that on the basis of an individual patient, in most clinical circumstances, the development of drug resistance is “probably irrelevant.”

To Linder, the more pertinent question doctors must face is: “Is this prescription more likely to help my patient or hurt them?” The answer is that it’s more likely to hurt; unnecessary antibiotics provide no benefit but pose risk of adverse events, allergic reactions, and disruption of healthy microbiomes, which can provide an opening for opportunistic pathogens, such as Clostridioides difficile (which is classified as a “serious threat” in the CDC’s newly updated antimicrobial resistance threat report.)

“For these non-antibiotic-appropriate diagnoses, prescribing antibiotics is medically incorrect and could itself be considered a form of dishonesty or lying mainly to assuage the patient,” Linder wrote. That dishonesty is corrosive, he said, quoting philosopher Sissela Bok, who wrote extensively about lying and, even specifically, about lying to get antibiotics. In 1978, Bok noted that antibiotics are “sometimes used as placebos” and many parents “come to believe that they must ask for the prescription of antibiotics every time their child has a fever or a cold.” But Bok argued that when clinicians prescribe medications more likely to harm than help, such “practices lacking in candor” threaten “the entire institution of medicine.”

Linder concludes by reminding readers that “Clinicians’ obligation is to act in patients’ best interest, even if patients are hoping we do something different, even if patients do not like it, or even if patients lie about their symptoms.”

Thorpe and colleagues, meanwhile, conclude with a call to address the reasons patients lie in the first place, writing: “Strategies to improve communication about antibiotics are needed to address patient concerns, support understanding of appropriate antibiotic use, and strengthen patient-clinician relationships.”

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#309. Want to Sign With a Hollywood Agent? Start Making Fun of AI

“Hi there!” says an AI avatar of a clean-cut man dressed casually in a denim shirt, with a mostly empty bookcase in the background. “I’m Clark from Marlow & Finch. To get us started, why don’t you tell me a bit about yourself?”

The real human on the other end of the call—Graham Raabe, in glasses and ball cap—is more than ready to dive in. “Happy to, and happy to be here,” he tells his AI job interviewer. “I’m Chick Bongo. I’ve spent about 10 years in sales. Really good at managing badger margin, spent quite a bit of time with sprocket moss, particularly proud of my goosebuckle.”

“Managing badger margin sounds like a serious skill,” the unfazed bot replies. “And that goosebuckle experience is impressive.” Raabe continues to answer Clark’s boilerplate questions with complete nonsense, the fake interviewer echoing most of it in mechanical tones of approval and amazement. When the interviewer inquires what kind of salary range “Chick Bongo” has in mind, Raabe replies, “Six hundred.” Clark interprets this to mean $600,000, calling it a “bold number,” but adds that he admires the “confidence” in the ask.

Raabe isn’t really after a new gig. Actually, in addition to his job as manager of a sales team in the fintech space, he is among a crop of comedians who have recently blown up online—and secured talent representation—by figuring out inventive ways to troll and satirize AI. Absurd, rapid-fire exchanges with agents like Clark have become Raabe’s signature comic routine, one that has doubled his Instagram audience from around 50,000 to more than 100,000 followers over the past two months.

Raabe tells WIRED that he’s been pursuing stand-up comedy and screenwriting as hobbies for the better part of a decade, and trained in improv and sketch at the renowned Upright Citizens Brigade theater. It wasn’t until May of this year, he says, that he started experimenting with office humor videos on Instagram and TikTok.

“I actually didn't start with any AI-adjacent content,” Raabe says. “It was primarily more of a down-the-middle, workplace comedy play, and I was just encouraged by the results and the feedback that I got.”

Raabe has a knack for clever linguistic play, and one of his earlier bits involved substitutions for stock or cliché phrases you might hear in a meeting: instead of “the ball is in your court,” he suggests in one clip, try “the hawk is on your glove” or “that’s your microwave beeping” or “the decision goblin lives at your address.”

Then Raabe started using AI bots to “quiz” him on this type of corporate jargon—his chatbot challenged him, for example, to come up with a euphemism for explaining that his team walked into a meeting unprepared. (“We brought forks to a soup party” was his twist on the phrase.)

Finally, Raabe hit upon the bizarro AI interviewer format. Though he’s never personally endured a bot screening for employment, he was aware of the trend and saw potential in the interview agents from the AI research lab Tavus. (“Screen thousands,” the tool’s marketing copy reads. ”Miss nothing.”) The Tavus bots, Raabe found, could be customized to deliver the conversational rhythms and escalation he needed for a video sketch, and he launched a popular series called “How to Fail Your AI Interview,” in which he derails calls with the avatars with digressive tactics—claiming to have known the bot in college, for example, or insisting on “icebreakers” before the interview begins.

“Most of my comedy is to play off straight men, and AI is the ultimate straight man to improv against,” Raabe explains.

The concept quickly took off, with commenters sharing their own frustrating experiences in real AI interview scenarios. It was around when he began this transition into AI comedy that he gained representation at Dulcedo Management, a talent agency with clients throughout North America, including influencers, models, athletes, and creators. That placed him in a comedy cohort with creators Matt Husk (@husk.irl) and Sam Wassef (@ahh.gpt), two other content creators whose viral AI trolling led to agent deals despite—or perhaps in some way because of—entertainment studios rapidly integrating the tech into production workflows.

Alex Melendez, associate director of gaming and entertainment at Dulcedo, tells WIRED that the company came across Raabe when he had fewer than 10,000 followers and were instantly taken with his sharp timing and original, well-executed premises. As for the AI interview videos, he says that Raabe is mining rich territory.

“There's something inherently funny about the contradiction surrounding AI right now,” Melendez explains. “We're constantly hearing about how it's going to transform industries and replace jobs, and then you see it struggle with something incredibly basic. That disconnect creates a lot of comedic opportunity.” He feels that Raabe and others “are giving audiences a way to laugh at something that can otherwise feel intimidating or overwhelming,” and that the rapid evolution of AI means a steady flow of new material.

“Every development brings another moment that makes people stop and think, ‘What is actually happening?’” Melendez says. “Comedy has always been a way to make sense of cultural shifts, and AI is no exception.”

And though AI may be the butt of these jokes, many tech developers and companies seem to be all for it. “I've gotten multiple DMs from people who are product managers at companies that build AI video avatars like this,” Raabe says. “They've told me that they love to see people having fun with the tools, and occasionally I've gotten messages from product managers who are like, ‘Thanks for pointing out that particular skill gap because now we know how to fix it.’”

Likewise, the surreal and wildly viral dialogues between Matt Husk and OpenAI’s ChatGPT have exposed the weaknesses of the LLM, forcing the company to acknowledge these shortcomings. In his videos, Husk (as he is known across his social media accounts) typically asks the chatbot for some kind of help, with his theoretical problems ranging from drowning in quicksand to simple challenges like counting to a hundred. Without fail, the chatbot cheerfully botches the job, and it tends to gaslight Husk about getting the answer wrong if he presses it to admit fault.

Husk’s content has earned him some 2 million followers combined across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube, as well as a deal with the talent agency Unicorn, where he’s represented by Ali Fischbein, founder of the production company Lil Fish Comedy. (Fischbein declined to comment for this article.) And as with Raabe, Husk’s rise as a social media star has coincided with a role as pressure-tester for his favored product.

In April, on the tech podcast Mostly Human, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was prompted to react to a Husk video in which he used ChatGPT as a stopwatch and found that it measured a span of a few seconds as lasting “around 10 minutes.” Altman laughed at the glitch, claiming that it was a “known issue,” and predicted that it would be another year before the voice model could set an accurate timer.

Not everyone in this scene is examining areas where AI might be improved, however. Sam Wassef, who has more than 860,000 followers as @ahh.gpt on Instagram, instead embodies a humanoid parody of a chatbot, delivering a pitch-perfect impression of the inanities and non sequiturs you’ve come to expect from these pioneering models, often while guzzling water by the gallon. Wassef’s shorts featuring this blathering character make up a mysterious countdown—he is a third of the way through a planned run of a hundred posts—and have expanded to cinematic scope. One of the latest videos sees him prattle on about the bright future of AI as the camera gradually reveals that he is standing alone in the center of a barren mall among dark, empty storefronts.

Wassef is signed with talent managers Mikayla Haycock and Adam Loria at Night Media, who declined to comment for this article. Their involvement is more evidence that the entertainment world is looking for people with inventive angles on the AI zeitgeist, which, as Melendez says, is an indicator that they can apply the same comedic skill set to other topics and platforms. The ultimate goal for a client like Raabe, Husk, or Wassef, he explains, “is for audiences to become invested” in them as a performer, not just “the format or trend” that gave them their start. The name of the game is growth and longevity regardless of where public discourse may go next.

“Virality can open the door,” he says, “but it's the talent behind it that builds a lasting career.”

#307. Germany's search for a nuclear waste site

Finland has become the first country with a final storage facility for nuclear waste. Germany is still searching for a site, while some countries have yet to start. Costs are expected to total many billions of euros.

Hardly any environmental and political challenge is as complex as the disposal of radioactive waste from nuclear power plants. In almost all of the world's nuclear-powered nations — some 31 countries currently operate or once operated nuclear power plants — the issue remains largely unresolved. This is despite the first large-scale nuclear power plant going online 72 years ago in the Soviet Union.

Finland recently became the first country in the world to approve a repository for radioactive nuclear waste. Located 400 meters (1,300 feet) underground on an island in western Finland, it is situated at the site of one of the country's two nuclear power plants. The project took around 40 years to complete.

Yet in every other country, including Germany, the problem remains unresolved. To make an everyday analogy: The garbage has already been placed outside for collection, but the garbage truck has not yet arrived. There is simply no landfill to take it to. It is not a pleasant sight, yet hardly anyone wants to live near such a site.

Germany has made some progress: The specially established Federal Company for Radioactive Waste Disposal (BGE) has now been searching for a suitable site for almost ten years, one that, like the Finnish repository, would be located deep underground.

Most experts have long agreed on one point: Nuclear waste, especially the spent fuel elements from nuclear power plants, which will remain radioactive for many thousands of years, must be stored underground.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany hopes to identify a site for a final repository by 2050. But that is still a long way off, which is why Environment Minister Carsten Schneider of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) wants to examine whether the search process can be accelerated.

And, the government says, at least there is a roadmap in place. "Russia, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Japan have not yet advanced their procedures as far as we have," ministry spokesperson, Stephan Gabriel Haufe, said at a regular government press conference this week. "Finland is certainly the country making the fastest progress worldwide. But Germany is among the leading countries."

This week, the BGE announced that only 5% of Germany's land area, spread across 11 of the country's 16 states, remains under consideration as a potential site for a final repository. The agency is consulting geologists, nuclear experts, and physicists, as well as citizens and politicians. What is already clear, is that the nuclear waste generated during decades of nuclear power production will remain in Germany.

Most of the waste is currently stored at or near the sites where it was generated. These include the 19 former nuclear power plants currently being decommissioned, as well as several research facilities.

In 2011, following the reactor disaster in Fukushima, Japan, Germany decided to phase out the commercial use of nuclear energy, and the last nuclear power plant was shut down in 2023. The waste, however, remains in interim storage.

"It must be shown that a repository will remain safe over a very long period of time," said BGE spokesperson Dagmar Dehmer. "In Finland, that means 100,000 years; in Germany, Switzerland, and France, one million years. But no matter how far into the future scientists project, the effort involved is enormous. It requires a detailed analysis of developments over time, the interactions between geology and technology, and the decay of radionuclides, as well as an assessment of how these factors affect safety."

The procedure is indeed complex: First, potential sites are evaluated for their geological suitability. Will the rock formation remain stable at a depth of 400 meters? Could groundwater become contaminated? The goal is to identify a location where the repository would be surrounded by a rock layer around 100 meters thick, providing a natural barrier. Suitable geological formations include layers of clay, granite, and rock salt.

As the requirements become progressively stricter, fewer and fewer potential sites remain under consideration. Other factors, such as proximity to major cities, come into play only much later in the process. Few communities are likely to welcome a repository for radioactive waste, whether in an urban area or in the countryside.

Building and maintaining trust is also part of Dehmer's job. She often has to explain why it is important to deal with the legacy of the nuclear age, regardless of where people stand on nuclear energy.

Finland has succeeded in doing so, Dehmer believes. "There is a high level of trust in government action in Finland," she said. "The country's supervisory and licensing authority, STUK, is one of its most respected institutions. Germany can learn from Finland by remaining consistent, avoiding frequent changes in direction, and demonstrating the patience needed to achieve a successful outcome."

The disposal of nuclear waste is extremely expensive. Even today, the search for a final repository and the storage of nuclear waste at former reactor sites cost around €1.4 billion ($1.6 billion) per year.

Experts estimate that the final repository itself will cost roughly €14 billion ($16.4 billion) once completed. If all goes according to plan, 28,000 cubic meters of radioactive waste will eventually be stored deep underground on a permanent basis.

This article was originally published in German.

#306. CEOs are tired of being held responsible for gun regulation

Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.

In 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law. In 2019, they called abortion bans “bad for business.”

After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.

Recently, more than 1,000 companies promised to voluntarily curtail their operations in Russia in protest of Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Dick’s Sporting Goods stopped selling semi-automatic, assault-style rifles at stores and Citigroup put new restrictions on gun sales by business customers after the mass shooting at a high school in Parkland, Florida, in 2018.

A year later, after mass shootings at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas, and a nightclub in Dayton, Ohio, Walmart ended handgun ammunition sales.

Corporate leadership has long been vocal on the issue of gun control – in 2019 and again this past summer nearly 150 major companies – including Lululemon, Lyft, Bain Capital, Bloomberg LP, Permanente Medical Group and Unilever – called gun violence a “public health crisis” and demanded that the US Senate pass legislation to address it.

That’s why corporate America’s silence in the wake of the latest mass shooting at a school in Nashville is so jarring. The United States has come to rely on the increasing power of large corporations as political advocates.

But Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a vocal advocate of corporate social responsibility who has a direct line to major CEOs around the globe, said that top executives are forlorn. Their previous efforts haven’t done much to push the needle on gun control legislation and without more backing, they don’t know what else they can do at the moment, he said.

Before the Bell spoke with Sonnenfeld, who runs Yale School of Management’s Chief Executive Leadership Institute, a nonprofit educational and research institute focused on CEO leadership and corporate governance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Before the Bell: CEOs have been quiet about gun reform since the latest mass school shooting in Nashville, have you heard anything about plans to speak out?

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld: Where is everybody else? Where is all of civil society? CEOs are just one group of people and it’s like we’re turning to them to be our saviors on every topic. They’ve joined causes with valor and nobility but they can’t just be taking cause after cause as if there’s nobody else in society. The social change that happened in the 1960s wasn’t being led primarily by CEOs. Social changes really happened when we saw the interfaith activity of clergy locking arms and canvassing legislators. We saw campuses alive and aroused. Where’s all the student activism?

The CEOs are still the most active even if they’re less active than they were six months ago. They’re not there as hired hands of shareholders to fill the role of politicians and civic leaders. They’re there to join that chorus, but they don’t want to be the only one singing.

So is this what you’re hearing from top CEOs? Have they gotten tired of advocating?

I just got off of a CEO call on voting rights and this morning we had a forum on sustainability – CEOs are still the most active on these fronts. It’s the same thing on immigration reform. If a CEO was working an 18 hour day on a 12 day week, they still couldn’t address all of the issues that need addressing.

The nation’s CEOs are waiting for everybody else to join them. They don’t need to restate something they’ve already stated. They’ve jumped in the pool, where’s everybody else?

So what do you think has led to this complacency amongst Americans and the growing reliance on CEOs to advocate on our behalf?

They’ve taken a very strong stance and they’ve gone out further than the general public. They are where the general public is on surveys, but they’re not where the general public is on action in the streets. So we’re ready for others to now do something. Enough already on saying ‘what are the CEOs doing?’ Social capital is as valuable as financial capital. CEOs understand that in their soul, they want there to be social capital. They want there to be public trust, but they need the rest of civil society to join them. And that’s their frustration.

But don’t these CEOs hold the purse strings in terms of donating to powerful politicians?

You would think that, but since the 2020 elections much less of campaign contributions have come from big business. Since the 2021 run on the Capitol, a lot of businesses either had an official moratorium or they’ve given mere pennies to politicians. The common impression on the street that CEOs are controlling campaign purses strings is 100% wrong.

Tesla reported. a modest 4% rise in sales in the first quarter compared to the final three months of last year, despite a series of price cuts on its lower priced vehicles and talk by CEO Elon Musk about strong demand at those lower prices.

The first quarter also marked the fourth straight quarter that Tesla has produced more vehicles than it has delivered to customers. Some of that may be due to the ramp up in production at two new factories, one in Texas, the other in Germany, which opened last spring, and a lag between that increased production and sales.

Tesla said there was an increase in the number of its more expensive models, the Model S and Model X, in transit to Europe, the Middle East and Africa, as well as to the Asia Pacific region.

But it does mean that over the last 12 months Tesla has produced 78,000 more cars than it has sold, suggesting that talk of strong demand by Tesla executives may not be backed up by the numbers.

“Early this year, we had a price adjustment. After that, we actually generated a huge demand, more than we can produce, really,” said Tom Zhu, Tesla’s executive in charge of global production and sales. “And as Elon said, as long as you offer a product with value at affordable price, you don’t have to worry about demand.”

#305. Dartmouth's provost warned us about AI cheating—but his own AI use cost him his job

People who love AI don’t always love telling others they used it.

On August 9, 2026, Dartmouth College Provost Santiago Schnell wrote a Washington Post op-ed called “Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there’s a deeper problem.” This week, Schnell discovered the depths of the problem himself as he resigned from the university after an advisory committee found that he failed to disclose significant AI use in an academic paper and in the Washington Post op-ed, even though publishers required such disclosure.

Schnell didn’t make it especially easy for the committee to investigate his AI use; the report uses the term “insufficient cooperation.” He did turn over his Dartmouth laptop, but he did not turn over logs from his personal LLM accounts related to the writings in question. Nor did he agree to meet with the committee.

The committee did get access to the Claude enterprise account Schnell had used through Dartmouth, though. This shows him using the LLM as a tool for revising his papers, finding and fixing bugs in code, and editing or generating figures. For instance, Schnell would run his papers through Claude and ask things like:

I am getting read[y] to submit the enclosed paper, its supplementary materials and the enclosed repo to ChemSystemsChem. This paper is not biological, but rather chemical. Imagine that you are a reviewer for this paper with expertise in nonlinear chemical dynamics and mathematical chemical kinetics. What would be your referee report for this paper?

This is quite a bit different from asking Claude to write your entire paper for you, and Schnell has long insisted that he used AI as an editorial aid and discussion partner. He told Semafor that he had used chatbots “to refine a few arguments” and “check for grammatical errors.” He told one journal editor that he “used AI as an editorial tool” to “help refine sentences, improve clarity, and the expression of arguments.” He had not disclosed his AI use to an academic journal, he said, because he “did not understand that this type of AI-assisted editing required disclosure.”

Indeed, Schnell’s own description of what he did with AI doesn’t sound, on the long list of AI-powered sins, like it would rank near the top. But it’s hard to know. As the Dartmouth committee points out, the full scope of Schnell’s AI use was unclear to them. The committee believes that Schnell’s public statements may understate “the nature of the Provost’s actual AI use” and says that Schnell regularly “went beyond his other public descriptions of his use of AI in writing.”

We do know that Schnell also asked LLMs to take TeX files and “make the corrections to the files, and the repo. If you have to generate new figures, please provide them to me. Let me know what you change in the repo, and text files so that I can take a look into it.”

Whatever you think of his actions, Schnell repeatedly failed to disclose them. It is certainly possible that he thought his AI use was on par with a spelling or grammar checker, though one Claude exchange raises questions about whether Schnell wanted to hide traces of LLM activity in his work. From the committee report:

Provost Schnell’s Claude logs reflect that he uploaded to Claude a manuscript of a forthcoming article entitled Academic Freedom and Catholic Mission: The Procedural Overlap Zone in University Governance and prompted Claude: “Are there many signatures of AI writing in this article?” Schnell later submitted a revised manuscript that incorporated the kinds of changes Claude suggested.

Schnell has now resigned. Dartmouth, though, is barreling ahead with AI. The university calls itself the place that “launched the field of artificial intelligence” back in 1956, when “the term was coined and the foundational question was asked: Can machines solve problems once reserved for human minds?” Seventy years later, Dartmouth is hosting a conference called “What Must Remain Human?” that will feature a student hackathon sponsored by Anthropic and speakers like Mira Murati and Yann LeCun.

Despite the scandal, Dartmouth President Sian Leah Beilock wants more AI. (She wrote a piece for The Atlantic in September, called “Why I Want More AI at Dartmouth.”) What’s crucial, though, is that the school’s leaders should “hold themselves to the highest standards,” she said. This appears to mean one main thing: disclosure.

In announcing Schnell’s resignation, Beilock wrote that “each of us brings a different perspective on how and when to incorporate AI into our work and our lives. Moreover, keeping Dartmouth at the forefront of AI inevitably means leading through an environment that is fluid and fast-changing. That is why, as leaders, it is so critical that we model the transparency and human judgment that we expect from our students and scholars.”

What does “disclosure” mean? In a September 2026 paper on AI detection tools, called “Who Wrote This?”, Schnell himself goes to great lengths to argue that “human-written” or “AI-written” is far too simple a binary. In his view, everything will become a mix of human judgment and AI work, and there’s nothing wrong with that. The key for him is that the human author takes full responsibility for the text, however it was composed and edited.

In the paper, Schnell lays out his method for producing it. It’s worth quoting at some length:

In September 2026, I asked OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Pro whether an AI-written essay could ever be identified with certainty, and I suggested connecting the problem to Turing’s imitation game and to the “reverse” Turing test posed by AI-text detection. GPT-5.6 Pro connected the question to binary hypothesis testing and statistical decision theory, proposed early structures and titles, identified candidate literature, and generated portions of early drafts. I chose the problem, journal, audience, and eventual direction of the argument. I decided which examples and results should remain central, including the decision to retain the Liang study while confronting it with important counterevidence. I checked the cited literature, rejected or corrected claims that I judged inaccurate, corrected mathematical and conceptual errors, and reorganized the argument.

In revising the manuscript, I rewrote most sections and added substantial explanations. I occasionally asked GPT-5.6 Sol to provide language-editing assistance for sections I had rewritten. I created the figures and made the final decisions about the mathematics, interpretation, sources, organization, and wording. I take full responsibility for the resulting manuscript.

Before submitting the manuscript for publication, I also asked GPT-5.6 Pro and Anthropic Claude Fable 5.1 to review it critically and identify issues that reviewers might raise. I evaluated the issues they identified and made corrections where I judged them warranted.

Despite all this assistance, Schnell resists the idea that AI is a “co-author.” Instead, he writes, “Calling [the paper] ‘coauthored’ would introduce a different confusion. Mathematical tools have long made substantive contributions without thereby becoming authors… The point is not that the software contributed nothing. It is that contribution and authorship are different roles.”

He is not against disclosure, as he makes clear by describing his method. Yet curiously, when submitting other papers for publication, he did not disclose his AI use even when required by publishers.

Confused about the rules in an age where even universities are pushing AI? So are many students. New survey data unveiled at this weekend’s conference shows that 61 percent of college students think AI helps explain difficult concepts, and half believe that they produce better work after talking through issues with AI tools. But “70 percent of the college students in the survey indicate that take-home work has become unfair due to AI, with 39 percent feeling pressured to use it because their peers do.” Among Dartmouth students, 92 percent of them fear “that AI can hurt writing skills.” And many of them believe their peers are using far more AI than they actually are.

Not everyone is racked with existential doubt over how to deal with AI, though. Dartmouth student Eli Moyse wrote in a September op-ed that Schnell should be fired because “a fetishization of AI to earn publicity for the College has rotted the brain of our top academic.”

#301. When You Should—and Shouldn’t—Use AI to Search the Web

If you've interacted with the likes of Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini, you've noticed that in addition to everything else they do, these AI chatbots can search the web for you. Depending on what you’re looking for, it can be easier to find more relevant results through a chatbot, which may explain why Google is so keen to push AI Mode for its own search engine.

When asked to search the web, the latest versions of these bots are combining elements of traditional web search (they're essentially just googling on your behalf) with knowledge they are able to pull out of their training data. Everything is then packaged and formatted in the now-familiar, polished generative AI style.

It's the added AI elements on top of the traditional googling where the differences come in, and that means AI-powered search may not always be the best option.

If you're looking up something simple and widely known—like the height of the Empire State Building—then AI search is a pretty safe bet. Not only is information like this easy to access online, the “autocorrect” probability patterns favored by large language models mean there's a near-certain chance that the results you see will include the right information.

If you just need a quick look-up, AI is OK. The more obscure the question, though, the closer you need to look at the answer. If you've asked something less well known, like the fifth-billed actor in an obscure television show, there might only be one or two references to it on the web, and an AI might choose the wrong one.

One of the takeaways from recent Stanford University research is that when AI finds an accurate source, it's very good at pulling the right information out of it. Where it tends to fall down is in not finding accurate sources (either because there aren't any or because the query has been misinterpreted) and presenting a confident answer anyway.

AI search is also helpful when you have a complex query that a standard Google search wouldn't be able to parse: "I need to know the best restaurants in San Francisco for a family of five who want to spend no more than $200." AI is able to query and collate multiple sources in response to a search like this, and then present a well-synthesized answer. A traditional web search would give you a list of blue links that most probably just rank San Francisco restaurants by more basic criteria.

Again though, sources are crucial. AI bots have never been to San Francisco or eaten there. They are relying on public accounts on the web, written by people who have. Where there are no exact page matches, they'll look for related words (like "affordable" or "family") and generate an answer.

For queries where there's lots of information online, like San Francisco restaurants, AI web search can feel incredibly useful. For less popular destinations and more specific requests ("dining tables shaped like stars"), you need to be more careful with the results, as the way that AI joins the dots then becomes less reliable.

So, with the caveat that you should always do some kind of double-check, AI web search works best for common queries that are likely to lead to a lot of accurate, up-to-date information online. In both the way they process search queries, and package together and synthesize answers, AI chatbots are a significant upgrade on googling.

The way generative AI bots and LLMs are put together means they work best when paraphrasing, synthesizing, and summarizing. But these processes can also introduce mistakes. If your search needs precise details (like a celebrity quotation, a report stat, or a device specification), a traditional Google search may work best.

Heading to Google and searching the old way is also likely to be better if you want full control over the sources used. Offloading web searches to AI is convenient, but you're relying on them to interpret your search correctly, find the right sources, and then extract accurate information from those sources. It saves time, but it's more opaque.

If you know the websites you trust most for technology news, for example, you can prioritize them in a traditional web search in a way that AI might not be able to. Researchers from UC San Diego have found that AI web searches will sometimes pick sources because they're more relevant to the query, rather than because they're ranked as more authoritative.

That means a personal blog might get chosen above a professional health care site if the AI deems it to be a closer match to what the user is actually searching for. This is a choice that you would be much less likely to make when scanning a traditional list of results, as you'd typically pick the one you trusted the most.

Other areas where traditional searching still wins out are for breaking news (there can sometimes be a lag in the timeliness of the data AI pulls up) and for high-stakes searches where you absolutely cannot make a mistake—searches related to health, the law, or your finances, for instance.

If you do feel like an AI approach is needed, be sure to double- and triple-check the sources the chatbot has used, which should be linked inside the answer. If you're in any doubt, you can ask the AI for clarification on where something was sourced from, to make sure it isn't an LLM invention.

Classic Google searches can still turn up false information on the web, of course, but you're in a much better position to discern what's true and accurate and what isn't without a chatbot in the middle. For queries where that's more important than convenience and speed, there's still a place for the old way of searching the web.

#300. Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours

It’s still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic’s verified Cursor account.

An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers’ machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident.

The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorion said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account.

“It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorion CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorion has more details here.

Anthropic has yet to issue public notice of the incident to customers.

Cursor said that the malicious extension attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor using an added attacker-controlled SSH key, enabling the local SSH service and opening a reverse SSH tunnel. The code was written to work on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Because Cursor extensions run with the permissions of the tool’s Integrated Development Environment, the backdoored version likely would gain access to local files, source code, and developer tooling once it was installed.

Cursor said the capabilities of the backdoor include:

Phorion said the theft of variable names allowed the operator to quickly take inventory of cloud credentials and API tokens stored on a compromised device, likely so it could prioritize which machines to target in follow-up attacks.

Bugs in the malicious code for Windows and macOS prevented the backdoor from working in some cases. Phorion said that despite the coding flaws, “the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.”

Cursor said company personnel worked with the cloud provider hosting the server the reverse shell connected to so that infected devices could no longer reach it. Personnel also removed the backdoored version from the marketplace and blocked further distribution. The company also shut down the VSCode Marketplace to rotate keys, audit access controls, and confirm no other extensions were compromised. The marketplace is now open.

It remains unclear why Anthropic isn’t publicly warning customers of the threat and why it and Cursor aren’t explaining how the supply-chain compromise happened. Neither company answered questions seeking this information.

Anyone who installed or updated Anthropic’s VS Code extension from Cursor between 5:27 am ET and 4:35 pm on Thursday should consider themselves affected, although it may be wise for anyone who has recently done so to also consider themselves potentially infected. Both Cursor and Phorion list various indicators of compromise, including IP addresses and cryptographic hashes.

#298. Ethnic Germans in Kazakhstan face legacy of the Soviet Union

Kazakhstan is struggling to deal with the legacy of the Soviet dictatorship. Some 85 years ago, Stalin deported hundreds of thousands of people: Some 400,000 ethnic Germans living in the USSR were sent to Kazakhstan.

She wants to keep history alive. Yunna Kinereish, 22, is studying public relations in Kazakhstan's modern capital, Astana. She describes herself as a Kazakh German.

"I am German by ethnicity. But I also feel that I'm Kazakh, because I keep the traditions with my family, and I have this mentality," she told DW.

Kinereish, who belongs to the Wiedergeburt (Revival) Association of Germans in Kazakhstan, is one of 223,000 Kazakh Germans living in the Central Asian republic of Kazakhstan today.

Kinereish recently acted in a play at the association's youth theater that told the fate of her Russian German forebears.

From the 18th century onward, Germans were incentivized to leave Germany and settle in the Russian empire, including in Ukraine's Black Sea region.

But after the armies of Hitler's Nazi Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941, Soviet dictator Josef Stalin started deporting hundreds of thousands of Germans living in Russia and Ukraine to Siberia and Kazakhstan.

Innocent people who had nothing to do with Nazi Germany's invasion and atrocities were collectively held responsible by the Soviet power and denounced as spies and collaborators.

There were more than a million deportees, of whom at least 200,000 died as a result of expulsion, hunger, and forced labor.

"My family is part of this history, these terrible times. They were driven out of the Ukrainian village Kleinwärter, a settlement of ethnic Germans in Ukraine."

Yunna Kinereish says she was very moved by the personal stories she and her friends had brought to the stage at the House of Friendship, where the association has its office. "It's not easy for me, because it all touches my heart very deeply. I actually feel like crying. But when I'm on stage ..., I have to be strong."

The modern-looking House of Friendship in the capital Astana is the center for German culture in the city. Financed primarily by the German government, it offers language courses, engages in social work and fosters a culture of remembrance, focusing on the themes of deportation and repression under the Soviet regime.

Yunna Kinereish doesn't only present the history of her people on stage: She is also documenting it on film. In 2025, she made a film about German women incarcerated in ALZhIR (Akmolinsk Camp for Wives of Traitors to the Motherland), among the most infamous in the Soviet Gulag system.

During Stalin's brutal campaign of political repression and state-sponsored terror in the 1930s, a period known as the Great Terror, the Soviet Union established its biggest camp system in Kazakhstan. 18,000 women passed through the ALZhIR camp alone. These women were imprisoned there only because their husbands had been convicted of being traitors or enemies of the people. Among them were 167 ethnic German women, whose stories are told in the film.

The memorial for the ALZhIR women's camp is located just outside the gates of Astana, which only became the capital in 1997.

Astana's roads are permanently clogged with traffic. There are almost no pedestrians, and no cyclists at all. The city is growing, with new buildings shooting up all along the outskirts of the city. Beyond them is the barren steppe; the village of Akmol is about an hour's drive away.

Before entering the actual ALZhIR museum, the visitor passes through the Arch of Grief, a huge steel construction that commemorates the suffering and forced labor the women endured. The museum itself contains personal items that belonged to the female prisoners, models of their primitive quarters, original documents and photographs.

One of the photos is of Gertrud Platais, a woman with German roots who spent years incarcerated in ALZhIR. Platais was a print worker from Lower Silesia, part of modern-day Poland. She married Karl Eduard Platais and became a Soviet citizen. In 1938, during the Great Terror, her husband was arrested. Gertrud was convicted, too as a "relative of a traitor to the homeland."

She was transferred to ALZhIR, in a region where temperatures hit 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) in summer and minus 40 degreees Celsius in winter. Here, she was forced to work as an embroiderer until 1946. After this, she was banished for life to the huge Karaganda Corrective Labor Camp, known as Karlag. Gertrud Platais wasn't rehabilitated until 1956. Hers is just one story documenting the terror of the Soviet system on Kazakh soil.

Karlag was by far the biggest camp system, and its complex covered an area about 22 times the size of New York City. Karlag was not just a prison camp, but a huge economic and agricultural complex. Almost one million people passed through it between 1931 and 1959.

Around 10,000 prisoners are believed to have died here between 1940 and 1950 alone: of starvation, cold, sickness, and the effects of forced labor.

The museum sits in the middle of the Kazakh steppe, near the city of Karaganda, about 250 kilometers south of Astana. It is located in the building that used to house the camp system administration. Visiting German historians and specialists are slightly puzzled: People were not tortured or tormented in this building, it was simply where the administration was done.

Here, interrogation and torture cells have been reconstructed, and everything is underscored by melodramatic music pouring from ubiquitous loudspeakers. It comes across as staged rather than authentic. As at the ALZhIR memorial, the Karlag museum has few visitors. Even well-educated young Kazakhs probably don't know about it."

Many people in Kazakhstan, and certain areas of politics, have almost no interest in coming to terms with the country's often brutal history," says Katherine M. Erdman. An American anthropologist and archaeologist at the Nazarbayev University in Astana, she has been researching the Gulag system for about a decade now.

"We wanted to find out where exactly the camps were, and how they can still be recognized today." Erdman and her students relied on modern technology such as drone flights, but conducting interviews and research on the ground was also a part of it.

"In many regions, the landscape has been shaped by forced labor," Erdman says. Factories were often constructed alongside the primitive living quarters. Houses were built using bricks made by forced laborers.

The researchers share their findings directly with neighbors and with local administrations. "Often we're just met with apathy, or flat-out rejection," says Erdman. At a time of economic and social advancement, many don't want to be reminded of the inglorious aspects of the past.

Erdman says there is a desire to demonstrate to the international community that the country is dealing with the dark side of its history, but that she often experiences lack of interest and even rejection. The academic has been conducting research in Kazakhstan for a decade, but there is no state funding for a further lectureship.

The Kazakh German Yunna Kinereish is one of the young people in Kazakhstan who want to ensure that the past is not forgotten. "My ancestors survived the Gulag system in Kazakhstan," she tells DW. "So it's important to me that we don't forget our roots, and that what our forefathers experienced and suffered is passed on."

This article, originally published in German, was written in the context of a study trip organized by the Federal Foundation for the Study of the Communist Dictatorship in Germany. Since 1998, the foundation, funded by the German taxpayer, has dedicated itself to studying and reappraising the former communist dictatorships in Germany, the GDR, and other countries.

#296. Birdbuddy vs. Birdfy: Which Budget Smart Feeder Should You Buy? (2026)

Hard to believe, but smart bird feeders have been around for six years.

The idea started with Birdbuddy (then styled Bird Buddy), which launched a Kickstarter campaign in November 2020 for the world’s first app-connected, AI-powered smart bird feeder. Birdfy followed in 2021 with its first camera-equipped feeder, and today the two companies remain the most popular brands in the smart bird-feeder space, with a sizable catalog of offerings, including smart bird baths and smart nesting boxes.

Thanks to two new releases from Birdfy and Birdbuddy, you can now get a premium smart bird feeder experience for under $100—something that just a year or two ago would have cost $200 or more.

I tested both Birdfy’s Rookie and Birdbuddy’s Nook in my backyard for four weeks each, noting annoyances, especially helpful features, and which features were available without a subscription.

While both have a significant number of pluses and minuses, Birdbuddy’s Nook, despite costing $20 more and failing to capture every visit, came out just slightly ahead due to its more premium hardware experience.

Released in October of last year, Birdfy’s Rookie was positioned as a smart feeder for beginners, with USB-C charging only, no solar (though you can buy a more expensive model that has it), and no complicated assembly process. It functions basically as a lightweight gravity pet feeder with a 1.3-liter seed capacity and a camera on the side—just snap the three main pieces together, charge the camera, and you’re good to go. It can only be pole- or wall-mounted, not hung.

While I loved the simplicity of the Rookie and appreciated that it uses the same excellent app as the pricier Birdfy feeders, the 1080p camera’s picture quality was noticeably lower than the Nook’s, and while it did capture every bird that visited, there were also plenty of false-alarm motion detections.

I also found some significant drawbacks to the design over my four-week test. First, though the feeder itself is IP66 rated for water resistance, there’s no overhang on the roof, which means water is going to get into the seed if it rains (as it did off and on throughout my testing period).

Second, the lid just sits loosely on the top, so it kept blowing off whenever there was a big gust of wind. And third, perhaps most frustratingly, because the camera is on the side, it didn’t do the greatest job capturing larger birds, though the camera lens stayed relatively clean, being farther away from the action, and small-bird shots were well framed. Birdfy advertises the battery charge as lasting seven weeks, but my test unit lasted less than two.

One big advantage the Rookie has, however, is its seed capacity. At 1.3 liters, it’s only slightly less voluminous than Birdfy’s popular original feeder, which packs 1.5 liters. (Though note that this still pales in comparison to Birdfy’s Bamboo feeder, a top pick in our guide to the Best Smart Bird Feeders, which holds 3.5 liters.)

Feeder capacity aside, Birdfy’s app is well designed and simple, and it makes it easy to see which birds visited that day. You can even watch your feeder on TV if you have Roku—the Birdfy app is available on devices running Roku OS 15.1 or higher. Best of all, as of November 1, Birdfy offers unlimited automatic AI-based identification without a subscription, which is a rarity among smart bird feeders. Birdfy’s ID is pretty decent, with nearly no mistakes during my test.

If you want to spring for more storage or longer video recording (free tier is limited to 5 GB and 20 seconds), you can opt for Birdfy Plus for $80/year or Birdfy Pro for $150/year.

Birdbuddy’s Nook launched in late October this year and is also aimed at beginners and budget-conscious shoppers. It looks a lot like Birdbuddy’s flagship Home (previously the 2 Pro), just smaller and squatter. It has the same thick plastic construction with a roof to keep out rain, but the Nook’s hinged lid makes filling a breeze. (Note that the $99 version does not come with the extended perch or solar roof, as pictured.)

Like the Home, the camera is a half-sphere about the size of a ping-pong ball that pops in and out with a magnet; you can position it vertically or horizontally depending on which style of photos you prefer. My test unit came with the solar panel, so I was not able to test the battery life of the camera, but know that the Nook’s battery only delivers 3,900 mAh compared to the Rookie’s 5,200 mAh.

The Nook shoots in 2K HDR, resulting in noticeably crisper imagery and sound. Unlike the Rookie’s side camera, the Nook’s is centered on the feeder—which makes for better full-bird shots, but its close proximity means it tends to get dirtier and smudged more easily than the Rookie’s side camera. I was also surprised by how fast the seed disappeared—within a day in some cases. Birdbuddy states that its seed hopper holds 0.9 liters, or 3.8 cups, which is only slightly less than the Rookie, but the difference in empty rates was noticeable.

My test unit also came with the optional Extended Perch for bigger birds like Steller’s jays and crows, though the big birds in my yard have always managed to find a way to visit the Birdbuddy Home, which has Birdbuddy’s usual tiny perch, so I’m not entirely convinced this is worth the extra $40. However, I do like that I can hang the IP67-rated Nook, especially since its pole-mount option doesn’t have a fastener. This means it tends to swing around when it’s mounted on a 1-inch-diameter pole, especially when larger birds land and take off.

Birdbuddy’s strength has always been its app, which remains easy to use and presents a library of shareable photos from each bird visit, though its interface is quickly being bested by newer brands like Kiwibit and even Birdfy, which just began offering AI ID for free with all its feeders. (Birdbuddy’s app also offers free AI ID, which is excellent, but you have to manually engage it for each photo, making it harder to see at a glance which species visited that day.)

Birdbuddy cameras have also historically struggled to capture all bird visits, and while the Nook was advertised to have a faster wake time, it still missed many bird visits I saw, though I did notice more captures than previous models, with no false alarms.

One new feature of the Birdbuddy app—and one I have not seen before—is the ability to ID other birds from sounds in the background, à la Cornell Lab of Ornithology’s Merlin ID app. It currently states it’s a “free preview,” though, so I suspect it will ultimately be locked behind a subscription tier. Still, I found it to be a neat complement to the Nook’s superior onboard microphone. Other features requiring a subscription (Birdbuddy Premium for $70/year or Birdbuddy Family for $99/year) include Ultra resolution, guest access to the livestream, and the ability to name individual birds.

If you’re looking to spend under $100, the Rookie is a perfectly respectable smart bird feeder, with excellent free AI ID. However, if you want the whole package, I have to give the edge to the Nook. It won’t show you every bird that visits, which is disappointing, but you’ll get great shots of the ones that do, and its sturdy housing and versatile camera make it a great value that will hold up well in inclement weather.

#294. Supersonic airliner in doubt as company shifts to powering AI data centers

Boom’s airliner may be delayed, and its data center power business lost a customer.

Boom Supersonic CEO Blake Scholl recently declared “it’s time for a renaissance in energy and in supersonic flight” as the supersonic airliner company unveiled a Colorado factory dedicated to making gas turbines for AI data centers. But Boom may be facing turbulence after early backers for both ventures have questioned the company’s delivery timeline or backed out entirely.

One of the company’s first customers, United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby, has expressed doubts about Boom’s original plan to deliver the first Overture supersonic airliner in 2029. Kirby’s latest frank assessment came during an interview with the Office Hours: Business Edition podcast that appeared on October 28, 2026.

“‘29 is their official timeline,” Kirby told podcast host Monica Langley. “It’s not going to happen in ‘29—it’s going to take longer.”

Boom first made headlines for flying its XB-1 demonstrator aircraft in 2024 and 2025 to demonstrate a “boomless cruise” concept that harnesses the Mach cutoff phenomenon. Such a feat involves flying just beyond supersonic speeds at higher altitudes under specific atmospheric conditions, so that the aircraft’s shockwaves refract upward and minimize the impact on the ground.

The company’s plan to revive supersonic air travel has been backed by the Trump administration via efforts to ease regulations. In June 2026, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposed a new rule overturning a long-standing ban on commercial supersonic flights over the United States following an executive order from President Donald Trump.

Boom’s press releases have previously described achieving aircraft certification and carrying the first paying customers by 2029. The company has conditional agreements with American Airlines, Japan Airlines, and United Airlines involving non-refundable deposits of unknown amounts that would allow the airlines to fully purchase the Overture aircraft once it becomes commercially available.

But United CEO Kirby pointed out that Boom still has “a lot of hurdles to overcome” while developing Overture and getting the supersonic airliner certified by the FAA. “So it’s not a guarantee that they’ll overcome,” he cautioned during the podcast interview, even though he praised Scholl and the company in general.

This follows Kirby’s earlier comments back in March that put the chances of Boom’s Overture airliner entering commercial service at “50-50.” Ars has reached out to Boom for comment.

Although Boom completed building the factory intended for production of the Overture airliner in 2024, the facility, located at Piedmont Triad International Airport in Greensboro, North Carolina, has mostly sat dormant since that time. That has raised questions for North Carolina state leaders who provided more than $50 million in taxpayer funding to help build the Overture factory.

Since October 2025, NASA has separately been doing test flights involving the experimental X-59, which has a long, needle-like nose designed to reduce the sonic booms from supersonic flight. But this is a completely different approach than Boom’s use of the Mach cutoff flights.

Much of Boom’s recent focus has been on developing natural gas turbines to power AI data centers as an additional revenue stream. On October 22, the company unveiled another factory in Centennial, Colorado, dedicated to producing a 42-megawatt natural gas turbine called Superpower for data centers.

The Trump administration’s public support of Boom was once again evident as US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright participated in the event alongside Colorado Governor Jared Polis.

Boom described its new Superpower factory as making turbine parts while still undergoing construction. It aims to deliver the first gas turbines to AI data center customers in mid-2027 while ramping up annual production to 25 turbines in 2028 and 50 turbines by 2029.

Boom’s detour into powering data centers coincides with many tech companies prioritizing natural gas as the primary power source to get their projects up and running. Some data center developers are even using “mobile gas generators strapped to semitrucks” or “aeroderivative turbines originally designed for aircraft and warships,” according to the market intelligence platform Cleanview.

However, Boom CEO Scholl also acknowledged the recent loss of a $1.25 billion deal that would have seen data center developer Crusoe purchase 29 of Boom’s gas turbines, in a post on the social media platform X on September 25. Crusoe has been involved in building Texas data centers for Oracle, Google, and Microsoft that draw upon various power sources, including natural gas and renewables.

Scholl said Boom “will be delivering about 250MW of Superpowers next year to other sites” but did not specify the AI data center customers that may be using the gas turbines.

Still, Boom has characterized the development of a gas turbine for data centers as being synergistic with its design of the Symphony engine for the Overture airliner. During the October announcement, it also described having completed a prototype turbine core, called Sprint Core, that is intended to eventually power both the Superpower gas turbine and Symphony engine for the airliner.

That turbine core is set to undergo testing at the Colorado Air & Space Port, with Boom planning to fire the turbine for the first time before Thanksgiving. That would be a concrete development milestone, but the company still has much to do in proving it can get both its AI data center and supersonic airliner ventures off the ground.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.
