#293. Ukraine: Six-day localized ceasefire in Oleshky comes to end

A US-brokered ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region ended on Sunday night with no violations reported. But Russian airstrikes continued in other parts of Ukraine.

A temporary truce in Oleshky in southern Ukraine ended at 11 p.m. local time (10 p.m. CET)

Oleshky evacuees arrived in Ukrainian territory via Belarus after a long journey

Russian strikes continue elsewhere in Ukraine, knocking out power to tens of thousands of people across regions, including in the capital Kyiv

We've moved coverage to a new bloghere. Below is a roundup of events from Russia's war in Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday, October 31 and November 1.

Hundreds of people returned to safety in Ukraine after a localized ceasefire paused fighting between Russia and Ukraine in the front-line town of Oleshky.

Residents in the city lived under Russian occupation for four years, and the situation there worsened this year.

A temporary truce brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump allowed for people to leave the besieged city.

They traveled on a bus through Russia and Belarus to enter Ukrainian territory.

The Ukrainian Air Force said on Sunday evening that its public air raid alert app had been hacked.

For ​a short ​time, the app ‌showed the capital, Kyiv, and other areas subject to ‌a nuclear alert. But ​the abnormality later disappeared.

"The air alert ​app appears to have been ⁠subjected ​to enemy influence," ​the air force ​said on ‌Telegram. "There is no radiation threat! Stay ⁠calm and follow ⁠our ​updates on our channel!"

Local residents in the southern Ukrainian region of Kherson said the six-day ceasefire in and around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky had been a "breath of fresh air."

"We have to use this time to get things done," Volodymyr Omeltchenko, a 38-year-old gardener, told the AFP news agency. "We're pruning the rose bushes for winter."

Pope Leo XIV, who had pressed Russia to agree to the truce, said he hoped the temporary pause would "strengthen the desire for dialogue and lead to new concrete peace initiatives."

However, a Ukrainian military officer, speaking on condition of anonymity, expressed concern, telling AFP that the fighting would be "worse than before" when it resumed.

He said Russian forces had taken advantage of the calm of the past week to amass new troops and ammunition stocks, and collect intelligence on Ukrainian positions.

The longest truce in  the war in Ukraine, which was limited to the southern Kherson region, in and around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, ended on Sunday after Russia refused the offer of an extension, Ukrainian officials said.

"The ceasefire, which was in effect from October 27 to November 1, has ended," confirmed Ukraine's Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets.

Lubinets described the temporary truce as having been an "important step in our joint humanitarian efforts" with Russia.

Neither side reported violations of the truce, with a Ukrainian lawmakers having described the halt in fighting as having been the "biggest de-escalation since 2022."

The Ukrainian military evacuated a further 167 civilians from the partially occupied southern region of Kherson on Sunday, the army's general staff confirmed shortly before a localized six-day ceasefire was due to expire.

Among the evacuees were 22 children and 21 people with limited mobility, according to the announcement.

The temporary truce in and around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky is set to expire at 11 p.m. local time (10 p.m. CET).

Local governor Olexander Prokudin called on residents in the region to remain alert and warned people not to enter or approach areas close to the Dnipro river which flows through Kherson.

Ukrainian officials said the intensity of Russian drone and artillery strikes remained high in those areas.

Ukraine offered to extend the US-brokered ceasefire for the Kherson region but Russia refused, a senior Ukrainian official told the AFP news agency.

The truce, which only applied to the southeastern region of Kherson, expires at 10:59 p.m. local time (2059 GMT) on Sunday evening.

The official told AFP that the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry had made the offer but "the Russians don't want to."

The ceasefire, which the White House says was brokered by First Lady Melania Trump, began on Tuesday and has allowed for a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

Around 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the ceasefire took effect this week. They were given the choice of leaving the area to territory controlled by Ukraine or Russia, or of staying in the city, which has been resupplied during the truce.

US President Donald Trump called for the ceasefire to become the "starting point for lasting peace."

"The ceasefire across Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region has provided residents with the freedom to move, access to food, clean water, medicine, plus a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack," Trump said on social media. "Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace."

A Russian drone attack on Koziatyn in central Ukraine has killed at least three people and injured four others, including three children, local authorities said Sunday.

Vinnytsia regional military administrator Nataliya Zabolotna said on Facebook that a 13-year-old girl was among those who died.

"Two five-year-old children and a 16-year-old boy" sustained injuries, she said, as well as a 24-year-old man.

The victims were injured when a drone exploded between a residential building and a school, officials said.

Russian drone strikes were also reported in the western region of Chernivtsi. One person was injured and an administrative building was severely damaged, regional military administrator Ruslan Osypenko said.

Foreign ministers from countries making up the G20 refused to take part in the traditional group photo with Russia's Sergey Lavrov.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio canceled the event because of the boycott, as Russia's war in Ukraine and Moscow's diplomatic isolation from many Western countries overshadowed the summit.

Residents evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky have arrived in Ukrainian-held territory after a rare localized ceasefire enabled civilians to leave.

Speaking to DW, evacuees described years of isolation, food shortages, and regular shelling, with some saying they survived by eating grass and dogs as supplies ran out.

The rescue operation brought families back together at a reception point in northern Ukraine, where relatives, volunteers, and local residents welcomed the arrivals after their journey through Russia and Belarus.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with his Turkish counterpart Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Istanbul on Saturday evening for talks that the Ukrainian president said included preparations for a three-way summit between Ukraine, Russia and the United States.

He said the meeting would be held in the first half of November.

"President Erdogan and I discussed the prospects for this format and other possibilities, including ways to involve Turkey and all of Europe, as well as the possibility of holding meetings here in Turkey," Zelenskyy said.

"At every level, Russia must be sent signals that there is no alternative to peace and that support for Ukraine will not diminish."

Previous rounds of talks between Ukraine and Russia brokered by Turkey failed to yield a lasting peace agreement.

Describing the meetings as "important and substantive," Zelenskyy said he and Erdogan had also discussed security issues concerning shipping through the Black Sea.

"This includes food security, and today President Erdogan and I agreed to work on a Black Sea grain corridor to ensure that the corridor exists and operates effectively," the Ukrainian leader told a press conference.

A ceasefire limited to the Kherson region in eastern Ukraine that was brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump was set to expire on Sunday evening, after neither Russia nor Ukraine announced an extension.

The rare truce, which began on Tuesday, is the longest since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The ceasefire allowed for a humanitarian mission to the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

While neither side reported violations of the ceasefire, Russian strikes continued overnight, with fresh power outages reported across Ukraine on Sunday, its energy ministry and president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian strikes on the Russian-occupied region of Luhansk killed at least four people since Sunday evening, Russian-backed local authorities said.

Hundreds of thousands of households lost electricity after overnight Russian strikes hit energy infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said.

In a post on X, the Ukrainian president said energy infrastructure in four regions — Dnipro, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, and Khmelnytskyi — had been struck.

"Substations, transformers, and power lines that supply electricity to our people's homes were targeted. Repair crews are working everywhere. As of now, hundreds of thousands of families remain without power," Zelenskyy said Sunday.

He added that "massive Russian attacks on Ukraine's other critical infrastructure are also continuing unabated."

"The intensity of the strikes is very high," he said, accusing Russia of seeking to exploit Ukraine's shortage of interceptors used to shoot down ballistic missiles.

Zelenskyy repeated his call to the US, Europe and Ukraine's other partners to do more to deliver missiles and other weaponry to better defend against the Russian attacks.

"These deliveries cannot take years. Russia is destroying infrastructure and killing our people right now, and it is betting on ballistic missiles this winter. Accordingly, decisions on air defense must also be implemented now," the Ukrainian president said.

Russia wants the opening rounds of renewed peace negotiations to involve only Moscow, Kyiv and Washington, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said.

Asked whether European countries should participate, Ushakov pointed to Russia's existing contacts with the United States.

"We have working contacts with the Americans," Interfax quoted him as saying. It was therefore "logical" for at least the first rounds to take place in a trilateral format, he added.

A drone attack caused "significant damage" to an industrial facility east of Moscow, a Russian governor said, following Ukrainian reports of a strike on a major oil refinery.

#289. Everything to know about Black Friday 2026: Best deals, sale dates, how to shop smart, and more

We're officially only weeks away from one of the biggest shopping events of the year: Black Friday.

There's still about a month until the shopping holiday officially starts, but deals start to roll out much sooner than the Friday after Thanksgiving. How much sooner, you ask? Try right now. In fact, our deals experts have already been tracking price drops for the past two weeks.

That doesn't necessarily mean you should start frantically adding deals to your cart, but it does mean that it's good to head into the mega-sale event with a plan. From knowing when sales from retailers like Amazon and Best Buy start to knowing which products will likely go on sale to preparing your own shopping list, we've got you covered on everything you need to know ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

This year, Black Friday falls on Nov. 27. While retailers often start featuring their best markdowns on Black Friday itself, there are plenty of early deals worth shopping in the lead-up. Most retailers' official sales do start before the actual day, so shopping strategically ahead of time can save you from missing out on a deal entirely (or dealing with the chaos the day after Thanksgiving).

The mega-retailer just wrapped up its October Prime Day sale, but naturally, it's also getting in on the Black Friday action. While Amazon hasn't released official sale dates yet (it's still in the final days of the Holiday Beauty Event), last year's Black Friday sale started over a week before the official day. As soon as we have available dates for Amazon (and other retailers), we'll update this guide. Speaking of...

Amazon: While no official dates are available just yet, 2025's Black Friday sale started on Nov. 20 — eight days before Black Friday on Nov. 28.

Best Buy: Like Amazon, Best Buy hasn't announced any official dates yet, but promised a return of the day after Thanksgiving sale with some of the best tech prices of the year, plus a new batch of deals dropping for Cyber Monday. Most deals will be available online and in-store, with some exclusive to in-store sales. Following past precedent, Best Buy will also drop special deals through November, in the lead-up to the sale.

Walmart: Walmart has three major sale events throughout November: the early Black Friday sale from Nov. 12 to Nov. 15, the Black Friday sale from Nov. 23 to Nov. 29 (with deals online only from Nov. 23 to Nov. 26), and the online-only Cyber Monday sale from Nov. 30 to Dec. 2.

Target: Target hasn't released its full Black Friday lineup yet, but we do know its first Early Black Friday sale kicks off Nov. 5 to Nov. 7. From Nov. 1 to Dec. 24, Target's Deal of the Day offer kicks off, featuring new deals every day. Every weekend after Nov. 7, the retailer will also drop new limited-time holiday offers.

Considering prices went up this year on pretty much Apple devices except for AirPods, Black Friday will be the time to pick up new Apple devices. The short answer: Apple products will absolutely be on sale this Black Friday. The slightly longer answer: the best place to pick up Apple products during Black Friday sales will be at retailers like Amazon, Walmart, or Best Buy, which often duke it out to see who will drop a MacBook or pair of AirPods to the record-low price first (or, more impressively, keep it in stock the longest).

As for Apple itself holding Black Friday sales, the Apple Store features its own Black Friday sale every year: a free gift card for future use with the purchase of select devices. We expect to see the same this year, so we recommend picking up your Apple devices elsewhere if you're looking to save as much cash as possible.

With Black Friday feeling like a month-long (and then some) affair, what are the deals worth shopping now? It's an especially relevant question in 2026, a year that saw many historic price increases across everything from laptops to Kindles. In other words, shopping smart has never been a smarter decision, which is why we've gathered some of the best early Black Friday savings so far.

The more apt question is what doesn't go on sale during Black Friday. That's to say, if there's a product you're looking to grab on sale, whether that be a new TV or paper towels, Black Friday is the time to do it.

Beyond the deals we have listed above, we expect to see more savings on MacBooks, Windows laptops, video games and consoles, robot vacuums, regular stick vacuums, drones, trading cards, books, board games, and power tools. This list is by no means exhaustive — if there's a good deal worth writing up, you'll likely find it in our deals coverage.

The best Black Friday deals generally last through Cyber Monday, which falls on Nov. 30 this year. Some deals do linger through the week, and some Cyber Monday sales (such as Walmart's) are scheduled to extend beyond Cyber Monday proper. And as Target's deal-of-the-day sale demonstrates, there are almost always Black Friday-worthy sales through essentially Christmas. That said, for the best shot at scoring big savings (and for catching a deal while it's still available), shopping during Black Friday weekend is typically a good rule of thumb.

Bethany Allard is a Los Angeles-based shopping reporter at Mashable covering beauty tech, dating, sex and relationships, and headphones. That basically means she puts her hair through a lot, scrolls through a lot of dating apps, and rotates through a lot of different headphones. In addition to testing out and rounding up the best products, she also covers deals for Mashable, paying an especially obsessive amount of attention to Apple deals and prices. That knowledge comes in handy when she's covering shopping holidays like Prime Day and Black Friday, which she's now done for three years at Mashable.

#288. Oh captain, our captain: Ars staff remembers Patrick Stewart

“For huge numbers of people, I will always be Jean-Luc Picard. … We created an admirable individual.”

Along with the rest of the world, we at Ars are mourning Sir Patrick Stewart—the beloved award-winning actor best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise—who died Wednesday at the age of 86.

A statement released by Stewart’s representatives said:

We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia. He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.

Through the actor’s X account, the family has requested that, in lieu of flowers, memorial contributions be made to the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund and the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources.

Born in Yorkshire, England, in 1940, the acting bug bit Stewart at the age of 12, when his English teacher handed out scripts for Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice and asked young Patrick to read the part of Shylock—a role the adult Stewart would later play for the Royal Shakespeare Theater (RSC), among many other parts. His signature bald head emerged early, around 19, thanks to alopecia. He briefly worked as a cub reporter and a furniture salesman before winning a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theater School, and he landed his first professional role in 1959, playing a marooned pirate in a production of Treasure Island for the Lincoln Repertory Company.

Stewart worked regularly in theater and on British television, and his big break came in his late 40s. The actor was conducting master classes on Shakespeare at the University of California, Los Angeles, when a TV producer developing TNG heard him lecture and thought he would make a perfect captain for the Enterprise-D. Creator Gene Roddenberry wasn’t initially keen on the choice, but Stewart’s audition changed his mind. The rest is television history.

On Instagram, fellow thespian Sir Ian McKellen—who first met Stewart when both were young actors with the RSC and co-starred as Magneto in the X-Men films—recalled the day Stewart told him about the Star Trek offer.

“’But Patrick, think of your stage career in the UK,'” McKellen recalled saying. “‘Do you really want to risk—getting lost in Hollywood for years and years?’ Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did.”

Stewart himself never expressed anything but pride in the role. “For huge numbers of people, I will always be Jean-Luc Picard, and that’s fine,” he told The Independent in 2003. “I really believe we created an admirable individual.”

TNG ended in 1994, but it wasn’t long before Stewart created another iconic role, starring as Professor Charles Xavier in 2000’s X-Men, alongside McKellen as Magneto. He reprised the role in six more films and voiced the character in multiple video games.

He was a serious actor who never took himself too seriously, relishing Shakespeare, Ibsen, and Beckett but also throwing himself into comedic TV appearances on Saturday Night Live, The Daily Show (he was a “special correspondent” for several segments in 2012), and Sesame Street. Who could forget his timeless “Soliloquy on B,” channeling Hamlet? Or his daily readings of Shakespearean sonnets that helped us all get through the COVID-19 pandemic? He voiced Napoleon in 1999’s Animal Farm, CIA Deputy Director Avery Bullock on American Dad and, earlier this year, Sir Nitchfield in the delightful Sheep Detectives.

In between acting gigs, Stewart found time for charity work, advocating for such causes as domestic violence prevention and PTSD awareness among members of the armed forces, drawing on his own childhood being raised by an abusive father. All of this made Stewart one of the most beloved actors of our time. Tributes to Stewart are all over social media today, as celebrities and regular folk alike reflect on everything the actor’s work has meant to them over the years, including these heartfelt words from his lifelong friend McKellen:

Before everything else, Patrick was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire, the proud county in the north of England which he loved to the end. You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.

Ars staffers share their own reminiscences about Stewart and what he meant to them below.

I had the good fortune to literally bump into Sir Patrick Stewart outside Bond 45 in Midtown Manhattan (when it was on 45th Street). I was coming out of the restaurant with a couple of colleagues one evening when I turned right into him. When my eyes met his, I entered a state of total confusion. I knew he loved and even played Broadway, but it didn’t register why he was here, right next to me.

Fortunately, I recovered—but then, for some unknown reason, I said in a pirate voice, “Scuse muh, Capt’n!” But he didn’t miss a beat, smiled, and took a posture of “after you good sir!” I immediately chuckled like a fool and then added that I loved his work both on and off the stage. He thanked me, and we kept on rolling. I am thankful to this day that I didn’t say something corny like “two to beam up.”

What struck me about the exchange was that, as brief as it was, he did not appear annoyed in the slightest. And while I know he is a world-class actor, he also seemed genuinely appreciative of the comment. I am grateful today that I got to share my appreciation with him, awkward though it was.

Warmth. Humanity. Decency. Honesty. Integrity. Intellectualism. These are but a few of the traits I associate with Captain Jean-Luc Picard. At a time when our leadership in the United States, and many other countries around the world, regularly showcases the opposite of these characteristics, is it any wonder that we dearly miss the captain of the Enterprise-D? Picard first graced our TV screens in the late 1980s, a super impressionable time for me. As a result, for a time, that is how I expected most leaders would behave. Alas, no.

I’m sure everyone has their favorite Picard scenes, but for me it came at the very end of The Next Generation; we had all gotten to know and love the bridge crew so well, and it felt so bittersweet that it all was ending. There was Jean-Luc, who had maintained his professional distance for seven years, joining his crew at the poker table. And now, not just the series is over, but so too is the era in which Patrick Stewart was alive and making the world a better place. It’s a little darker outside.

With Patrick Stewart’s death, there will be plenty of people remembering all of the Star Trek: The Next Generation moments when he ably portrayed Captain Picard as the moral and diplomatic core of the show. And for sure, Stewart’s meaty and memorable monologues in episodes like The Drumhead, The First Duty, Darmok, Chain of Command, and more will be long remembered by sci-fi fans and studied by actors honing their craft.

But the most lasting Captain Picard moments for me are often the ones where Stewart got to let his hair down (so to speak) and show some rare emotional vulnerability in what was usually such a composed and professional character.

I’ll remember watching Picard wrestling with and crying to his brother after the trauma of being overtaken by the Borg, or chasing a dream-world grandson around on his hands and knees. I’ll remember the pain in Stewart’s eyes after a psychic implant revealed his true feelings for Dr. Crusher or when he was forced to struggle with the weight of sending a new romantic interest and subordinate on a dangerous mission. I’ll remember countless small moments like Picard downing a shot of Aldebaran whiskey with a time-shifted Scottie, being duly chagrined by a Captain Picard Day banner during a video call with an admiral, or pretending to be the barber while thwarting smugglers on an otherwise empty ship.

It’s these smaller emotional character moments—and Stewart’s ability to make so much of them—that added depth and roundness to Captain Picard’s character over the years. And that continued all the way up to Next Generation‘s very final moments, where Stewart captures the wistfulness and regret of Picard finally deciding to join the senior staff poker game. “Five card stud, nothing wild… and the sky’s the limit.”

As a very casual Star Trek viewer, I only really began to grasp the depth of Patrick Stewart’s acting when I became enthralled by the silver screen chemistry between him and co-star Ian McKellen in the X-Men film franchise. The love-hate relationship and emotional vulnerability that Stewart and McKellen instilled in their roles as old-friends-turned-rivals has resonated with me throughout the years, and I still have deep appreciation for how the actors’ real-life friendship grew from that acting experience.

I also count myself extremely fortunate to have seen Stewart and McKellen perform together in a Broadway stage revival of the play Waiting for Godot in 2014. I’m sad they won’t be performing together again, but whenever they had the opportunity, they shone brightly indeed.

Hope and altruism are central themes in Stewart’s iconic roles, and they resonated most with me during one of my lowest moments.

Ever the one to inspire, Stewart’s role as Professor X in many X-Men films encouraged people and mutants to see the best in themselves and in each other. In 2014’s Days of Future Past, his pep talk extended to new ears: a younger, disillusioned version of himself (played by James McAvoy), and he may have well been speaking to me, too. Professor X’s telepathic abilities transcend space, time, and reality—don’t question it too much.

Upon the film’s release, I was freshly laid off from my hometown newspaper after the copy desk saw its numbers cut in half. (What was already a skeleton crew became less than that.) It wasn’t lost on me that being a cynic and malcontent was partly why I wasn’t picked to remain at the paper. In my late 20s, I questioned many of the decisions that set me on my journalism path, unsure what would happen to my career.

The younger Charles Xavier finds himself in a similar spot: angry with himself, with other people, and with the general state of things—and he’s seemingly out of a job. The older Professor X reminds his younger self that people can overcome their self-defeating flaws. “Just because someone stumbles and loses their way doesn’t mean they’re lost forever.”

Younger Chuck laments being tormented by people’s accounts of their pain, something a person who reads the news for a living can relate to. I try to unplug from Cerebro—er, my computer—when I’m off the clock. Xavier doesn’t have that luxury. The constant voices have driven him to despair and left him increasingly jaded.

But older Xavier calls him out, saying it’s his own mindset that’s holding him back. “We need you to hope again,” he says.

Therein lies the answer to Xavier’s malady: hope. And, as it turns out, the advice was also applicable to a young journalist in a crumbling industry. Incidentally, Stewart also found himself at a career crossroads as a young man, though he wasn’t too far along a chosen path, according to the Hollywood Reporter.

At 15, he got a job at the local newspaper, The Dewsbury Reporter, where he was tasked with interviewing bereaved family members when someone in town died. Journalism turned out not to be his passion, and he spent much of his free time with drama groups. His editor finally told him he had to choose between acting and journalism—and he quit on the spot.

Maybe if I had an Englishman’s commanding baritone, I would have made the same choice.

Ryan Whitwam, senior technology reporter:

Patrick Stewart was a prolific actor, but I will always associate him most with Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek: The Next Generation, a show that made a real impression on me as a nerdy kid. It was refreshing to see a leader who valued science and reason—someone who didn’t immediately reach for their phaser. Despite the sometimes silly sci-fi subject matter, Stewart never seemed like he was too good to be spouting technobabble, even though he was famously skeptical of the role at first. Stewart’s portrayal of Picard elevated the series and helped it to age into a classic that I (and I’m sure many of you) still enjoy.

I also appreciate that he took so many different roles in movies and TV during his post-Trek career. Whenever I saw Patrick Stewart pop up on my screen or heard his voice unexpectedly come out of a cartoon character, it was a reminder of how happy TNG made me over the years. I’ll miss that, and I’ll miss knowing that Patrick Stewart is out there being a kind, thoughtful guy off screen.

Lee Hutchinson, senior technology editor:

The version of Patrick Stewart that lives in my head will most often be the noble starship captain who taught us life lessons every Friday night at 7 pm on channel 39. But while Stewart was obviously fantastic at portraying Picard’s stentorian and often stuffy formality, I was surprised when I discovered that the man behind the uniform was… surprisingly hilarious.

I tuned into his early 1994 Saturday Night Live appearance expecting an endless series of Trek riffs, but what I got instead was a sketch about an erotic cake shop run by a weirdly scatological baker. My confusion gave way to giggles—it was a one-note joke, but the image of Stewart in an apron talking about “sexy cakes” has stuck in my head for decades. He committed to it every bit as hard as he committed to following the Prime Directive, and at 16, it made me realize that anyone who could go from “The first duty of a Starfleet officer is to the truth!” to that and sell them both with equal intensity and sincerity was not a one-note actor. This was a man with a hell of a lot of range!

The performance that brought me the most joy, though, was his turn on Ricky Gervais’ Extras, where he played a version of himself as an actor, delivering career advice to Gervais. The scene is a masterclass in expectation subversion, something Stewart often seemed to revel in. I won’t spoil it for the two or three readers who still haven’t had the pleasure, but I will say that to this day my wife and I still say, “I’ve seen everything, I’ve seen it all!” at each other regularly in conversation.

Farewell, Sir Patrick. You gave us so much. Thank you.

Like many Gen Xers, I grew up loving the original Star Trek series. But The Next Generation held a special place in my heart. From the moment it premiered, I was captivated by the mind-bending concepts it explored. Jean-Luc Picard quickly became one of my favorite characters. I admired his intelligence, leadership, and moral integrity. He was the quintessential Starfleet captain, and he made balding cool in a way only Michael Jordan could rival.

Years later, I discovered what would become my favorite Patrick Stewart performance: his formidable portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge on Broadway and in the 1999 adaptation of A Christmas Carol.

For me, the movie remains the definitive version of Dickens’ classic, and watching it has become a cherished family holiday tradition. During the COVID lockdowns, we eagerly tuned in to Stewart’s readings of Shakespeare, and of course, his solo multipart rendition of A Christmas Carol. A roaring fire, some warm drinks, and his perfect Shakespearean accent made everything seem right with the world.

Sir Patrick Stewart will be greatly missed in the Marlin household.

Growing up in the US, raised by Brits, there was something quietly thrilling about seeing a Yorkshireman handed the captain’s chair. Better still, it made TNG legitimate in the eyes of my parents—a classically trained Shakespearean actor wouldn’t be involved in anything unserious, surely. As I came of age in 2000, there he was again as Professor X. Of course he was. Who else could it have possibly been? Beyond the roles, though, he just seemed to be a genuinely good man, the Mr. Rogers and Weird Al tier of human being. And when the world was upside down at the height of COVID, there he was, reading me a daily sonnet.

#286. HSBC's top execs face tense shareholders calling for a breakup

HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.

At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on issues ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.

In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a plan to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.

HSBC's biggest shareholder reignites debate about breaking up the bank

Tucker said the board was unanimous in its opposition to the resolution, stating plainly: “It would not be in your interest to split the bank.”

He said the board had previously reviewed a range of options for restructuring the bank, and concluded that such alternatives would “materially destroy value for shareholders,” including dividends.

“Our strategy is working,” Tucker told the room of more than 1,000 shareholders. “Our current strategy is moving dividends up.”

HSBC has been facing calls to separate its Asian business from the rest of the bank over the past year.

Shareholders in Hong Kong — where HSBC is a mainstay of many retail investors’ portfolios — contend that the London-based lender’s performance has been dragged down by its businesses in other regions.

Quinn addressed those complaints head-on Monday, saying “our profits in Hong Kong and the UK are no longer being dragged down by underperformance elsewhere. The group is performing well as a whole.”

Pressed later by a shareholder on the issue, Quinn said a breakup of the bank would result in “significant revenue loss” because much of its business relied on cross-border transactions.

Investors have also been unhappy with HSBC scrapping its dividend in 2020, at the request of British regulators. They argue that if the lender cordoned off its activities in Asia, it would no longer have to expose Hong Kong shareholders to requests in other jurisdictions.

Christine Fong, a district council member in Hong Kong, said she represented about 500 small shareholders who had been affected by the dividend cancellation.

“Street hawkers, taxi drivers or teachers — they all relied on the dividend to pay for their regular expenses, like mortgage, insurance payments, school fees,” Fong told CNN.

“That’s why, three years ago, what HSBC did upset those small minority shareholders.”

Fong has now joined calls for shareholders to vote in favor of the proposal for the bank to spin off its Asian business, despite the lender bringing back its dividend in 2021, albeit at a lower level.

Ken Lui, an activist shareholder in Hong Kong who put the resolution together, doubled down on his call for support ahead of the meeting Monday.

The resolution will require 75% of votes to be passed in May, but “nothing is impossible,” he told reporters outside the meeting venue.

Lui, who said he personally held a stake worth 100 million Hong Kong dollars ($12.7 million), laid out plans for his team to focus on “targeted outreach to institutional shareholders to present our case and gain their support.”

His group will also canvass 18 districts of Hong Kong “to tell HSBC shareholders that they finally have a chance to speak for themselves and protect their rights through voting,” he added.

HSBC is also facing pressure from its largest shareholder.

Ping An (PNGAY), China’s biggest insurer, holds an 8% stake in HSBC and has backed calls for the bank to rethink its structure.

In a series of remarks made public by the Chinese firm last November, Huang Yong, chairman of Ping An’s asset management arm, said “we will support any initiatives including a spinoff that are conducive to improve HSBC’s performance and value.”

Since then, the insurance giant’s views haven’t changed, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The source told CNN that Ping An has been calling for HSBC to explore a reorganization, with an eye on boosting its valuation and simplifying its regulatory obligations around the globe.

The insurer has not recommended a specific path forward but will support any initiatives, including a spinoff of its Asian business, that could boost its stock performance or value, the person added. Ping An did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how it planned to vote at the upcoming general meeting.

HSBC’s leaders were also asked Monfday why the bank had scooped up the British unit of SVB following the stunning collapse of its parent in the United States. The purchase was made for £1 ($1.20) last month, just days after SVB had folded.

Critics have questioned HSBC’s ability to perform adequate due diligence on SVB UK’s customers because of how quickly the deal came together.

“Did HSBC look into the clients of SVB in detail? Say, the financial statement — whether they can pay back the loan?” said Fong.

HSBC buys SVB's UK business, ending 'nightmare' for British tech

Quinn and Tucker defended the acquisition, calling it a good business opportunity that allowed the bank to gain hundreds of innovative startups as customers. They pushed back on the notion that management hadn’t had time to carry out proper due diligence.

Tucker also weighed in on recent tumult in the banking industry, saying he did not expect an “immediate impact” on HSBC.

“After the collapse of a number of smaller regional banks and the takeover of Credit Suisse, the share prices of all banks have been suppressed,” he noted.

But he said he did not believe such developments represented “a systemic risk” to the sector. “I do expect a period of uncertainty” before nerves settle, he added.

#285. 5 ways to get Amazon Prime for free (or way cheaper)

Amazon's free trials are only the beginning.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

It's easy to justify the price of Amazon Prime when you take advantage of Prime Day deals or have a gift delivered tomorrow, just in time. But when you've paid another $14.99 and only bought a USB cable this month, the numbers are not as attractive.

If Prime's sticker price is a no-go for you, you might be able to get away with paying less. You may qualify for six months of Amazon Prime at no cost. There are also discounted Prime plans that cost half as much as a regular monthly membership, or even less. You could also have the option to get Prime through someone in your household, your employer or a benefit bundled with another service.

If you qualify, Amazon's standard 30-day free trial is the simplest way to get Prime at no cost. With this trial period, you'll receive Prime benefits like fast shipping, exclusive discounts on some products, improved Alexa and access to Prime Video, all without having to pay any initial subscription fee. This can be especially useful if you're joining prior to Prime Day or in preparation for the holiday shopping season where a single month of service is enough.

Other plans provide different ways to save. Prime for Young Adults gives eligible new members six months of free service. Afterward, they can choose to pay $7.49 monthly or $69 annually. Eligibility covers adults ages 18 to 24, as well as higher-education students of any age. To qualify, you must provide proof of your age or school enrollment.

Prime Access costs $6.99 per month after a 30-day free trial for eligible new members receiving qualifying government assistance or meeting Amazon's income requirements. It includes all the same perks as the standard Prime membership, and is open to SNAP or Medicaid recipients. Double-check your eligibility, since current Prime members may be able to transition to the discounted membership.

Also, the program limits who can participate. In October 2025, Amazon ended its Prime Invitee program, which previously allowed members to share free shipping with people outside their household. Friends at another address can no longer receive your free shipping benefit through that program. Note that free trial and Prime for Young Adults members cannot share their Prime benefits through Amazon Family.

Free Prime memberships are available to eligible US employees at Amazon, while Whole Foods announced that its hourly workers will receive the same benefit beginning January 1, 2027. If you work for either company, checking your benefits could save you from paying for Prime twice.

Metro by T-Mobile began bundling Prime with select plans in 2018, but stopped offering the perk to new customers on September 17, 2026. Eligible legacy customers can still keep it, so before you switch carriers or make adjustments to your plan, check what your existing setup includes. You could potentially lose out on a free membership if you change.

Existing Navy Federal Visa Signature Flagship Rewards cardholders receive a $139 statement credit toward an annual Amazon Prime membership paid with the card, but that's no longer open to new applicants. It's been replaced by the newer Flagship Premier card, which offers a $100 airline credit instead.

If you have the Flagship Rewards card, be aware that the annual fee increased from $49 to $95 on November 2, 2026. After that, the net annual savings from the Prime credit will be $44 if you count no other card benefits. According to Navy Federal, it may take six to eight weeks for the statement credit to appear on your account.

There are other offbeat methods to getting a lower-cost Prime subscription. Programs like Microsoft Rewards give you points that you can redeem toward gift cards, including Amazon gift cards to put towards Prime. If you're a frequent Amazon shopper, the Amazon Prime Visa grants five percent back on all Amazon purchases with Prime, which can help cover the cost of a subscription. And low-income customers who qualify for Spectrum's Internet Assist plan can get Amazon Prime for no extra cost.

#284. How to know if a USB-C cable is waterproof

Always check the IP rating when purchasing a waterproof USB-C cable

Some USB-C cables are waterproof, but you need to learn to recognize which ones. Widely available from online retailers, including Amazon, they're likely to feature seals to protect the connection and ship in a variety of types, including male, female, and angled cables. But do the seals work? The International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) has developed the IEC 60529 standard, a globally accepted Ingress Protection code that shows how well an enclosure (such as a USB-C plug) resists solids and liquids.

The first number in this code represents dust protection, while the second shows water protection. Under this code, waterproof USB-C cables should have an IP67 or IP68 rating. These cables are most frequently used in specific tough environments, such as manufacturing, construction, maritime and electric vehicle charging systems — anywhere exposed to water, weather or accident. When choosing a cable, what matters most is the IP rating (even for other gadgets, like your phone):

The USB-C standard does not specify water resistance, which means that while ordinary cables may survive a splash, nothing is guaranteed and water exposure comes with some risks. USB-C is versatile, ubiquitous and complex. Take a connector apart, and you'll find it contains 24 contacts, which may connect to data or power wires inside the cable. (That's 20 more pins than found in USB-A, which helps account for the faster data transfers.) If water gets inside the connector, it can cause a short circuit that may damage your equipment, while long-term moisture exposure can corrode contacts. There's also the risk that short-circuited wet cables can overheat, potentially causing a fire. You should never plug a wet cable — even a waterproof one — into a device.

USB cable protection is usually achieved with a silicone rubber seal, gasket, or locking collar around the connector to protect against water ingress. Some rely on threaded bayonet couplings, with a rubber seal that compresses as the collar is tightened, creating a watertight link. Cables designed for extended water exposure may use a tough synthetic rubber, such as neoprene. An even tougher material called fluoroelastomer (FKM) is frequently used where chemical or solvent resistance is required.

If the contacts show no corrosion, you can generally use the cable safely again once it dries. To dry a cable, unplug it, shake the connector ends to force water out, and let it dry for 24 to 48 hours. Don't try to dry the cable with a hair dryer, as the heat can damage the cable, and don't use rice, as it can introduce grit and dust into the connector. If a cable becomes hot when using it after drying, replace it.

Brands of waterproof cables, such as Atlavox, Yale, and the more industrial-grade L-Com, are available at good DIY/tech retailers and also at Amazon. You should ensure the cable you choose is IP-rated, rather than simply being water resistant. Basic waterproof cables are available for around ten dollars, while ultra-rugged waterproof cables for the toughest environments can cost ten times that. Finally, when purchasing one of these cables, you should always check the official IP rating, as a cable that doesn't provide this may not deliver what you need.

#283. Flesh-eating screwworms spread to third state and are attacking pets

USDA has identified 74 animal cases in US since parasitic flies invaded in June.

For a genuine fright this Halloween, you can turn your gaze to the southern border, where ravenous, flesh-eating maggots are festering and have taken to eating people’s pets.

This week, the country’s New World Screwworm (NWS) infestation spread to a third state, Arizona, which joins New Mexico and Texas in being plagued by the horrifying parasites. To date, 74 animal cases have been identified in the US since the flies re-invaded the country in June.

The flies lay hundreds of eggs in wounds and moist orifices of animals, and the resulting voracious maggots feast on their victims. The maggots resemble screws and tortuously bore and twist into living flesh, causing severe, sometimes fatal wounds before dropping to the ground to develop into adults.

Because of their ability to ravage livestock, the flies were eliminated from the country in the 1960s through aerial releases of sterile male flies, which thwart successful breeding. For years, they were held at bay using a biological barrier along the Darién Gap at the border of Panama and Colombia. But the barrier was breached in 2022, and the flies have made their way back to the US through Central America.

While they are largely seen as a threat to the livestock industry, they can also devastate wildlife, domestic pets, and in rarer cases, humans. According to the latest data from Mexico’s Ministry of Health, the country has confirmed 806 cases of human screwworm infestations since the flies reemerged. Nine people died from the savage maggots.

In the US, most of the 74 confirmed cases have been in livestock. But some of the cases have been in domestic pets, mainly dogs. Just this week, the US Department of Agriculture recorded four new cases in domestic dogs—which includes the new detection in Arizona—as well as a domestic cat in New Mexico. That brings the pet total to 10 cases since the flies reemerged. The US has also detected one case in a wild elk, which was reported last week.

Arizona’s agriculture department said this week that the state’s index case was identified in a dog in Cochise County, which borders both New Mexico and Mexico. A local veterinarian examined the poor pup on October 26 and found a wound on the canine’s back that was “heavily infested with maggots consistent with NWS characteristics.”

“We remain prepared and vigilant, and we urge all livestock owners, pet owners, and other animal industry partners to continue to monitor animals closely and report any unusual wounds consistent with NWS immediately,” the state said in an announcement.

The USDA confirmed the infection and said it was working closely with Arizona on a joint response to the expanded infestation.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#282. Ceramic vs Titanium Apple Watch: Which material is better for overall durability?

Ceramic and titanium are both premium Apple Watch materials, but they excel in different ways.

Comparing Apple Watch casing materials, specifically titanium and ceramic, comes with varying degrees of counter-intuition. For one, titanium models feature ceramic components. Second, ceramic is harder than titanium, though titanium is the stronger material overall. There is a winner, but winning comes with caveats. Titanium is the better choice for consumers shopping primarily for long-lasting durability, but it's not as scratch-resistant as ceramic. As you can see, the comparison is a bit more complicated than the general assumption that titanium is the superior material.

In terms of abundance, titanium is the most practical premium option, since Apple hasn't manufactured a primarily ceramic Apple Watch casing since the Apple Watch Series 5. With the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple is bringing back the ceramic option (Pearl White and Midnight Blue), but that leaves ceramic several generations behind in terms of abundant, recent-generation availability.

Both the ceramic and titanium Series 12 models feature a sapphire crystal front, so there's no separation there. But the case itself is a different matter. Ceramic is the better option for buyers who hate scratch buildup on their watch casings and want that gleaming, glossy surface for the long term. Titanium is the best bet for those who tend to walk into doorframes and drop delicate items. You know who you are (author included). Plus, the titanium option is noticeably lighter at 44.9 grams versus the ceramic version's 51.3 grams.

Apple Watches are fairly sizable, so more surface area is visible and exposed. Ceramic is the optimal choice if you care more about a pristine-looking case. Ceramic is exceptionally resistant to surface scratching and is the better option for office wear, formal occasions, or for anyone whose primary cosmetic concern is light scuffing now and then.

Hardness and scratch-resistance don't mean invulnerability, however. In fact, it's the hardness of the material that increases its impact liability. Titanium's tolerance of sharp, concentrated impacts makes it the safer watch for highly active Apple Watch enthusiasts. Apple heavily markets the health and fitness aspects of the Apple Watch, naturally drawing in people with active lifestyles or jobs. A welder will be much better off with titanium, while a hair stylist will get along fine with ceramic.

It makes for an interesting choice at the end of the day. Sure, titanium is tougher overall, but ceramic tends to maintain that premium finish. Nobody wants to wear an ugly watch, especially not one that retails at $399 for the lowest tier. At the same time, that exceptional ceramic vibe is more vulnerable to something as simple as knocking an arm against a metal doorframe.

Even if we toss aluminum into the mix, titanium still wins the overall durability matchup. It simply has the best balance of resistance and lighter weight. Ceramic is the scratch-resistant option, which will carry more weight for some. Apple also makes an aluminum Apple Watch, and it's a practical alternative mostly in terms of lower weight and cost. The 46mm aluminum Series 12 weighs 39.5 grams, lighter than its ceramic and titanium counterparts.

The aluminum version lacks the sapphire crystal screen, instead featuring a ceramic-covered Ion-X glass that Apple claims is 60 percent tougher than its earlier Ion-X iterations. Unfortunately, aluminum is susceptible to dents and cosmetic scratches, and its display glass is more vulnerable, despite the fanciful name. Still, if you're looking for a budget option that still looks great and offers all the same options, it's a prudent choice.

At the end of the day, no Apple Watch is indestructible. There is no adamantium resource for Apple to exploit. A protective case can reduce the risk of damage if you're inclined to purchase one separately, but it will add bulk and obscure that premium finish you paid for. Regardless of the winner, Apple manufactures strong watches, but you'll want titanium for resilience, ceramic for long-term polish, and aluminum for a lightweight, less expensive option.

#281. France opens attempted murder probe after protest attack

Paris prosecutors have opened an attempted murder investigation after a Molotov attack on police. France reported 779 arrests during nationwide protests and Halloween night, fewer than on previous weekends.

Paris prosecutors opened an attempted murder investigation Sunday after a Molotov cocktail was thrown at security forces during a demonstration in the French capital.

Prosecutors said explosive projectiles targeted about 15 gendarmes as well as police officers. No suspects have been arrested over the attack, and investigators were still establishing the number and severity of injuries.

The attack took place at Porte de Charenton, where Saturday's march ended. Photographs and video from the AFP news agency showed an incendiary device exploding at a gendarme's feet and setting his protective equipment alight.

Prosecutors said reported injuries included second-degree burns and tinnitus, although those details remained provisional. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez described the attack as an attempted murder.

The Interior Ministry reported 779 arrests nationwide during the demonstrations and Halloween night. The figure includes both events, updating Saturday evening's provisional total of 565. Authorities said the later part of the night passed without major incidents.

Paris prosecutors separately reported 105 arrests in the capital: 88 linked to the demonstrations and 17 to Halloween night. They said 89 people remained in custody, including at least 22 minors.

The protests focused on high living costs and government policies. The ministry put nationwide turnout at 320,000, while unions estimated nearly 500,000 participants.

The nationwide arrest total was below the 1,314 recorded during the previous Saturday's mobilization and the 2,628 on October 17, when widespread rioting and looting broke out. Authorities had increased security ahead of Halloween amid online calls for violence.

#279. Once again, NASA is asking for ideas to rescue Hubble from certain death

The space agency solicited ideas for reboosting Hubble four years ago, but they didn’t go anywhere.

The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century.

NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope’s orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction.

The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or conduct a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies’ current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope’s performance, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry.

“The requirement includes that the boost and/or servicing mission must not harm the HST and that this mission is expected to occur by 2032,” NASA wrote in the RFI. The contractor would be responsible for providing the launch vehicle, servicing spacecraft, mission operations, and “crew if applicable.”

NASA is not committing to buying a Hubble rescue mission, but officials want to know who might be interested in mounting such a mission, how much it would cost, and which companies would have a realistic shot at reaching Hubble before it falls out of orbit and burns up on reentry. Orbital dynamicists currently predict that it will likely happen in 2033 or 2034 without intervention, but reentry forecasts can change based on solar activity.

It took 24 years for Hubble, which lacks onboard propulsion, to glide from its 2002 altitude of 362 miles (583 km) to its current orbit some 292 miles (470 km) above Earth. A reboost to NASA’s requirement of 373 miles (600 km) would likely keep Hubble in orbit for at least 25 more years.

You’ll be forgiven if you’ve heard this before. Jared Isaacman, a billionaire commercial astronaut, approached NASA in 2022 about a servicing mission to Hubble with a team of astronauts on SpaceX’s Dragon spacecraft. He proposed funding most of the mission, which would have reboosted Hubble by at least 30 miles (50 km). Engineers also studied using Dragon to attach a rescue pod onto Hubble with new gyroscopes to overcome problems with the telescope’s debilitated pointing system.

NASA also released an RFI in 2022 for other teams to share how they might boost Hubble’s orbit. The agency received eight responses, including a joint robotic reboost proposal from Astroscale and Momentus to pair their satellite servicing technology and in-space transport capabilities.

Agency officials announced in 2024 they would not pursue a reboost mission after reviewing the responses. Mark Clampin, the head of NASA’s astrophysics division at the time, said the servicing plans from Isaacman and SpaceX “were really just notional concepts.”

Fast forward to 2026. Isaacman is now NASA administrator, and the satellite servicing industry is maturing. Northrop Grumman launched the world’s most sophisticated robotic servicing satellite earlier this year in a partnership with DARPA, the Pentagon’s research and development agency. Smaller startups like Astroscale and Starfish Space have contracts for servicing and refueling demos with the US Space Force and NASA.

So it’s not unrealistic to think the commercial industry could reboost and service Hubble by 2032, given enough time and resources. That was one of the lessons learned from NASA’s last-minute bid to rescue one of its smaller space telescopes, named Swift, from an impending reentry.

NASA awarded a $30 million contract to a startup named Katalyst Space Technologies last year and gave the company just nine months to develop a mission to fly up to Swift, grab onto it, and propel it to a higher orbit, extending its useful lifetime. Remarkably, Katalyst built a rescue satellite and launched it by the deadline and got within about 6 miles (10 km) of Swift. Ground teams decided not to move closer after problems with Katalyst’s power and reaction-control systems.

The Swift rescue attempt showed a servicing mission doesn’t need to cost billions of dollars, as one of NASA’s now-canceled servicing demo projects was predicted to cost. But Hubble is a significantly more expensive asset than Swift, so if NASA goes forward with a rescue mission, the agency would like to give a contractor more than $30 million and nine months.

NASA does currently not have any funding allocated to procuring a Hubble reboost or servicing mission.

“Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible,” Isaacman said in a NASA statement. “If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the Universe.”

A crewed servicing mission like the one Isaacman envisioned in 2022 is unlikely to happen now. SpaceX aims to retire its Crew Dragon fleet by 2030. In a post on X, Isaacman wrote that he expects the new RFI will “draw interest from robotics companies.”

NASA’s newer flagship observatories, sometimes described as successors to Hubble, are not actually one-for-one replacements. Hubble is tuned to observe the Universe in visible and ultraviolet light, while the Webb and Roman telescopes peer deeper into the infrared Universe. Astronomers will likely have to wait for the launch of NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory in the 2040s for an improvement on Hubble’s visible and ultraviolet vision.

“Commercial industry has rapidly evolved in recent years to offer new capabilities for in-space satellite capture and servicing,” said Nicky Fox, NASA’s associate administrator for science. “Given the time we have until Hubble’s anticipated reentry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow.”

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#278. Which Samsung S Pens can be located using SmartThings Find?

Your Galaxy phone might warn you about a missing S Pen but finding it is a different story.

Leave your Galaxy S26 Ultra's S Pen in an office meeting room and the phone can warn you it hasn't been returned to its slot. That's useful until you realize that it can't tell you where inside the room it might be. The warning isn't a tracking feature, just a reminder.

Samsung retired the Galaxy Note series, but its S Pen lives on. The company introduced S Pen support to the Galaxy S21 Ultra in 2021 and added a built-in S Pen slot to the S22 Ultra a year later. The S Pen name has been used for a variety of pens, ranging from battery-free pens on older Galaxy Note phones to Bluetooth-enabled pens and larger styli for tablets and foldables. However, only one is officially compatible with SmartThings Find.

The S Pen Pro is the one you're looking for. Samsung unveiled it with the Galaxy S21 Ultra in January 2021, then released it alongside the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Z Flip 3 that August (only the Fold 3 supports it). Compatible phones also include the Note 10 and Note 20 series, Galaxy S21 Ultra through S26 Ultra and Z Fold 4 through Z Fold 6.

Sold separately for $100, it's a larger, rechargeable stylus with a USB-C port under its cap, a dedicated pairing button and a switch for compatible Galaxy devices. It's also the only S Pen Samsung officially supports for tracking via SmartThings Find. There's one problem, however: it won't fit in the Galaxy S26 Ultra's built-in pen slot, which isn't exactly convenient for something you're worried about losing.

Bluetooth doesn't guarantee tracking functionality, either. In 2018, Samsung added a Bluetooth-enabled S Pen to the Galaxy Note 9, letting users remotely activate the camera and control some apps. Similar capabilities were carried over to later Note models and the Galaxy S22, S23 and S24 Ultra. However, none of their built-in S Pens can be found via SmartThings Find.

Samsung removed Bluetooth from the S25 Ultra's S Pen and the S26 Ultra was the same. Tablet owners also face variations. Some Galaxy Tab S Pens support Air Actions via Bluetooth, while others, such as the pen on the Tab S9 FE, don't. The S Pen Fold Edition and Creator Edition also lack Bluetooth, so neither supports SmartThings Find. Bluetooth support alone doesn't make an S Pen trackable, and Samsung's naming conventions don't make that distinction especially clear.

To prepare the S Pen Pro for tracking, charge it, select the appropriate mode and hold its Connection button for three seconds. Tap Connect when prompted and make sure you're signed in to your Samsung account.

Next, open SmartThings, head to Life > Find and open the three-dot menu. Select Settings > Allow devices to be found and enable Offline finding. Offline finding needs to be enabled first, so you'll want to do this before losing the pen, obviously.

1. Open SmartThings > Life > Find and select the S Pen Pro, swiping between device cards or opening the device menu if needed. 2. Tap Refresh to update its location on the map. 3. Select More > Navigate for directions, or swipe up on the pen's details to access Navigate and Blink light, which flashes its indicator when searching nearby.

The separate Samsung Find app also lists the S Pen Pro under its Devices tab.

For other S Pens, refer to Settings > Advanced features > S Pen > More S Pen settings > Warn if S Pen is left behind (if available). As I mentioned earlier, the S26 Ultra can notify you if the pen is not placed in its slot for a while after the display is turned off. It won't pinpoint the pen's location, but a warning before you've gone too far could save you some searching.

If the pen is gone for good, make sure that the replacement pen you buy is compatible with your device. Samsung currently lists a replacement Galaxy S26 Ultra S Pen for $55 in the US.

#277. How to clean your PlayStation 5 without damaging it

There’s no need to tear down your PlayStation 5 to do a basic maintenance cleaning, but you shouldn't neglect this either.

Cleaning a PlayStation 5 isn't as exciting as playing its best games, but it's important to do on occasion. With PlayStation 5 prices climbing, you don't want to suddenly be in the market for a new console because of a total lack of maintenance. Dust buildup in the system restricts airflow and makes your system work harder to cool itself. But overzealous cleaning can be dangerous, too.

When cleaning your PS5, it's best to keep it simple and only go deeper if needed. Never start right after using the system. Prepare it for its dust exorcism by shutting it down, unplugging all cables and letting it cool before setting it on a flat, clean surface. To start, wipe off the outside surfaces to remove any dust or grit visible from the exterior. Don't use bleach or chemically treated cloths, and you shouldn't be excessively forceful while cleaning. Just give it a modest wipe-down with a clean, soft cloth, as Sony advises in its safety guide [PDF].

While you may see people recommending rubbing alcohol and other cleaners, be aware that a PS5's internal and external components include ABS, polycarbonate (PC) and a blend called PC-ABS. Each has its own chemical vulnerabilities. Sony specifically recommends against using alcohol, as it may discolor the system or degrade its materials.

A lot of this stage is focused on the outside vents. You can vacuum them if needed, but stick with a small handheld vacuum or a compressed air and vacuum combo. Don't use something heavy-duty like an industrial shop vac. Take your time and use a cotton swab to catch any dust the vacuum won't grab. A soft brush (an old toothbrush works) is helpful for scraping off caked-on dirt.

In the next step, you'll handle anything you can't reach from the outside.

Once you're done with the exterior cleaning, it's time to take off the covers for a more comprehensive cleaning. These are designed to be removed, but they're fairly flimsy, so take it slow. The way to do this differs depending on whether you have an original PS5 or a Slim/Pro system. See Sony's instructions for removing the covers for illustration.

With the covers removed and set to the side, use the same microfiber cloth and handheld vacuum to catch any accessible trapped dust. You don't have to disconnect the fan or remove any internal screws; just get what you can access on both sides. If you use canned air, be careful not to spin the fan, which can generate an electric charge that damages the system. Use a cotton swab to jam the fan blades before blowing towards it. Look for the triangular "dust catcher" spots, which Sony specifically designed to gather debris for removal.

If you want to go deeper, you're able to, but you run the risk of damaging internal components and Sony's warranty excludes damage caused by unauthorized opening or work inside the PS5. Beyond pulling the covers and cleaning what's accessible there, proceed at your own risk. You'll need a TR8 Torx Security screwdriver to remove the fan screws.

When you're done, reverse the earlier process to reinstall the covers, then reattach the stand before you reconnect the console and set everything back up again. Failing to reconnect the covers properly could result in problems with airflow, potentially shortening the life of your PlayStation 5, so make sure they are aligned and connected correctly.

Using your system in either vertical or horizontal placement is perfectly fine, since the console is designed for both. Just make sure you use the stand, no matter which orientation you decide on. You can technically position the console vertically without a stand, but it's much easier to tip over and being on the ground makes it more susceptible to dust.

The original PS5 comes with an adjustable base that works in both positions, but the PS5 Slim and PS5 Pro only come with horizontal stands; vertical stands are sold separately for $30. Cleaning out dust optimizes the console's ability to circulate air, but all that work isn't as effective if you place the console improperly.

Make sure there's at least four inches of space between the console and walls, preferably with nothing overhead. Don't place the console in a cramped space like the inside of an entertainment center. It's also wise to clean the area where your console spends most of its time. Wipe down the dust and vacuum the space well so you don't have to open your system for cleaning as often.

#275. This is the right way to clean your vinyl records

The answer depends on your budget — and how hardcore you want to get.

There's no one right way to clean a record. If anything, there's a different answer for every budget — and even then, 10 enthusiasts might give you 10 different answers. No matter your situation, though, some TLC for your vinyl collection is better than none.

Most record crackles come from dirt and debris. Dust sits on the surface and is the easiest to clean. "Grime," for lack of a better term, settles into the grooves and is harder to remove. And then there are scratches, which are a different problem altogether. Unfortunately, nothing will fix them. Such is life with vinyl.

For regular maintenance, a carbon fiber brush is one of the easiest places to start. Rest it lightly on a spinning record for a few turns, then sweep it off toward the edge. This won't do much if your record needs a deep cleaning, but it keeps the loose dust from piling up.

An air duster, whether canned or electric, is another option to blow off surface dust. If you use the canned variety, be sure to hold it upright so it doesn't spray propellant. And keep all air blowers away from the record player's needle.

As their name suggests, anti-static guns are indeed handy for static, which can attract dust. Keep in mind that they won't remove dirt; they just make it harder for dust to stick to the record in the first place.

Don't neglect your needle, either. It's worth buying a small stylus brush, which you move gently from back to front to clean your needle. Stylus cleaner gel is another option: lower the needle onto the sticky pad, repeating a few times until the tip is clean.

Wet cleaning is the next step up. Whether that means hand-washing a record or using a machine, this approach is much better than brushing at removing dirt that's sunk deep into the grooves.

Fluid made for records from reputable companies is a simple and cheap option. Spray the liquid on a soft brush or pad rather than straight onto the record, move in circles along the grooves and avoid wetting the label. Some do this while the record is spinning, which would be convenient if not for the risks: It can strain the turntable motor and get liquid on the player. It's safer to do it by hand, even if it takes a little longer.

Diluted alcohol shows up in plenty of commercial record fluids and tends to be fine for brief contact with vinyl. You can make your own with isopropyl alcohol-based cleaner, but it's often stronger than you need, so mix about two to three parts distilled water with one part alcohol. You can add a drop of plain, unscented dish soap to the mix, too. Just be sure to rinse with distilled water afterward to avoid residue. No matter what, don't let alcohol go anywhere near old 78s, as it can dissolve the shellac and damage the record.

If you're willing to spend around $80 to $125, a record washer like the Spin-Clean (or a similar model from a reputable competitor) can be a worthwhile investment for your vinyl collection. There's nothing too complicated about its design: put cleaning fluid and distilled water in the reservoir, place your record between the brushes, and give it a good spin. The machine cleans both sides of the record at once while avoiding the label. Change the fluid often, especially when it turns cloudy. The Spin-Clean also includes drying cloths.

No matter which method you choose, don't use just any cloth for drying. Stick to microfiber, and never machine-dry it; air-dry instead, since a dryer can leave lint and fibers on the cloth. Also, avoid fabric softener when washing them. After wiping, set your records on a cheap dish rack to dry completely before they go back in the sleeve or on your turntable.

Casual vinyl collectors will be fine with everything we've already covered. But if you're willing to spend real money, ultrasonic cleaning is the gold standard. Instead of scrubbing, these machines dip the record in a bath and use high-frequency sound waves to create tiny bubbles that burst against the record. That loosens stubborn grime from the bottom of the grooves, going much deeper than a brush or standard wet-cleaning can reach.

The big drawback is the price. The cheapest ultrasonic cleaning machines start at over $100 and require a lot of setup. All-in-one machines like the HumminGuru, which spin, clean and dry the record, start at several hundred dollars. Premium models like the Degritter climb well into the thousands.

Vacuum record-cleaning machines, like the Record Doctor VI (around $350), are another premium option. You scrub the record with fluid, then the machine sucks it back out of the grooves for you, which is a big step up from wet-wiping. If you're forking over that much money, though, ultrasonic is generally more thorough. And if you already own a wet-dry shop vac, there there is a budget option: the $30 Vinyl Vac wand is an attachment that gets you into the vacuum game without spending much.

But before you dive into these premium options, take a step back and ask how serious you want to get about your collection. Unless you're all in and have money to spare, a Spin-Clean is a more modest investment that will still get most of the job done.

Not all vinyl maintenance advice you read is useful. Avoid wiping records with Windex or other household cleaners, as they can leave residue. Ditto for paper towels, as they can shed lint. Skip tap water, which can leave mineral deposits in the grooves; distilled water is your friend.

How you handle records can matter as much as your cleaning method. Hold them by the edges and label, and keep them away from the sunlight and heat. Store them upright in polyethylene or poly-lined paper sleeves. And after a cleaning, it's worth using a new inner sleeve, since the old one can put dirt right back on the record.

Beyond that, some wear and tear will be out of your control. Try embracing the mindset that the imperfections are inevitable and interesting. Nobody wants to scratch or damage their prized records, but a little surface crackle is part of the charm.

The head of Serbia's criminal police directorate has been arrested and charged with abuse of office, state media reported on Sunday.

Marko Kricak is accused of suppressing and manipulating an investigation into the murder in May of a suspected criminal underworld figure in a Belgrade restaurant.

The 42-year-old was seen as a supporter of defeated Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, whose right-wing populist camp was defeated by the opposition Student List in parliamentary elections on October 25.
