#273. How using one earbud more than the other can cause uneven wear and tear

For the sake of your earbuds' health, you may want to curb the habit.

Back in the day, some of you might remember the popular gadget known as a Bluetooth headset or earpiece. It's not a pair of wireless headphones with a mic attachment or one of the best gaming headsets, as the term more commonly describes today. It was a single bud, sometimes with a tiny boom mic, that wrapped around and sat on or was positioned in your ear. The purpose was to make it easier to take hands-free calls without completely blocking out the world around you. You would see businesspeople walking around with these all over, some wearing them all day as a sign of prestige (and maybe a bit of self-importance). They were eventually replaced with wireless earbuds that can work in mono mode, meaning you can place one bud in your ear and use it the same way. But doing so all the time is not necessarily a good idea.

Using one earbud more than the other can create an uneven usability balance, which can lead to quicker wear and tear on the one bud you use most often. Beyond that, charging cycles are limited with devices, and when you need to charge one bud more often than the other, it is more likely to drain faster. It's important to understand how this works and what you can do to avoid issues while still being able to talk hands-free.

As noted, wearing one earbud more means it goes through more battery cycles than the other. Even though they both charge in the same case, if one bud is at 50% and the other at 80%, it will logically take longer and more power to recharge the one with less battery life. While the simple solution is to alternate buds, some wireless earbuds use a master/slave setup where one bud offers the primary connection to the phone and transmits data to the other. In these cases, only the master bud can be used in mono mode, so you don't have that option. That said, most newer earbuds outside of some cheaper entry-level models support mono playback from either bud thanks to the role-swapping design. This includes some of the best wireless earbuds, such as the Samsung Galaxy Buds and Google Pixel Buds. So, if you are set on wearing just one, it's best to go with a model like this and switch to even out the imbalance.

But note as well that wearing just one bud often for things like phone calls consumes more power, as does the Bluetooth transmission process. This means its battery per use, as well as overall battery, will drain more quickly. Removing one bud more often from the case can also cause charging imbalances, which can further impact battery wear. When you want to listen with both buds, you may find that the bud you use more often dies before the other, resulting in forced mono mode. With master/slave buds, this means you won't be able to listen at all.

The best way to avoid these issues is to stop wearing just a single bud. Doing so is useful for taking a quick call every now and then, or maybe for listening to a translation of a lecture or meeting in one ear. But try to limit how often you do it. If the reason is that you still want to be aware of your surroundings, consider a pair of wireless earbuds that have transparency or ambient mode. Activate this mode to let in ambient sounds to hear the waitress coming by the table, talk to a friend, hear a pilot announcement on a plane, or simply be more aware of your surroundings, even with both ears plugged. Some can even switch to this mode automatically when they detect voices.

Some people like to wear a single bud while driving, the legality of which varies by state and location. Rather than doing this, use the speakerphone function of your phone, potentially through a system like Apple CarPlay or Android Auto. If you want to take private calls while others are in the vehicle, consider buying one of those old single-bud Bluetooth headsets or using an old pair of buds you have lying around that you aren't as worried about causing an imbalance.

If you're stuck on using only one bud often, you can still find single Bluetooth earpieces from brands such as Poly and BlueParrott, though these are mostly designed for professional use and are much bigger than the ones from decades past. Otherwise, limit single-bud usage to only when necessary and use a pair with role-swapping and switching. Or, better yet, find a set with transparency mode and rely on that while wearing both buds.

#272. AI glasses can replace your prescription glasses, but should they?

AI glasses have a lot of benefits, but they're still not the best option for everyday glasses.

Most of these AI-powered smart glasses are essentially regular glasses with extra tech built into them. From the outside, most of them look just like any other pair of glasses — if you look at a pair of Ray-Ban Meta from a distance, you probably couldn't tell they're smart glasses. Because they look so much like regular glasses, their lenses can also be replaced with prescription lenses. Ray-Ban lets you order a pair of Meta's smart glasses with prescription lenses already installed — all you have to do is upload your prescription, and they'll take care of the rest.

But there are other things you should consider, such as weight. Regular glasses usually weigh between 20 and 30 grams (0.7 to 1.1 ounces), but smart glasses can weigh up to 80 grams (2.7 ounces). Wearing a pair of these for a few hours is fine, but you start to feel the weight when you wear them all day long. Battery life can be an issue, too. AI glasses last an average of 3 to 5 hours before the battery dies. That's fine if you only use them occasionally, but wearing them all day will require you to constantly recharge the battery. They'll still work as regular glasses, but you'll lose all the AI features. The technical limitations alone make them more of a second option than a replacement for your everyday glasses.

There have also been many reports of AI glasses being banned from corporate environments. Usually, the camera is the main concern, but even if you don't turn it on, audio can be a problem, too. A simple real-time translation feature could end up uploading confidential conversations to a third-party server. Meta, for example, has been facing scrutiny for allowing outsourced workers to access intimate images and videos captured by its AI smart glasses. The company claims that the content is sometimes reviewed by humans for the purpose of improving the product experience.

Then there's the social aspect, which has led some people to decide to stop wearing AI glasses in public — the Meta Glasses backlash is changing how people use them. With so many negative stories about them, users have become afraid of being labeled as stalkers or weirdos. So while you can definitely get AI glasses with prescription lenses, they're not yet the best option for your everyday glasses.

#271. 10 iPad widgets you probably didn't realize existed

Basic iPad widgets are great, but there are many more exciting ones to discover.

Many iPad owners never truly grasp the capabilities of widgets. Adding a basic Weather, Calendar or Photos widget is limiting; they can do a lot more than just show the temperature and your next meeting, but many of the most useful ones go unnoticed. With iPadOS 27, Apple even brought extra-large widgets to Today View, giving them more room to take advantage of the bigger screen.

Between Apple's in-house widgets and third-party options, there's something for new iPad owners and power users alike to discover. To explore your available widgets, touch and hold an empty spot on the Home Screen of your iPad, tap Edit and then hit Add Widget. Depending on the app, you may have various options, including different sizes. Then, just place the widget where you desire.

In case you weren't already aware: you can turn an existing app icon into a widget by touching and holding it, then picking a widget size from the menu. However, not all apps support this.

If you're always waiting on a package, Parcel's widget is great for showing upcoming deliveries without opening the app. It supports up to 300 delivery services, including UPS, USPS, FedEx, DHL and Amazon Logistics, and there's also a map widget in different sizes that shows where a package is.

Getting deliveries into the app is easy. By connecting your Amazon account, orders are added automatically, which means no copying and pasting tracking numbers. For everything else, you can scan a shipping label's barcode with the built-in scanner instead of typing out a long tracking number.

Parcel isn't limited to your iPad, either. It has a native Mac app, and you can manage your deliveries from any browser through Parcel's web access, so your packages follow you across devices. The free version can only track three deliveries at a time and doesn't include push notifications. To remove those limits, you'll need a Premium subscription for $6.99/year.

Instead of launching the Home app every time you need to make a quick change, its widget lets you take quick actions like switching lights on/off. It's one of Apple's interactive widgets, meaning it can perform a task without opening the app. It also works for locking and unlocking garage doors, as long as you have a HomeKit-compatible controller.

You have full control over what the widget shows. Simply touch and hold it, tap Edit Widget and pick the accessories and scenes you want it to display. Using this, the bedroom lamp or scene that turns everything off at night stays within reach, while accessories you rarely touch stay out of the way.

The widget works with smart accessories like bulbs, LED strips and smart plugs, and what you can control depends on the accessories you own. It's built for simple on and off actions, though; you still have to open the app to adjust values like brightness and color, or setting the thermostat. For quick toggles from the couch, however, it's much faster than digging through rooms in the app.

This isn't your typical weather forecast widget. (Not Boring) Weather is built around a 3D, video game-inspired design with interactive visuals, giving your Home Screen some character. The widget can show details like temperature, conditions, precipitation, UV index and wind, and it's available for the Lock Screen as well as the Home Screen.

The design is playful and the data comes from established sources like Apple, AccuWeather, Foreca, and the National Weather Service (adjustable in the app's settings menu). It also covers severe weather alerts for heat waves, storms, flood risk, hurricanes and blizzards, so the fun visuals don't come at the expense of safety information.

The Find My widget tracks your Apple devices, AirTags, third-party Find My items and trusted people right on the Home Screen. Each one appears with its last known location, so you can see where your keys or backpack were last spotted without opening the app and waiting for the map to reload. That comes in handy when you're rushing out the door and can't find your keys.

The app behind the widget is more capable than you think. Find My can locate devices even when they're offline or powered off by using the Find My network. This relies on nearby Apple devices to anonymously and securely share their location. You can also turn on Notify When Left Behind, which alerts you if you leave a device somewhere unfamiliar.

Endel creates AI-powered soundscapes to help you focus, relax or sleep, and it adjusts them on the fly to help with your circadian rhythm. Its widgets give you quick access to the app's modes from the Home Screen, so you can start a soundscape in one tap.

This makes Endel's widget especially appreciated on an iPad that doubles as a work or study device. Instead of hunting for a playlist before starting your session, begin a focus soundscape straight from the Home Screen and get to it. All soundscapes are also available offline, so the app keeps working on a flight or anywhere without a reliable internet connection.

The free edition of Endel includes four classic soundscapes: Focus, Sleep, Relax and Move. Each free session is capped to 10 minutes, though you can restart as often as you want. A premium subscription unlocks the rest of the library: Colored Noise with nine colors to choose from, Dynamic Focus, artist collaborations and Spatial Orbit, which is an immersive Spatial Audio experience. The premium tier also adds Focus Timer, which joins Endel's focus sounds with timed work sessions. It's available as a subscription or a one-time lifetime purchase; prices on the website are cheaper than App Store subscriptions, with "special discounts" often available.

Apple's stock Mail widget has more capability than showing your inbox. You have the option for it to display recent unread emails, messages from your VIP list or any other mailbox. Tapping an email in the widget will open that message directly in Mail.

The VIP option suits anyone who primarily cares about emails from a handful of people, like a manager, a client or a child's school. Once those senders are marked as VIPs, their messages sit on your Home Screen instead of getting buried under newsletters and promotions.

Adding someone to your VIP list takes only a few seconds. Open an email from the person in question and tap the header with the sender info. Then tap the sender's name and choose View Contact Card, followed by Add to VIP on the resulting screen. Repeat for everyone whose emails you never want to miss, then all these people will appear up in Mail's VIP mailbox across the widget and app.

If no existing widget looks quite right on your iPad, Widgetsmith lets you design your own. You can craft widgets for the date, time, weather, calendar, reminders and photos, then adjust the fonts, colors and layout to match your Home Screen. It can customize your Lock Screen as well, so both screens share the same aesthetic.

The standout feature of this widget is scheduling. Widgetsmith is able to show different widgets at different times of day, so the same spot on your Home Screen could show the weather in the morning and your calendar during work hours. Recent updates added clear and frosted styles so your wallpaper shows through, plus a photo background that places an image behind a widget.

Widgetsmith also includes a built-in weather tool with air quality, pollen and tide information, though that requires a premium subscription (starting at $1.99 a month).

It's easy to lose an hour to doomscrolling without noticing. To keep an eye on this, the Screen Time widget offers a reality check on the Home Screen or in Today View without having to dig through Settings. The smaller size simply shows your daily total, while the larger option adds a rundown of the apps and categories you've spent time on.

The widget is more useful with iPadOS 27, as it adds Schedules and Time Allowances. Time Allowances put a cap on the amount of time you can spend in categories like Entertainment, Games and Social Media, while Schedules control which apps are available at different times of the day.

This makes the widget particularly helpful for parents setting up an iPad for their kids. A quick glance shows whether the cartoons have run long, and the new limits come in handy to cut off excess usage automatically.

Craft is a docs and planning app in the same vein as Notion, and its widgets go further than most. You can pin a specific document for one-tap access, show a list of Recent Documents, or keep a Tasks widget in view and check off to-dos without opening the app. Lock Screen widgets add shortcuts for quick actions, like creating a document or starting a Quick Entry.

Craft is built around Daily Notes for planning your day, and a dedicated Daily Note widget keeps yesterday's, today's or tomorrow's note a tap away.

If you keep your work and personal notes separate, Craft's widgets respect that. Each widget can be set to a specific Craft Space, so you could keep your work tasks on one widget and personal documents on another. Craft's widgets are also available on iPhone and Mac.

The setup works especially well on iPad, where you can fit multiple Craft widgets side-by-side without crowding the Home Screen. For instance, you might set up a Tasks widget next to a Daily Note widget, making the Home Screen your simple planning dashboard.

The app is free, but there's a premium subscription (available monthly or yearly) that unlocks all features and removes some limits.

Many iPad owners overlook Apple's Journal app. It arrived with iPadOS 26, and is arguably a better fit there than on iPhone, since the bigger screen gives you more room to write and jot down your ideas. On iPad, you can type with the on-screen or a physical keyboard, or handwrite entries and add sketches with an Apple Pencil.

The Journal widget brings that habit to your Home Screen. It can show your current streak or surface writing prompts that change throughout the day, and that small prompt makes it easier to build a journaling habit without hunting for the app. iPadOS 27 added more control over writing streaks, letting you track them daily or weekly.

The app is flexible: you can keep multiple journals for different parts of your life, such as one for travel and another for work purposes. Since journals are personal by nature, you can lock the app with Face ID, Touch ID or your passcode so nobody can read your entries.

#270. The FDA wants to pull its approval of a drug. It’s not so easy.

The regulator says Tavneos was approved on the basis of manipulated study data. Should patients still have access to it?

In May 2021, the US Food and Drug Administration released a lengthy briefing document on an experimental medication for a rare autoimmune form of vasculitis that often damages the kidneys and lungs. The agency was on the fence about whether to approve the treatment, and it wanted an independent advisory committee to weigh in. Among the questions at hand: Was the drug meaningfully better than existing therapies?

Participants in the study, which had been conducted by the California biotechnology company ChemoCentryx, did appear to have slightly higher rates of symptom remission after one year. But according to the FDA, it was hard to interpret the results because the study’s design had been less than optimal. Some advisory committee members expressed a similar view. The effect of the drug, said one, “is just not well verified by this study.”

At the same time, many patients, and some physicians, saw in the data a potentially helpful medication, one that might lessen patients’ reliance on steroids, which are highly effective but often cause severe side effects.

The advisory committee ultimately voted narrowly to recommend approval, and the FDA followed that advice, greenlighting the drug on October 7, 2021. The drug, marketed as Tavneos, started making its way into clinics. A year after approval, ChemoCentryx was acquired by Amgen, one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies. The cost, even today, isn’t minor: $220,000 per year, according to Drugs.com. In fiscal year 2025, sales of Tavneos reached nearly half a billion dollars.

This financial windfall has unfolded despite a long-roiling investor lawsuit—one that incidentally uncovered what the FDA today believes is evidence that ChemoCentryx employees manipulated the data in the pivotal trial submitted to the agency. In April of this year, the FDA issued a letter proposing that Tavneos be withdrawn from the US market, citing reports of serious, sometimes fatal, liver injury, and arguing that the drug now lacks “substantial evidence” that it works.

These revelations have triggered a dramatic cascade of events. This summer, the New England Journal of Medicine retracted a paper describing the clinical trial and Tavneos was taken off the market in the European Union. The United Kingdom has announced that it, too, will remove the product from the market. And on October 29, a court hearing is expected to proceed over Zoom to consider a proposed $69 million settlement for the lawsuit.

But the fate of Tavneos, at least in the United States, is far from sealed. Amgen has pushed back against its critics, insisting that—whatever the details of ChemoCentryx’s data handling—its drug works as advertised and should stay on the market. In July, the company submitted a 104-page document to the FDA stating that “the totality of the evidence supports the continued availability of TAVNEOS.”

Some patients and academic experts also believe the drug is an important treatment option. “This appears to be an efficacious medication,” said Eric Roberts, an epidemiologist at the University of California, San Francisco, who co-authored an independent registry study of Tavneos.

The dispute is emblematic of the FDA’s longstanding struggle to regulate drugs of uncertain efficacy, said Reshma Ramachandran, a physician and co-director of the Yale Collaboration for Regulatory Rigor, Integrity, and Transparency. Absent more rigorous studies, either before or after a drug goes on the market, Ramachandran worries, “we’re just going to be living in uncertainty in terms of whether or not these drugs actually work.”

For American consumers, the saga of Tavneos also raises potent questions around the safeguards in place to ensure the integrity of drug approvals, particularly when a relatively small company conducts the pivotal trial and has so much riding on the success of a single drug.

Chloe Cusano was a 20-year-old college student when she was struck, this past December, with unbearable pain in her legs, as well as bouts of breathlessness from routine tasks like walking upstairs or bending down to retrieve her dog’s water dish. After going to the emergency room, she was hospitalized for more than two weeks, during which she was diagnosed with ANCA-associated vasculitis, or AAV, an umbrella term for a group of rare diseases in which the immune system mistakenly attacks its own blood vessels. When it was first identified, the condition was usually fatal.

Over the past four decades, scientists have developed drugs that allow many AAV patients to live a relatively normal lifespan. Because the disease can rapidly lead to organ failure, particularly of the kidneys and lungs, patients are immediately started on a high dose of steroids to rapidly tamp down inflammation. They also typically receive slower-acting medications that target the underlying disease process.

Steroids, however, have severe side effects. Within a month and a half of going on the steroids, Cusano recalled, she gained 40 pounds. Her emotions were “just like crazy,” swinging from intense sadness to anger. She had trouble falling asleep, and when she did fall asleep, she was haunted by another side effect: nightmares. “I did not like it at all,” she recalls.

AAV patients may need to take steroids for months to years, and Tavneos was supposed to replace or reduce their use.

David Pisetsky, a rheumatologist and researcher at the Duke University School of Medicine, was on the FDA advisory committee that considered the ChemoCentryx trial data. He voted against recommending approval, in part because many patients in the control group received just one round of a slower-acting medication — rituximab — in addition to steroids when, in the real world, they would have received two, according to Pisetsky. The trial’s design, he said, made the results difficult to interpret.

In an editorial in the journal Rheumatology, Mike Putman, medical director of the Vasculitis Program at the Medical College of Wisconsin, and co-authors would later make a similar case: Patients in the comparison group did not receive treatment consistent with the current standard of care. “It is somewhat debate-able about what the ‘standard of care’ would have been” when the study was done, Putman wrote in an email to Undark. “We had not yet established rituximab as maintenance therapy at that point, though most people were already doing that.”

Other members of the advisory committee were persuaded, including Walter Kraft, a clinical pharmacologist and researcher at Thomas Jefferson University. He voted yes to approval. “I felt the evidence, though limited, met the societal and therapeutic goals,” he said during the meeting. Requiring another trial, he added, could delay the drug’s approval by several years.

But that vote, he told Undark in a recent interview, was “based upon an assumption that the sponsor was following the rules of the road.”

These days, a significant number of drugs approved by the FDA start out at a small company with few or no medications on the market, said Sean Nicholson, an economist at Cornell University. Large companies increasingly recognize that their comparative advantage is not in developing breakthrough science, which is more likely to come from “nimble, small startup biotechs,” so rather than trying to compete, Nicholson said, a big company will look to buy or partner with the smaller company.

That’s what happened with ChemoCentryx, which was bought by Amgen for nearly $4 billion one year after the FDA issued its approval of Tavneos.

When bringing a drug to market, small companies face a slightly different set of incentives from large companies, said David Ridley, a health economist at the Duke University Fuqua School of Business. A large company with many products in its pipeline may more readily abandon an experimental drug rather than invest in costly late-stage testing. “Small companies have more to lose,” he wrote in an email to Undark. “The entire company can be at stake. That urgency can drive them to work harder and move faster.”

“In rare cases,” he added, “they might cut corners.”

Back in May 2021, Tavneos’ approval appeared far from certain. Almost immediately after the FDA released its briefing document for the advisory committee meeting, ChemoCentryx’s stock value plummeted, and its shareholders sued for securities fraud.

Four years later, as part of that lawsuit, a report was filed, alleging that ChemoCentryx had not, in fact, followed the rules of the road. The report indicated that the company’s own trial analysis originally found that the patients receiving Tavneos had not achieved better one-year remission rates than the patients who received the usual treatment.

After company employees unblinded the trial data—meaning they looked to see which study participants had actually received the drug and which had received a placebo—they selected a handful of patients whose remission status would be reassessed. This readjudication, as it is called by the FDA, violated the study’s protocol. What’s more, the agency alleges, the patients were cherry-picked to get the results the company needed for approval.

ChemoCentryx did not disclose the original results, nor the fact that it had reassessed the original data, to the FDA.

In December 2025, Tracy Beth Høeg became acting director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, or CDER.

In an email to Undark, Høeg noted that legally, she can’t speak to the specifics of how this issue came to her attention. But, she noted, “One of my key roles as CDER acting director was letting everyone know my door was open, and I encouraged CDER employees to speak openly with me, especially about matters potentially affecting public safety.”

“When I learned of this case,” she continued, “I distinctly remember thinking this story had so much intrigue that it could easily be made into a movie.”

But the repercussions, Høeg argued with unusual candor, are very real. “Essentially ChemoCentryx swindled billions of dollars by developing a drug that gained FDA approval only because they manipulated the data,” she wrote. Since the drug went onto the market, it has been linked to eight deaths and dozens of hospitalizations. “This can be a deadly drug,” wrote Høeg, “and we don’t know if it works.”

Such was the essence of the FDA’s letter sent in April to Amgen, in which the agency proposed to withdraw approval of Tavneos. The retraction of the Tavneos trial data by the New England Journal of Medicine followed two months later, at the request of the study’s two academic authors.

“This will be a pivotal moment for rheumatology,” wrote Putman, in a lengthy essay on Substack. It’s a story not just about Tavneos, he argued, but evidence that the normal systems of scientific oversight — including peer review and regulatory approval — “failed to detect a shocking case” of alleged data manipulation.

According to Amgen, ChemoCentryx’s actions were less than ideal, but they don’t amount to data manipulation—and they certainly don’t warrant withdrawal of Tavneos.

In the 104-page document submitted to the FDA this summer, Amgen said that ChemoCentryx’s re-adjudication doesn’t “align with the approach Amgen would have taken.” Amgen called it “unfortunate” that ChemoCentryx didn’t disclose its actions to the FDA, noting that it, too, had been in the dark about this.

Still, Amgen pointed out, none of the underlying data were actually changed, and the reassessment of the data, Amgen maintains, was “conducted to correct a small number of errors.” ChemoCentryx was not legally required to disclose the fact that it revisited the data to the FDA, Amgen maintains.

In an emailed response to questions from Undark that Alison Chartan, director of Amgen’s global media relations team, requested be attributed to a company spokesperson, Amgen reiterated many of the points made in the document submitted to the FDA. “As stated in our response to CDER,” the email noted, “the 2019 data readjudication conducted by ChemoCentryx followed a prespecified procedure to correctly and consistently apply prespecified trial rules to adjudicated outcomes. No clinical data were altered.” The email also emphasized the real-world impact a withdrawal would have on those currently taking Tavneos. “Preserving treatment options for these patients,” Amgen wrote, “is central to our mission.” (The company plans to present new data on Tavneos at a conference in November.)

The FDA does have the authority to withdraw its approval of a drug, said Patricia Zettler, a law professor at The Ohio State University who formerly served as an attorney for the Department of Health and Human Services. The law requires a stepwise approach. As an opening gambit, the agency must give notice and offer the drug’s manufacturer an opportunity for a public hearing. If the manufacturer can demonstrate a genuine disagreement about the facts, then the hearing may be held. After that, the FDA can withdraw approval of the drug. If Amgen disagrees with the decision, it could sue the agency.

All of this leaves patients and physicians in a potentially protracted state of uncertainty about whether Tavneos actually works.

Amgen says it does. To make its case, the company has pointed to an independent re-adjudication of its pivotal trial, conducted by researchers at the Duke Clinical Research Institute, part of the Duke University School of Medicine. Although the drug still didn’t meet the FDA’s bar of higher one-year remission rates, the study participants who received the drug fared no worse on this measure. The company also pointed to real-world data, meaning data collected via routine medical care, suggesting that Tavneos can indeed reduce steroid use.

Chloe Cusano is among those who would like to see Tavneos retain its approval. She received it while in the hospital and credits it with helping her taper off steroids more rapidly. Roberts, the UCSF epidemiologist, said his team’s registry study found low rates of drug-induced liver injuries among patients in the U.S., a finding he characterized as “incredibly reassuring,” particularly when care is coupled with careful monitoring. It’s important to keep in mind, he said, that the current alternative to Tavneos is “much higher levels” of steroids.

Under the law, Tavneos “really shouldn’t remain on the market,” said Joshua Skydel, a clinical fellow in rheumatology at Yale New Haven Hospital and a researcher at the Yale Collaboration for Regulatory Rigor, Integrity, and Transparency. The FDA has standards for drug approval, including substantial evidence of safety and effectiveness. In this case, the pivotal trial has been called into question, and several of the studies that Amgen has pointed to have yet to be published: “I’d at least like to see them go through peer review,” Skydel said, “before hanging my hat on them.”

Høeg, meanwhile, is skeptical that clinical evidence gathered since Tavneos was approved will do much to support its case. “I suspect real world data, much of which were already available when we requested withdrawal in April, will not meet the FDA’s evidentiary bar for approval,” she wrote. “We do know the data were insufficient for ongoing marketing authorization [in] the EU and UK.”

Skydel additionally noted that at the time of Tavneos’ approval, the FDA requested that additional post-marketing studies be conducted. But Amgen has fallen behind on deadlines for those studies. “This episode really, for me, highlighted the way that drugs are allowed to reach the market with open questions,” Skydel said. “Our capacity to answer those questions is really only as strong as FDA and industry’s collaboration,” he continued, as well as FDA’s willingness to use its authority after a drug has gone on the market.

In its April letter, the FDA argued that the stakes of this debate go beyond patients with one rare disease, stating that withdrawing the drug “is critical to protect the public health and the integrity of the drug approval process.” Absent such a consequence, the agency stated, other companies will have an incentive to act deceptively.

Walter Kraft, who voted to recommend approving the drug based on what he knew at the time, also worries about the potential for knock-on effects. The clinical trial system “is built on a level of trust,” he said. “And when that trust is put into question for a narrow parochial gain, it puts the whole system at risk for other subsequent actors in the space.”

#269. China Renaissance suspends trading, delays results after founder's disappearance

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, said it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the company. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

China Renaissance said in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

In a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance said auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, company says

Trading in the company’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

Bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined company’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog launched an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement said. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.

#267. Android Auto could upset your work-life balance with its next update

A hidden Work Mode tile hints at support for employer-managed apps, but no word on when it might arrive.

Your commute could soon come with a little more office baggage. An Android Authority teardown of Android Auto version 18.0.664204 revealed a Work Mode tile, suggesting Google may be testing new Work Profile controls. The site's team managed to bring up the tile, which lit up a briefcase icon over the app drawer, but tapping the tile didn't do anything.

Supporting Work Profiles could make it easier to join work calls between appointments. Then again, it could also give the office another way to follow you into the car, which isn't exactly everyone's idea of a peaceful drive.

Using an Android Work Profile isn't the same as signing in to a second Gmail account. A Work Profile keeps employer-managed apps in a separate space and marks them with briefcase badges, while personal apps and data remain outside the company's management on employee-owned phones. To check if you have a Work Profile set up, look for separate Personal and Work tabs or apps with small briefcase icons in your app drawer. If neither appears, you probably don't have one, but you can navigate to Settings > Passwords and accounts to double-check.

Work Profile restrictions are especially apparent for video conferencing apps. Microsoft says Teams supports audio calls and meetings through Android Auto, but the integration doesn't work if the app is installed inside a managed Work Profile. Google Meet has a slightly different restriction. An active Work Profile call can appear on the dashboard, but upcoming meetings and call history from that profile won't show up. That's inconvenient for someone driving between appointments who wants to join their next meeting from the car's display.

A missing app isn't always a Work Profile problem, though. You might have hidden it from the Android Auto launcher. And if Android Auto is not working at all, a connection problem could be at fault. Neither issue has anything to do with Work Profiles.

On the drive home, a dashboard Work Mode switch could eventually silence work alerts while leaving personal calls and navigation untouched. For now, if your employer has set up a Work Profile on your phone, you can pause work apps using the Work tab in the app drawer or, on supported devices, a work tile in Quick Settings. Pausing stops work apps and their notifications without affecting personal apps.

Some Android phones with a Work Profile let you schedule work hours through Digital Wellbeing, but Samsung's version has lacked this option. Here's the interesting part: Google says that scheduling can't keep work apps paused for consecutive days, such as an entire weekend. The manual switch still has its uses.

Google hasn't said whether Android Auto's experimental tile will offer those controls. It hasn't been shown to pause notifications or launch work apps. Meanwhile, current Android Auto customization options won't get around the Work Profile restrictions.

Even if the feature arrives, drivers won't necessarily get access to every company app. Android Auto restricts app capabilities while driving, and employers control which apps are available inside Work Profiles. On company-owned Android devices, IT admins can also limit how long a Work Profile stays paused. Exceeding that limit may suspend access to personal apps and data.

#265. How to add and rearrange apps on your Samsung smart TV

It's a snap to reorganize your Samsung TV home screen.

Smart TVs make it easy to access streaming services as well as self-hosted media servers, such as Plex, without needing to buy an extra device like a streaming stick (though there are other reasons to buy a streaming device when you have a smart TV). But even if you have a smart TV, you might not be taking full advantage of it. Fortunately, it's easy to add new apps to a Samsung smart TV if the ones you want aren't already included when you first set it up.

If you only need the most popular streaming services, you might not need to do anything to get them running. Samsung smart TVs usually come pre-loaded with the Netflix, YouTube, Disney+, Prime Video and Apple TV apps, though that list can change depending on which apps are available in your particular region. For anything else (like these free channels for your smart TV), you'll have to download a new app from a built-in search feature on your TV. And after downloading those apps, you'll probably want to do some rearranging on your home screen.

To add new apps, first pull up the TV's home screen. Use your remote to select the search bar at the top of the screen and type in the name of the app you want to download. If you search for something that doesn't show up, it may not be available in your region or might not be supported by Samsung smart TVs at all — Samsung has even publicly banned some smart TV apps. Otherwise, you can just select the app's icon with your remote to install it. If you don't have a specific app in mind but want to see what options are available, you can also find a selection of what's available, sorted by category, in your TV's apps menu.

Once an app is finished installing, a button to add it to the home screen should appear. If you've already navigated away and want to pin an app later, you can still find everything you have in the apps menu on the home screen. Just press and hold on the one you want to pin to the home screen, and the option to add to home will appear.

You can also rearrange apps once they're on the home screen to sort them in whatever order works best for you. On the home screen, use the remote to select whichever app you want to move, and press and hold the select button to open a menu. For older TV models, you might need to use a different command to open the menu, such as pressing the down key. Then select the move setting, and you can slide individual apps left and right. If you want to remove an app from the home screen or delete it entirely, you can do so from this same menu.

#264. Russia's giant new radar in Kaliningrad raises alarm in NATO

Russia is nearing completion of what experts think is a giant radar complex in Kaliningrad, capable of monitoring much of Europe. Experts warn the project could intensify the military standoff between Moscow and NATO.

The Kremlin is getting closer to opening its 'new eye' on Europe. Construction of a towering radar complex is almost complete in Russia's highly militarized exclave of Kaliningrad, according to reports.

From above, the three radiating arms of the sprawling facility, each more than 500 meters (1,640 feet) long, look like some sort of alien lifeform has left its mark on an otherwise undisturbed stretch of forested nature reserve. You could actually compare it to a landing platform or launch pad for Moscow's massive intelligence-gathering network.

While Russia has not confirmed it is building the structure, security expert Vaidotas Malinionis said the radar will be so big, it will be able to see beyond the earth's curvature. The retired commander from Lithuania told DW the over-the-horizon (OTH) radar network near Gvardeysk will have a surveillance range of about 3,000 kilometers (1,864 miles), allowing Russia to peer into almost every corner of Europe, as well as right across Ukraine.

The system would reportedly allow Russia to intercept satellite communications and detect aircraft movements and ballistic missiles.

"The goal and the purpose of this radar is observation of long-distance targets and early warning capabilities. We still don't know if it is operationally capable of doing that, but it is definitely being constructed right now," Malinionis added.

The British newspaper The Times reports that the systems are primarily intended for the detection and jamming of electronic signals, citing the Finnish-Polish space and defense technology company ICEYE.

"They would be able to use it in offensive operations, to get more information about specific targets," explained Malinionis.

"And if they were able to get an early warning about the movement of NATO troops, in the case of an invasion on NATO's eastern frontier, then they would gain more time for decision-making."

Speaking to DW from the shores of the Baltic Sea, Latvian geopolitical analyst Evija Djatkovica warned there is a significant downside for NATO to this old Soviet technology being revived when it comes to the increased use of new tech in the warfare of today.

"It will help Russia close existing loopholes in detecting low-flying objects, making the rapidly developing integration of drones into regional defense doctrines less effective," she claimed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Times report goes on to say that ICEYE defense company sees Russia's expansion of its OTH radar system as proof that Kaliningrad is being developed into a hub for advanced military sensors and electronic warfare systems.

"The new radar signals an intensifying contest between Russia and NATO for military supremacy and control of the Kaliningrad region," Djatkovica underlined.

"This is a potentially dangerous situation, since further militarization on both sides could be expected and, at some point, a preemptive strike becomes an option to deny the other side an unacceptable advantage over the region,” she warned.

Russia has already alerted NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to blockade Kaliningrad. The potential flashpoint and Russian outpost is situated on the Baltic Sea, wedged between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania– on the very doorstep of the alliance's eastern flank.

The exclave is only 200 kilometers from west to east and 100 kilometers from north to south. However, from what Malinionis asserted, Russia's smallest federal region or oblast packs a punch.

"According to some sources, they have the capability to deploy up to 100 nuclear warheads in Kaliningrad. And some sources say they have already started deploying some there – although that is yet to be confirmed," the former commander pointed out.

ICEYE claims to have discovered another large circular antenna complex some 50 kilometers west of Gvardeysk, near the city of Chernyakhovsk, according to the German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ). More than 20 signal and electronic warfare facilities are reportedly peppered throughout the Kaliningrad region.

Satellite images also reveal new shelters for fighter jets at the Kaliningrad-Chkalovsk military airfield, according to the FAZ report. Other images show launch pads at the mobile S-400 surface-to-air missile site in Baltiysk, meaning the systems could well be operational.

"These factors clearly depict the strategic importance of territories around Kaliningrad for both Russia and NATO," said Djatkovica. "For Russia, among other things, Kaliningrad's geographic position and nuclear arsenal stationed there allow it to project threats against most European capitals."

This is where the gargantuan radar comes into play, according to her. "Because of the radar's long reach, other European regions from North to West will also become more exposed to Russia's surveillance and military actions."

She sighed, saying the good news is that every escalatory step that Russia takes, with repercussions for European countries even further away from its borders, the more the whole continent takes Moscow seriously as a direct threat.

"Russia's malign signals should motivate the West to keep up with rearmament, which, in turn, will make NATO and Europe's collective deterrence more credible."

Djatkovica used the example of Poland, which has been transforming its offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea into NATO surveillance infrastructure.

In another step towards integrating newer technologies, German arms producer Rheinmetall is building Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites in conjunction with the firm ICEYE. They beam down precise pictures of troop movements and enemy positions, even at night or in bad weather.

The images will be used on NATO's eastern flank and by the Bundeswehr brigade stationed in Lithuania. The first SAR satellites are set to be launched into orbit on a SpaceX rocket in early 2027.

Malinionis agreed that adaptation is the most important lesson to be learnt for European leaders in times of Russian aggression. But he had another point to make. "There is also one disadvantage for this new Russian radar. Because it's so huge, it's a pretty easy target!"

#263. 6 Google Maps features that work better on Android Auto vs. CarPlay

I tested Google Maps on both systems in the same car, and Android Auto made several everyday navigation tasks noticeably easier.

Google Maps is available on both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay, but it's not the same experience — even when using the same app in the same car. I performed identical searches, route changes and simple navigation tasks back to back on both systems using the same infotainment screen.

Generally speaking, the fundamentals are close. Both provided me with a speedometer, lane guidance, incident reporting and alternative-route suggestions, as well as the standard controls for avoiding tolls, highways and ferries. The differences were much more apparent after I began using Maps for more than just getting from A to B.

The benefits of Android Auto range from minor interface details to features that still work better there than on Apple's offering. CarPlay does recover a few points, but Google Maps generally feels more at home on Google's own platform. Shocking, I know.

The clearest difference is how Gemini is accessed, and it still gives Android Auto an edge in two areas.

First, Gemini is easier to invoke on Android Auto. I could start talking to it without touching the screen. Late in my testing, a Gemini button also appeared in Google Maps on CarPlay, and it handled conversational searches and follow-ups once I tapped it. However, I couldn't summon it hands-free there. At the time of testing, Google's own help page still said Gemini wasn't available for CarPlay.

Second, route changes felt quicker on Android Auto. I asked it to locate a fuel stop on my route, then requested a pharmacy without reopening the conversation, and when I asked if there were other ways to get home, the options were immediately displayed. Gemini can search along a route, refine the results, add stops and show alternative routes. CarPlay could handle the same kinds of requests once Gemini was open, but it was noticeably slower in my test.

But it wasn't magic all the time. Gemini sometimes hung on a loading screen and failed to connect once during my test. However, being able to start those interactions without reaching for the display remains a significant benefit when the display is in the center of your dashboard, as it is in my 2025 Kia Sonet.

The third advantage became obvious when I was looking for places along a route. In my test, Maps showed me a number of options along with ratings and the additional time each option would take. Picking between a stop that's one minute away and another that adds six shouldn't require detective work.

CarPlay displays a series of results, one at a time, and has Previous and Next controls to scroll through the results. It can still provide valuable information like gas prices and detour times, but it takes more effort to compare several options.

The fourth difference was the interaction with the map. Android Auto kept zoom controls in easy reach, and pinch-to-zoom worked directly in my test. CarPlay made me enter its standalone map-control mode, and pinch-to-zoom didn't work for me.

That isn't to say that CarPlay cannot technically support gestures. Android Auto's navigation framework supports tap, scroll and pinch interactions, while CarPlay features its own map template and controls. In actual use (in my car anyway), Android Auto was less demanding when I needed to see farther down the road or check out another section of the trip.

It's a small difference in theory. But when you're trying to look ahead at an unfamiliar interchange, it starts to matter.

Google Maps also did more before I had even entered a destination.

Android Auto instantly displayed a Home shortcut with a live ETA and distance. In addition to Categories and Saved locations, the Recent section can also show recently visited locations and suggestions based on recent Maps searches.

That makes destination suggestions and shortcuts the fifth benefit. In my testing, CarPlay's initial Maps screen was a lot more bare-bones and required a search to reach the same information.

During my trial runs, Android Auto also made Google's fuel-efficient routing more transparent. It marked one of the choices as the most fuel-efficient and indicated the estimated fuel savings. Fuel-efficient routing isn't exclusive to Android Auto, as the same preference was also available on CarPlay in my test. But for me, Google Maps did a better job of explaining the recommendation on Android Auto.

One usability win for CarPlay here: Color-scheme controls for Automatic, Day and Night are easily accessible from the car screen's interface.

The sixth benefit is something I haven't been able to try in a gas-powered vehicle, but it's much more useful for compatible EVs in the US.

Google Maps can estimate battery consumption for a trip on supported Android Auto vehicles based on the vehicle's characteristics, traffic, road elevation data and weather conditions. Enter the current battery level, and it can then suggest charging stops, estimate the battery level at arrival and incorporate charging time into the ETA.

That's one step further than locating local charging stations. The charging stops are integrated into the route calculation, and that's just what you want Maps to do before the battery percentage gets too low.

A key drawback of Google Maps on iPhone is that its energy-efficient EV routes don't include charging stops. Android Auto's new battery-aware system can incorporate those stops into the trip and adjust the route accordingly. Google's announcement didn't mention a comparable CarPlay rollout. The rollout covers more than 350 EV models from over 15 brands in the US.

#262. How long is a new Apple TV actually supposed to last?

Older Apple TVs have received up to a decade of updates, but Apple doesn't promise that.

At $299, the new Apple TV 4K is a lot to pay for a little black box that sits under your TV waiting for you to pick a show to watch. The fourth-generation model will be available November 13 with an A19 chip, an improved Siri Remote and hands-free Siri controls. For that price, how many years can you expect it to last before the next upgrade beckons?

Apple doesn't guarantee how many updates will be available for tvOS or how long its streaming boxes will be supported. But its history is a pretty good indication. Older Apple TVs have received major software updates for eight to 10 years, with security patches continuing beyond that. The hardware may continue to function long after it exits official support, with software and app compatibility concerns the most likely reasons for replacing one.

While the Apple TV HD was introduced in 2015, and the first Apple TV 4K in 2017, both were updated to tvOS 26 in 2025. Plus, security patches were provided in tvOS 26.6 in July 2026. That's about 10 years of major software updates for the HD and eight for the original 4K, plus some security support.

The impressive streak came to an end in September 2026 with tvOS 27. Apple's new tvOS compatibility list begins with the second-generation Apple TV 4K from 2021, which means the 2015 and 2017 models can't get the latest operating system. Apple has not yet confirmed whether those older boxes will get additional security patches. It's not a guarantee that the new Apple TV 4K will get 10 years of support. Apple hasn't provided an estimate of how many years of tvOS updates to expect, so the best indication is its track record.

In contrast, Amazon promises at least four years of security updates for Fire TV devices bought new directly from the company, or through the model's published support date (if later). That's not the same as a major OS upgrade, but at least Fire TV customers have a minimum support deadline in writing.

Not being able to update to the latest version of tvOS doesn't make your Apple TV an expensive brick. Netflix still supports the Apple TV HD and first-generation Apple TV 4K, even though neither is eligible for tvOS 27. That could change as developers raise their minimum software requirements, potentially leaving older devices unable to install or update certain apps.

A better way to think about your Apple TV is to consider its performance, not its age. When menus start to become painfully slow, apps begin to crash or a service that you care about stops working, an upgrade makes more sense. Security is also a factor, especially if your Apple TV is used as a smart home hub and no longer gets patched.

Upgrading is a tougher pill to swallow with the newest release costing $299. Apple's Siri AI beta will also be available on the second-generation Apple TV 4K and newer (if the Home admin has an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad), so you don't have to buy the latest box just for Siri AI. The 2026 Apple TV 4K does have some significant improvements over the 2022 version, such as a faster A19 processor and built-in microphones for hands-free control. But it's a significant amount to pay if you're already happy with your current Apple TV.

Then there's the Siri Remote, which frequently finds itself in the sofa. If yours is lost or breaks down, you can use your iPhone as a TV remote instead of replacing the whole setup. Apple's latest Siri Remote is compatible with all Apple TV 4K models and even the 2015 Apple TV HD, and a replacement costs $59.

#261. Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged

A long flight home from feeding grounds messes with birds’ internal clocks.

Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling where the body insists it’s the middle of the night while the clock says it’s lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans.

A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass.

Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales.

From there, they head out to feed anywhere from a few dozen to more than 1,000 kilometers into the Atlantic. To get back, shearwaters are thought to work out where they are located using a map sense, possibly based on smells, and then use the Sun as a compass to set their direction.

The trouble with navigating by the Sun, though, is that it moves across the sky. “You can imagine an animal or a human that wants to travel south all day. At sunrise, when the Sun’s in the east, it needs to be traveling 90 degrees clockwise of the Sun, but by midday it needs to be traveling straight towards the Sun, and by sunset it needs to be traveling 90 degrees anticlockwise of the Sun,” Lewin said. Effective navigation by the Sun requires a clock that tells you what time of day it is. Birds, like nearly all animals, have such a clock built in. But the clock in Manx shearwaters is not perfect.

The birds recalibrate their internal clock at every dusk and dawn. This means that for every degree of longitude a bird covers between sunrise and sunset, its clock falls four minutes out of sync with local time. In consequence, a Manx shearwater misjudges where the Sun should be and veers off course clockwise when it flies east, or anticlockwise when it flies west.

Scientists had already shown something similar in other birds by catching penguins and quickly moving them across lines of longitude, but before Lewin’s study no one had clearly demonstrated it in wild animals moving on their own, mostly because the effect is small and so requires a lot of data to become apparent. But Lewin’s team happened to have just the right database.

Tim Guilford, Lewin’s supervisor at Oxford, and Chris Perrins, a long-time Oxford shearwater researcher, started fitting shearwaters with GPS tags in 2004, when the devices first became small enough for a bird this size. Two decades later, the team had tracks from 3,688 foraging trips made by 1,045 birds from colonies along the UK’s western coasts. Those trips last from one day to up to two weeks.

From this dataset, Lewin and his colleagues separated homeward flights, which the scientists say was rather simple. Foraging shearwaters make short, wiggly flights between dives. “When they are deciding to go back to their colony, they kind of switch into this mode where they are flying as fast as they can in pretty much a straight line continuously without stopping for really long periods,” Lewin said.

For each homing flight, the researchers worked out where the bird last saw the sunrise, at which point its clock should have matched local time. Then, at every GPS fix, they calculated how far east or west it had traveled since, and how much that would bend its Sun compass. Since they knew each bird was headed exactly to its burrow, they could compare those predictions with how the birds actually deviated from their course.

The time shifts were tiny. “About an hour is pretty much the maximum that we observed. Most of these are probably 15-minute, 10-minute time differences,” Lewin says. “For us, that would be pretty imperceptible, but it does still have an effect on their compass orientation that we can detect.”

Across 335 homing flights made out of sight of land, the birds veered just as the Sun compass predictions said they would. Because the study was not a controlled experiment, though, Lewin argues we need to be careful about causality. Still, the team calculated the biases that crosswinds, the Coriolis effect, or a magnetic compass might introduce, and none of those fit the data well. “Our observed biases match by far the best to the Sun compass biases that we would expect,” Lewin said.

The navigational errors apparently caused by jet lag reached up to around 15 degrees, which for birds was way less costly than one might expect. A bird with a map sense can check its position, notice it’s drifting, and correct. The team calculated that for a shearwater flying 1,000 kilometers east in a day, about the maximum the scientists observed, the average error would be roughly 7 degrees. If the bird keeps checking where it is, that adds only 5 kilometers to the trip.

The researchers also found that when shearwaters followed coastlines, they still drifted slightly closer to or farther from the shore depending on their expected compass error. Work done in Oxford two decades ago showed that homing pigeons with shifted clocks do the same, even while following a familiar road. This led researchers to hypothesize that birds may run two parallel navigation systems, one based on the compass and one on familiar landmarks, with the balance between them never tipping entirely to one side.

An alternative explanation, Lewin suggests, might be that they don’t know exactly where on the coast they are and use the Sun to pick which way to follow it. “We don’t quite know. And I think it’s an interesting question, especially as people try and design bio-inspired autonomous navigation systems,” Lewin says.

Lewin’s study could not answer whether Manx shearwaters suffer from other jet lag symptoms, like poor sleep or hunger at odd hours. “We’ve not been able to investigate that yet,” Lewin said. The next step for his team would be finding out whether the time shifts affect when birds forage, how much food they bring home, and their breeding success. Another question is whether more animals routinely experience jet lag. Lewin thinks it’s quite likely.

The same jet lag effect, Lewin said, could hit any organism with an internal clock that moves far enough east or west in a single day. That mostly means fliers, or animals living near the poles, where lines of longitude are packed closer together. The long-term goal is to find out whether animals that constantly suffer from jet lag evolved some ways to cope with it.

“In humans, if you do it a lot, in the long term it has really negative health impacts,” Lewin said. “So maybe we could take some inspiration from these animals that are constantly experiencing jet lag and see if there are ways that we can mitigate jet lag affecting humans.”

Science, 2026.  DOI: 10.1126/science.adz2542

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#258. Apple is reportedly launching three new iPads early next year

After launching its new iPad mini last week (along with the iPad-like iPhone Duo last month), Apple may launch up to three new iPad models early next year, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. Those will likely cover the rest of Apple's iPad lineup, including the base iPad, top-of-the-line iPad Pro and mid-range iPad Air, the report states. Each model will get key upgrades.

To start, the base iPad will reportedly gain access to Apple Intelligence, with an upgrade to the A19 processor and 8GB of RAM. It will also include Apple's new N1 chip and C1X modem, enabling Wi-Fi 7, sub-6 GHz 5G, faster speeds and reduced battery draw. The iPad Air, meanwhile, will get an OLED screen to match the iPad mini, along with the usual chip upgrades.

The iPad Pro will also get a processor upgrade from the M5, possibly to the new M6 or even a future M7 chip. To handle the extra heat it generates, particularly during AI tasks, the new model will likely have a new vapor chamber to better cool its interior (an upgrade first mentioned last year).

It will be interesting to see how Apple positions the new iPads, given the possibility of the iPhone Duo and new touchscreen MacBook Pro models invading their turf. Some buyers may find the HomeView smart display more convenient than an iPad in places like the kitchen. Still, Apple sells somewhere in the neighborhood of 60 million iPads per year, so the devices remain a vital part of its product mix.

#256. Dell XPS Googlebook review: Beautiful hardware for a useless platform

I can think of a few reasons to buy a Googlebook, but they're all pretty dystopian. Maybe every other computing platform has succumbed to a super AI-powered virus, leaving a Googlebook as your only option. Or perhaps Google has taken over the world and has started hunting down people who use Windows, Linux or macOS. In a world where a Googlebook is your only option, then the $1,000 Dell XPS Googlebook is probably the one to get. But in the real world, where you can get the exact same XPS hardware running on more flexible platforms with better developer support, the XPS Googlebook seems practically pointless.

But let's back up a bit and talk about Googlebook OS, Google's new laptop platform that's a combination of both Android and ChromeOS. It supports Android apps natively, it can synchronize and mirror apps from your Android phone, and it has Google's Gemini AI integrated throughout its interface. Technically, Googlebook OS should be an upgrade from ChromeOS, a platform built entirely around Google's web browser. But, after testing this laptop for the last week, I'd go so far as to say the entire Googlebook concept is a failure.

Who really wants a laptop running unoptimized Android apps? Why buy into an untested Google platform just to synchronize your Android phone, especially when you can mirror and sync Android device texts on Windows and Linux? And why would you pay the same exact price as a Windows PC for a computer that does so much less? While Apple, Microsoft and PC makers are sweating to push the computing industry forward this year, most notably with the launch of NVIDIA's RTX Spark and Apple's redesigned touchscreen MacBook Pro, Google has given us a new platform that is in many ways less useful than its aging Chromebooks.

For its first (and I'm hoping only) Googlebook, Dell took its recent XPS 13 design and refashioned it for Google's new OS. It still has a slim 2.2-pound metal case, making it one of the lightest systems in this size range, and it sports a 13.4-inch InfinityEdge screen. It's powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite chip with 16GB of RAM — the same hardware on the $1,000 Windows 11 XPS 13. There are only two USB-C ports on either side of the XPS 13 Googlebook, and, unfortunately, there's no headphone jack.

A multi-colored "Glowbar" occasionally lights up on the rear of the XPS 13 — something that Google highlights as one of the defining features of Googlebook OS — but it's ultimately superfluous. It can show your charging status and battery level, but it's not exactly solving any major problems for laptop users.

It's not unusual to see PC makers reusing their designs — many companies are also recycling their existing work for NVIDIA's RTX Spark chip. But at least that platform has a few halo products designed specifically for it, like the Surface Laptop Ultra. There's nothing highlighting what's truly special about Googlebook OS — arguably because there's not exactly much to show off.

I could tell you that the XPS Googlebook has a very nice screen, a comfortable keyboard and a very accurate touchpad. I could tell you that its slim design and light weight makes it easy to tote around without weighing down your bag. But really, you could have learned all of that from my review of the standard XPS 13 with Windows 11. Everything good about this system comes from Dell's excellent design work.

Once I started using Googlebook OS, though, it became instantly clear that Googlebook OS is simply a hot mess. It's fine for web browsing with Chrome and accessing Google apps like Gmail and Calendar, but support for Android apps via the Google Play store is mostly disappointing. Slack only works as a mobile Android app, allowing you to see a single channel or direct message, but there's no wider desktop view like you'd see on Windows or macOS. You also can't easily react to messages and images in Slack — instead, you have to perform a long click, as you would on a normal Android phone. Evernote, meanwhile, doesn't appear at all on the Googlebook Play Store. (And yes, I still use Evernote a ton. There are dozens of us!)

"Desktop optimized" Android apps function more like you'd expect on other laptop platforms. Notability, CapCut Pad and Luminar all offer more fully-featured apps for taking AI notes and editing media, but they're only useful if those apps are already part of your workflow. I can't imagine too many people will change their editing process just to find something compatible with Googlebook OS.

With no support for Audacity, I had to use Lexis Audio Editor to make some tweaks to a podcast file, but its basic interface seemed unsuited to more complicated edits. I might as well have just used an online editor like Audiomass (which, by the way, works just fine on Chromebooks). I also had to rely on Evernote's website to write this review, which required logging in every single time I turned on the XPS Googlebook, because the Evernote Android app was unavailable. I also eventually gave up on the Slack Android app and started using its web interface, which at least let me see all of my channels and direct messages.

I'm used to computers being gateways to sophisticated software and healthy developer support. Using the XPS Googlebook felt like being trapped in a computing stripmall: It's hobbled together by a variety of small apps of varying quality. Thank goodness for web apps, at least.

It's worth noting that Chromebooks also supported Android apps, so I don't believe there was actually a huge demand for a new Android-based computing platform.

I also wasn't impressed by any of the other Googlebook features: Syncing your Android phone to a Googlebook sounds nice in theory, but in reality it leads to redundant notifications if you have the same apps installed on both systems. You can also mirror an Android app from your phone — but again, why would you do that when you can run the app directly on the Googlebook? Given that you can already mirror Android phones and synchronize texts on Windows computers, I'm not sure why anyone would jump into a whole new platform just for these features.

Google being Google, of course, the company also crammed in as many Gemini AI features as it could into this platform. You can ask questions or edit media on the Gemini app, or wiggle the mouse pointer to ask the AI about things you encounter on the web or inside of apps. Gemini did a decent job of answering questions about products that we've featured on Engadget, but unless you absolutely want to lean on Google's AI, there really is no reason to buy a whole laptop just to have Gemini baked into everything.

Google's Rambler AI dictation feature, which lets you dictate text by speaking naturally, is also built into Googlebook OS, and from my testing it seemed to work pretty well. But it doesn't show you the text as you're speaking — it just shows a moving purple waveform, and that sometimes makes it hard to gather your thoughts or see what you were previously thinking. This is a big downside compared to just typing or using old-school dictation that used to be available on Android, but at least Rambler did a good job of cutting out natural "ums" and "uhhs," and it also formatted the text pretty well.

Battery life is another sign that the Googlebook OS platform is very unrefined. In the PCMark Android app benchmark, it lasted for 15 hours and 15 minutes, which is what we'd expect for a Snapdragon laptop. But during normal usage, I found that some apps ate up a lot of battery power without much reason. CapCut Pad managed to drain my battery by 50% in just one hour, even though it was simply sitting in the background, not doing anything. I simply couldn't trust the XPS Googlebook to last for a full day of work.

While the XPS Googlebook looks like a premium laptop, the fact that it's running an undercooked OS makes it something I can't recommend. Just get the $999 XPS 13 with Windows 11 instead — at least that gets you a mature OS that runs tons of apps and games. None of this is Dell's fault, as its XPS hardware is once again among the best in the PC world. But that doesn't matter if it's paired with yet another flimsy Google platform.

Sure, Googlebook OS will get more compatible Android apps down the line, and it may eventually turn into something more useful with upcoming AI features. But you shouldn't rush out to pay $999 with the hopes that it will get better. Why pay to be a beta tester? Google also hasn't been the best steward of its troubled platforms in the past, so I wouldn't be too surprised if Googlebook OS simply fades away due to lack of interest. This is the same company that couldn't optimize Android for tablets over the last decade.

The Googlebook launch may go down as one of the more baffling moments in computing history. Instead of delivering a true successor to Chromebooks – something that was similarly inexpensive, efficient and school-ready, but also ready for useful AI features – Google delivered a half-baked platform that's in many ways a step back. Not even Dell's excellent design can save the XPS Googlebook from the mess of Googlebook OS.
